title: Fasti
text:
1. The seasons set in order through the Latian year, with their causes,
and the constellations sunk beneath the earth and risen, I shall sing.
Receive this work, Caesar Germanicus, with a face at peace,
and steer the course of my timid vessel;
and, not turning away from a slight honour as a service,
come, propitious, with the favour I dedicate to you.
You will recognize rites unearthed from ancient annals,
and by what merit each day was marked.
There too you will find festivals belonging to your own house:
often you must read of your father, often of your grandfather;
and the prizes that they bear, marking the painted calendar,
you too shall carry with your brother Drusus.
Let others sing Caesar's arms: I sing Caesar's altars,
and whatever days he added to the sacred ones.
Approve my effort to advance through the praises of your kin,
and shake the trembling fears out of my heart.
Grant me your favour, and you will grant strength to my songs:
my talent stands or falls by your countenance.
This page, soon to undergo the judgement of a learned prince,
trembles, like verse sent to be read by the Clarian god.
For we have felt the eloquence of your cultivated speech
when it took up civic arms to defend trembling accused men;
and we know, when its current turns toward our own arts,
how great the rivers of your genius run.
If it is allowed and lawful, poet, guide a poet's reins,
that under your auspice the whole year may pass in happiness.
When the city's founder was setting the seasons in order, he fixed
that there should be twice five months in his year.
You knew arms, of course, better than the stars, Romulus,
and your greater care was to conquer your neighbours.
Yet there is also a reason, Caesar, that may have moved him,
and he has grounds by which to defend his error:
what is enough until the infant comes forth from its mother's womb,
this much of time he judged enough for a year;
for that many months, after a husband's funeral, the widow
keeps the signs of mourning in her widowed home.
This, then, was the foresight of robed Quirinus,
when he gave the year's laws to a primitive people.
Mars's was the first month, and Venus's the second:
she the founder of the race, he its very father;
the third took its name from the old, the fourth from the young,
and the crowd that follows was marked by number.
But Numa passed over neither Janus nor the ancestral shades,
and set two months before the ancient ones.
Yet, that you may not be ignorant of the rights of various days,
not every dawn brings the same office.
That day will be unlawful on which the three words are silenced;
that will be lawful on which the law allows business to be done.
And do not think their rights stand fast the whole day through:
a day that is now lawful was unlawful at dawn;
for as soon as the entrails are given to the god, all speech is free,
and the honoured praetor has unfettered words.
There is also a day on which it is right to shut the people in the enclosures;
there is one too that always returns after the ninth round.
Juno's care lays claim to the Ausonian Kalends;
on the Ides a white lamb, larger grown, falls to Jove;
the Nones lack a god's protection. After all of these
(beware that you be not deceived!) the next day is black.
The omen comes from the event, for on those days
Rome bore grievous losses, with Mars turned against her.
These words, said once for all, fixed throughout the calendar,
will stand, that I be not forced to break the thread of my account.
See, Germanicus, Janus announces a prosperous year to you,
and first in my song Janus is present.
Two-headed Janus, source of the silently gliding year,
you alone of the gods above who see your own back,
be propitious to the leaders, by whose labour the fruitful earth
and the sea hold their untroubled peace:
be propitious to your senators and to the people of Quirinus,
and with your nod unbar the shining temples.
A prosperous day dawns: favour it with tongues and hearts!
Now on a good day good words must be spoken.
Let ears be free of lawsuits, and let mad quarrels
be far off at once; postpone your work, envious tongue!
Do you see how the heavens shine with fragrant fires,
and how the Cilician saffron crackles on the kindled hearths?
The flame strikes the temples' gold with its own brightness
and scatters a trembling radiance over the topmost shrine,
and in spotless garments they go up to the Tarpeian heights,
and the people themselves take the colour of their festival,
and now the new rods go before, the new purple gleams,
and the conspicuous ivory feels its new burden.
The young bullocks, untried in toil, offer their necks for the blow,
the ones that the Faliscan grass fed in its fields.
When Jupiter looks down on the whole world from his citadel,
he has nothing but what is Roman to watch over.
Hail, joyful day, and return ever better,
worthy to be honoured by a people that rules the world.

title: Fasti
text:
Yet what god shall I call you, two-shaped Janus?
For Greece has no divinity to match you.
Tell too the reason why you alone of the heavenly ones
see both what is behind and what is before.
While I was turning this over in my mind, my tablets in hand,
the house seemed brighter than it had been before.
Then sacred Janus, wondrous in his double-faced image,
suddenly presented his two faces to my eyes.
I took fright, and felt my hair stiffen with fear,
and my breast was cold with a sudden chill.
He, holding a staff in his right hand and a key in his left,
gave forth to me these sounds from his foremost mouth:
'Learn, laborious poet of the days, lay fear aside,
what you seek, and take my words into your mind.
The ancients called me Chaos (for I am an ancient thing):
see of how long a span of time I shall sing the deeds.
This bright air, and the three bodies that remain,
fire, water and earth, were one heap.
When once this mass broke apart through the strife of its own parts
and, dissolved, went off into new homes,
flame sought the height, the nearer place took the air,
earth and sea settled in the middle ground.
Then I, who had been a ball and a shapeless mass,
returned into a form and limbs worthy of a god.
Even now, a small token of my once-confused shape,
what is in front of me and what is behind look the same.
Hear the other reason for the form you sought,
that you may know it at once, along with my office.
Whatever you see anywhere, the sky, the sea, the clouds, the lands,
all are shut and opened by my hand.
Mine alone is the guardianship of the vast universe,
and the whole right of turning its hinge is mine.
When it pleases me to send Peace out from her quiet dwelling,
she walks freely along unbroken roads;
the whole world would be steeped in deadly blood,
did not rigid bolts hold wars locked away.
I preside over the gates of heaven with the gentle Hours:
Jupiter himself goes out and returns by my office.
Hence I am called Janus; and when the priest sets before me
the cake of spelt and the meal mixed with salt,
you will smile at my names; for in the same rite I am called now Patulcius
and now, by the sacrificing mouth, Clusius.
No doubt that rude antiquity wished by alternating names
to signify my changing functions.
My power has been told. Now learn the reason of my form,
though already you see it in part for yourself.
Every doorway has two fronts, on this side and on that,
of which one looks toward the people, the other toward the household god;
and as your doorkeeper, sitting near the threshold of the front of the house,
sees the goings-out and the comings-in,
so I, the doorkeeper of the heavenly hall, look out
upon the regions of Dawn and of the West at once.
You see the faces of Hecate turned toward three directions,
that she may guard the crossroads split into three ways;
and I too, that I may not lose my time by twisting my neck,
am allowed to look both ways without moving my body.'
He had spoken, and by his look made plain that, if I wished
to ask more, he would not be difficult with me.
I took courage and, not afraid, gave thanks to the god,
and looking at the ground I spoke a few words:
'Tell me, come, why the new year begins in the cold,
when it had better been begun in spring?
Then all things flower, then is the new age of the season,
and the new bud swells on the laden vine-shoot,
and the tree is covered with leaves newly formed,
and the blade of seed comes up to the surface of the ground,
and the birds soothe the warm air with their concert,
and the herd plays and revels in the meadows;
then the suns are gentle, and the unfamiliar swallow appears
and builds her clay-work under the high beam;
then the field endures cultivation and is renewed by the plough.
This is the year's newness, and rightly should have been so called.'
I had asked at length: he, not delaying with many words,
gathered his answer thus into two verses:
'The shortest day is the first of the new sun and the last of the old:
Phoebus and the year take the same beginning.'

title: Fasti
text:
After this I wondered why the first day was not
without lawsuits. Hear the reason, Janus says.
'I entrusted the new-born season to the doing of business,
that the whole year might not be idle from its first sign;
for the same cause each man tastes his own craft by doing it,
and bears witness to no more than his usual work.'
Then I: 'Why, though I appease the other gods' powers,
Janus, do I bring you incense and wine first?'
'That through me, who guard the thresholds, you may have access
to whatever gods you wish,' he said.
'But why are glad words spoken on your Kalends,
and why do we give and receive prayers in turn?'
Then the god, leaning on the staff he held in his right hand,
said: 'Omens are wont to lie in beginnings.
You turn your timid ears to the first sound,
and the augur consults the bird he first has seen.
The temples and the ears of the gods are open, no tongue
frames idle prayers, and what is said has weight.'
Janus had ceased, and I made no long silence,
but joined my last words to his last:
'What do the date and the wrinkled fig mean,' I said,
'and the white honey given in a snow-white jar?'
'For an omen,' he said, 'that the year may follow the savour of these things,
and that the sweet year may finish the course it has begun.'
'I see why sweets are given: add the reason for the gift of coin,
that no part of your festival may slip from me.'
He laughed and said: 'Oh, how the times you live in deceive you,
if you think honey sweeter than coin once taken!
Hardly anyone did I see, while Saturn reigned,
to whose mind sweet gains were not dear.
With time the love of having grew, which now is at its height:
it hardly has further room to advance.
Wealth is now worth more than in the years of old time,
while the people was poor, while Rome was new,
while a small hut held Mars-begotten Quirinus,
and the river-sedge gave a scanty bed.
Jupiter scarcely stood at full height in his narrow shrine,
and in Jupiter's right hand was a thunderbolt of clay.
They decked with leaves the Capitol they now deck with gems,
and the senator himself pastured his own sheep;
nor was there shame in having taken quiet rest on straw
and put hay beneath one's head.
The praetor gave laws to the people with his plough just laid aside,
and a thin plate of silver was a crime.
But after the fortune of this place lifted its head high,
and Rome touched the highest gods with her crown,
both wealth and the frenzied lust of wealth grew,
and, though they possess the most, they seek for more.
They strive to gain in order to spend, to seek back what is spent,
and these very alternations are fuel to their vices.
So with those whose belly swells, suffused by dropsy's flood,
the more water they drink, the more they thirst.
Price now lies in price: wealth gives offices,
wealth gives friendships: the poor man lies low everywhere.
Yet you ask whether the omen of the coin is useful,
and why old bronze should please your hands.
Once they gave bronze: now the omen is better in gold,
and the old coin has yielded, conquered, to the new.
We too are pleased, though we approve the ancient ones, by golden
temples: such majesty befits a god.
We praise the old times, but use our own years:
yet each custom is equally worthy to be observed.'
He had ended his counsel; then again, gently as before,
I myself address the key-bearing god with these words:
'Much indeed I have learned: but why is a ship stamped
on one side of the bronze, and on the other a double-faced shape?'
'You might have known me under the double image,' he said,
'had not old time worn down the work.
The reason of the ship remains: a god who bears the sickle
came in a ship to the Tuscan river, when he had wandered the world.
On this land, I remember, Saturn was received,
when he had been driven from the heavenly realms by Jove.
Hence the people long kept the name Saturnian;
the land too was called Latium, since the god lay hidden there.
But a grateful posterity stamped a ship's stern on the bronze,
to bear witness to the coming of their divine guest.
I myself dwelt on the ground whose left side the gentlest wave
of the sandy Tiber grazes.
Here, where Rome now is, an uncut forest grew green,
and all this was pasture for a few oxen.
My citadel was the hill which the crowd, by my name,
calls — and this age calls Janiculum.
Then I reigned, when the earth could bear the gods,
and divinities mingled with the haunts of men.
Not yet had mortal crime put Justice to flight
(she was the last of the heavenly ones to leave the earth),
and in place of fear, shame itself ruled the people without force;
to give just men their rights was no labour.
I had nothing to do with war: I guarded peace and the doorposts,
and,' showing his key, 'these are the arms I bear.'

title: Fasti
text:
The god had closed his lips. Then thus I unloosed
my voice, the god's voice drawing out my own:
'Since there are so many Janus-arches, why do you stand consecrated in one,
here where you have a temple joined to two forums?'
He, stroking with his hand the beard combed down upon his breast,
at once recounted the warfare of Oebalian Tatius,
and how the light keeper, bribed with bracelets, led the Sabines
on a silent path to the height of the citadel.
'From there, as it is now, by which you go down,' he said,
'the steep slope ran down into the valleys and the forums.
And now they had reached the gate, whose opposing bolts
hostile Saturnia had drawn back,
when, fearing to join battle with so great a power,
I cunningly set in motion the craft of my own art,
and opened the mouths of the springs in which my power lies,
and shot forth sudden waters;
yet first I cast sulphur beneath the dripping veins,
that the boiling flood might shut Tatius from the road.
When, the Sabines driven off, its use had been perceived,
the place was given back, in safety, to its former shape.
An altar was set up for me, joined to a small shrine:
on it the spelt burns in the flames with its own offering-cake.'
'But why do you hide in peace, and open when arms are stirred?'
Without delay the answer to my question was given:
'That the road back may lie open for the people gone to war,
my whole gate stands open, the bolt removed.
In peace I close the doors, that none may slip away;
and, by Caesar's power, long shall I be kept shut.'
He spoke, and lifting up his eyes that look both ways
he surveyed whatever was in all the world.
There was peace, and, the cause of your triumph, Germanicus,
the Rhine had already yielded its waters as your servants.
Janus, make peace and the ministers of peace eternal,
and grant that the author of his work may not desert it.
Yet what I was allowed to learn from the calendar itself:
the fathers consecrated two temples on this day.
The island, which the river presses with its divided water,
received the son born of Phoebus and the nymph Coronis.
Jupiter has his share; one place held them both,
and the temples of the great grandsire are joined to the grandson's.
Who forbids me to tell of the stars too, as each one rises and sets?
That was part of what I promised.
Happy the souls who first took care to know these things
and to climb up to the homes above!
It is credible that they lifted their heads high above
human vices and human places alike.
Not Venus nor wine broke their lofty hearts,
nor the duty of the forum nor the toil of war;
no petty ambition, no glory smeared with paint,
no hunger for great riches troubled them.
They brought the distant stars near to our eyes
and subjected the heaven to their genius.
So is the sky reached: not that Olympus should bear Ossa,
and the Pelian peak touch the highest stars.
We too, under these guides, shall measure out the heaven
and set their proper days to the wandering signs.
So when the third night before the coming Nones has come,
and the ground is wet, sprinkled with heavenly dew,
the claws of the eight-footed Crab will be sought in vain: headlong
he will sink beneath the western waters.
When the Nones have arrived, rains sent to you from the black clouds
will give their signs as the Lyre rises.
Add four days drawn in order from the Nones,
and Janus must be appeased on the Agonal day.
The reason of the name may be the girded minister,
by whose stroke the victim falls to the gods of heaven,
who, about to dye his drawn knives in warm blood,
always asks 'Shall I act?' (agone), and does not act unless bidden.
Some think the Agonal day takes its name from the act (actus),
because the cattle do not come but are driven.
Some hold that this festival was called Agnalia by the ancients,
one letter being taken from its proper place.
Or, because the victim fears the knives it foresees in the water,
is the day itself marked from the beast's dread?
It may also be that the day took a Greek name from the games
in the custom of an earlier age.
And ancient speech called cattle agonia;
and in my judgement this last reason is the true one.
And though it is not certain, yet the king of the rites must appease
the powers with the mate of a wool-bearing ewe.
The victim is so named because it fell by the conquering (victrix) right hand;
the sacrifice (hostia) takes its name from conquered foes (hostes).

title: Fasti
text:
Of old, what could win the gods over to a man
was spelt, and a shining grain of pure salt.
Not yet had the foreign ship borne, over the seas,
the myrrh that weeps from its bark;
neither Euphrates had sent frankincense, nor India the costus,
nor were the threads of red saffron yet known.
The altar gave its smoke, content with Sabine herbs,
and the laurel scorched with no small crackling.
If there was anyone who could add violets to garlands
made from the meadow's flowers, he was rich.
This knife, which now opens the entrails of the slaughtered bull,
had no part in the rites.
Ceres first rejoiced in the blood of a greedy sow,
avenging her crops by the deserved slaughter of the guilty;
for she learned that in early spring the milky shoots
had been rooted up from the tender furrows by a bristly sow's snout.
The sow paid the penalty: warned by her example
you should have kept your teeth from the vine-shoot, goat.
Watching one as he pressed his teeth into a vine,
a man gave voice to such words, his grief not silent:
'Gnaw the vine, goat! Yet from it, when you stand at the altar,
there will be something to sprinkle on your horns.'
The truth follows the words: handed over for your harm, an enemy,
goat, your horns are sprinkled with poured-out wine, Bacchus.
His own fault harmed the sow, his fault harmed the she-goat too:
what have you, ox, what have you, gentle sheep, deserved?
Aristaeus wept, because he had seen his bees, killed root and branch,
abandon the honeycombs they had begun.
His sea-blue mother, scarcely consoling him in his grief,
added these last words to her speech:
'Cease your tears, my boy! Proteus will lighten your loss,
and will show how you may repair what has perished.
But lest he deceive you by changing his shapes,
let firm bonds hamper both his hands.'
The youth came to the seer and, his arms loosened in sleep,
bound the captured arms of the old man of the sea.
He, transforming, falsifies his face by his art:
soon, mastered by the bonds, he returns to his own limbs,
and lifting his dripping face with its sea-blue beard
said: 'By what art do you seek to repair your bees?
Bury the body of a slaughtered bullock in the ground:
what you ask of us, the buried beast will give.'
The shepherd does as bidden: swarms seethe from the rotting
ox: one creature's death gave a thousand lives.
Fate demands a sheep: wicked, she had cropped the vervain
that the pious old country-woman used to bring to the gods.
What is left in safety, when the wool-bearing flock
and the country-dwelling oxen lay down their lives on the altars?
The Persian appeases with a horse Hyperion girt with rays,
that no slow victim be given to the swift god.
Because once a hind was slain for the threefold maiden Diana,
now too a hind falls in no maiden's place.
I have seen the Sapaeans pour the entrails of dogs to Trivia,
and all who dwell near your snows, Haemus;
the stiff guardian of the countryside, the ass, is slain too;
a shameful cause indeed, but yet fitting for the god.
You were holding the festival of ivy-bearing Bacchus, Greece,
the festival the third winter brings back at its accustomed time.
The gods too came, the worshippers of the same Lyaeus,
and whoever was not a stranger to jests,
the Pans and the youth of the Satyrs prone to love,
and the goddesses who haunt the rivers and the lonely fields.
Old Silenus too had come on his swaybacked ass,
and he who frightens timid birds with his red groin.
Having found a grove fit for sweet feasting,
they lay down on couches clothed with grass.
Liber gave wine, each had brought his own garland,
a brook sparingly supplied the waters to be mixed.
Some Naiads were there with their hair flowing, with no comb's use,
others with their locks set in place by skill and hand:
one waits on them, her tunic gathered above the calves,
another, her bosom bared by her loosened robe:
this one bares her shoulder, that one trails her dress through the grass,
no bonds hamper their tender feet.
From this some kindle in the Satyrs a gentle fire,
and you, who wear your brows wreathed with pine;
they burn you too, Silenus of unquenchable lust:
it is your wantonness that will not let you be old.

title: Fasti
text:
But red Priapus, the glory and guardian of gardens,
of all those nymphs was captivated by Lotis;
he desires her, he longs for her, for her alone he sighs,
and he gives signs with a nod, and woos her with marks.
Disdain dwells in the beautiful, and pride attends on beauty:
she despises him with a mocking look.
It was night, and with the wine bringing on sleep,
the bodies lay vanquished by slumber in scattered places.
Lotis, last of all, beneath the maple branches on the grassy ground,
just as she was, weary with play, had lain to rest.
Her lover rises and, holding his breath, stealthily
bears his footsteps in silence, on tiptoe;
and when he reached the secret couch of the snow-white nymph,
he takes care that the very breath of his breathing make no sound.
And now he was poising his body on the grass close by:
yet she was full of deep sleep.
He rejoices, and, drawing the covering from her feet,
he had begun to go by a happy road toward his desire.
Behold, the ass that carried Silenus, braying with hoarse throat,
gave forth untimely sounds from its mouth.
The nymph rises in terror, and with her hands thrusts off
Priapus, and in her flight rouses the whole grove;
but the god, all too ready with his obscene part,
was a laughing-stock to all in the light of the moon.
The author of the cry paid the penalty with death, and this is
the welcome victim of the Hellespontine god.
You birds had been untouched, the comforts of the countryside,
a tribe at home in the woods and harmless,
who make your nests and warm your eggs with feathers
and pour forth sweet measures with ready throat;
but these things do not help you, because you have the crime of speech,
and the gods think you reveal their minds.
Nor is this false: for, as each is nearest to the gods,
so now by wing, now by voice, you give true signs.
Long safe, the brood of birds was at last slaughtered,
and the entrails of the informer delighted the gods.
So often the dove, snatched from her mate,
is burned, white, on the Idalian hearths;
nor did the saving of the Capitol help the goose to escape
giving its liver on the dish to you, dainty daughter of Inachus;
by night to the goddess Night a crested fowl is slain,
because with its wakeful voice it summons the warm day.
Meanwhile the Dolphin, a bright constellation, is lifted
above the waters and shows its face from its native depths.
The next day marks the middle of winter's division,
and the part that remains will be equal to the part gone by.
The next Dawn, leaving Tithonus behind, will look upon
the pontifical rite of the Arcadian goddess;
the same day received you too, sister of Turnus, in your shrine,
here where the Field is bounded by the Virgin water.
From where shall I seek the causes and the custom of these rites?
Who will direct my sails in mid-sea?
Instruct me yourself, you who have your name drawn from song,
and favour my purpose, that your honour may not go astray.
Older than the moon (if it is believed of herself),
the land takes its name from great Arcas.
Here was Evander, who, though famous on either side,
was the nobler for the blood of his sacred mother;
she, as soon as her soul had conceived the heavenly fires,
gave forth, with full mouth, the true songs of the god.
She had foretold that troubles were at hand for her son and for herself,
and much besides that time proved true.
For when the youth, with his all too truthful mother, was driven into exile,
he leaves Arcadia and his Parrhasian home.
To him, weeping, his mother said with manly courage:
'(Cease your tears, I pray) this must be borne by you.
So it was in the fates; no fault of yours drove you out,
but a god; you are driven from the city by an offended god.
You suffer no penalty deserved, but a divinity's wrath:
it is something to be free of guilt in great misfortunes.
As each man's conscience is to him, so within his breast
he conceives, for his deed, his hope or his fear.
Yet do not mourn as the first to suffer such ills:
that storm has overwhelmed mighty men.
The same was suffered by Cadmus, once driven from the Tyrian shores,
who halted, an exile, on Aonian soil;
the same by Tydeus, and the same by Pagasaean Jason,
and by others whom it would take long to recall.
To the brave man every land is his country, as the sea is to fish,
as to the bird is whatever lies open in the empty world.
Nor does the wild storm rage the whole year through:
and for you too (believe me) there will be a time of spring.'

title: Fasti
text:
Evander, his mind strengthened by his parent's words,
cleaves the waves in his ship and reaches Hesperia,
and now, at learned Carmentis's bidding, he had driven his vessel
into the river, and was moving against the Tuscan waters.
She looks upon the river-bank to which the shallows of Tarentum are joined,
and the scattered huts through the lonely places;
and just as she was, with her hair flung loose, she stood before the stern
and stayed the hand of the helmsman steering the course,
and stretching her arms far toward the right-hand bank
she beat the pinewood deck thrice with frenzied foot;
and to keep her from leaping, in her haste to set foot on land,
she was scarcely, scarcely held back by Evander's hand.
'Hail,' she said, 'you gods of the lands we sought,
and you, land destined to give new gods to heaven,
you rivers and springs, which this hospitable country uses,
and you nymphs of the groves and choirs of Naiads!
May the sight of you be a good omen to my son and to me,
and may that bank be touched by a happy foot!
Am I deceived, or shall these hills become mighty walls,
and from this land all other lands shall seek their laws?
To these mountains the whole world is one day promised:
who would believe the place holds so great a destiny?
And now the Dardanian pines will touch these shores;
here too a woman will be the cause of a new war.
Dear grandson, Pallas, why do you put on the fatal arms?
Put them on! By no humble avenger will you be slain.
Conquered, Troy, you shall yet conquer, and overthrown shall rise again:
that very ruin shall overwhelm the houses of your foes.
Burn, victorious flames, the Neptunian towers of Pergamum!
Is its ash for that the less high than the whole world?
Soon dutiful Aeneas will bring the sacred things and, another sacred thing,
his father: receive, Vesta, the gods of Ilium!
A time will come when the same man will guard both you and the world,
and the rites will be performed with a god himself their priest,
and the guardianship of the fatherland will rest with the Augusti:
it is right that this house hold the reins of empire.
Hence the god's son and grandson, though he himself refuse,
will bear the burden of his sire with a heaven-sent mind;
and as I shall one day be hallowed on undying altars,
so shall Julia Augusta be a new divinity.'
When with such words she came down to our own age,
her foreseeing tongue stopped in the midst of its sounds.
Stepping from the ships the exile stood on the Latian grass,
happy he, for whom that place was exile!
Nor was there long delay: new dwellings stood, and no other
on the Ausonian mountains was greater than the Arcadian.
Behold, the hero brings the Erythean oxen there,
the club-bearer, having measured out the long world's road;
and while his lodging is the Tegean house, the cattle stray
unguarded through the wide fields.
It was morning: the Tirynthian driver, shaken from sleep,
perceives two bulls missing from his count.
Searching, he sees no tracks of the silent theft:
fierce Cacus had dragged them, turned backward, into his cave,
Cacus, the terror and disgrace of the Aventine wood,
no light evil to neighbours and to strangers.
The man's look was dread, his strength matched his body, his body
was huge: the father of this monster was Mulciber;
and for a home a vast cavern with long recesses,
hidden, scarce to be found even by wild beasts.
Above the door hang heads and arms nailed up,
and the ground is white and foul with human bones.
The son of Jove was departing, part of his herd ill-guarded:
the stolen cattle gave a lowing with hoarse sound.
'I accept the recall,' he said, and following the voice
the avenger came through the woods to the unholy cave.
Cacus had barred the entrance with a broken crag for a bar;
ten yoke of oxen would scarcely have moved that mass.
He strains with his shoulders (the sky too had rested on them)
and by his effort shakes loose the huge weight.
And as soon as it was overturned, the crash terrified heaven itself,
and the ground sank, struck by the weight of the mass.
Cacus first joins battle, fighting hand to hand,
and fiercely wages the struggle with stones and stakes.
When this avails nothing, ill-bravely he flees to his father's arts
and vomits flames from his roaring mouth;
as often as he blows them out, you would think Typhoeus breathed,
and a swift lightning-flash hurled from Etna's fire.
Alcides forestalls him, and his three-knotted club, brought down,
sat thrice and four times in the man's face.
He falls and vomits smoke mixed with blood,
and dying beats the ground with his broad breast.
The victor offers one of those bulls to you, Jupiter,
and calls Evander and the country-folk;
and he set up for himself the altar called the Greatest,
here where the part of the city has its name from the ox.
Nor is Evander's mother silent that the time is near
when the earth will have had enough use of its own Hercules.
But the happy prophetess, as she lived most dear to the gods,
so the goddess holds this day in the month of Janus.

title: Fasti
text:
On the Ides the chaste priest in great Jupiter's shrine
offers to the flames the entrails of a half-male sheep;
and every province was given back to our people,
and your grandsire was called by the name Augustus.
Read through the wax masks set in order along the noble halls:
no man has attained titles so great.
Africa calls one its conqueror from herself, another bears witness
to the Isaurian or the Cretan powers subdued;
this man the Numidians make proud, that one Messana,
and another drew his mark from the Numantine city,
and Germany made both the death and the name of Drusus —
ah, wretched me, how brief was that valour!
If Caesar should take from the conquered so many names
as there are nations in the great world,
some are famous from a single deed, having titles either
from a torque taken, or from a helping raven.
Magnus, your name is the measure of your deeds:
but he who conquered you was greater in name.
And there is no step of surname above the Fabii:
that house was called Greatest by its own merits.
Yet all these are honoured with human distinctions:
this one alone has a name shared with highest Jove.
The fathers call sacred things 'august,' and 'august' are called
the temples duly dedicated by the priests' hands;
of this word too the augury hangs from its origin,
and whatever Jupiter increases (auget) by his power.
May he increase our leader's empire, may he increase his years,
and may the oaken crown protect your doors,
and, by the gods' auspices, may the heir of so great a surname
take up, with the omen by which his father did, the burden of the world.
When the third Titan looks back on the passed Ides,
the rites of the Parrhasian goddess will be performed anew.
For of old carriages bore the Ausonian matrons
(this too, I think, was named from Evander's parent);
soon the honour is taken away, and every matron resolves
to renew her thankless husbands by no offspring,
and, that she might bear no children, the reckless one with a hidden blow
shook out the growing burden from her womb.
They say the fathers rebuked the wives who dared such cruelty,
yet restored the right that had been taken away;
and now they bid that two rites be performed alike to the Tegean parent
for boys and for girls.
It is not lawful to bring leather into her shrine,
lest dead skins defile the pure hearths.
If you love ancient rites, stand by the one who prays:
you will learn names not known to you before.
Porrima is appeased, and Postverta, whether your sisters,
goddess of Maenalus, or the companions of your flight:
the one is thought to have sung of what had been long ago (porro),
the other of whatever was to come afterward (postmodo).
Bright Concord, the next day set you in a snow-white temple,
where lofty Moneta lifts her high steps:
now you will look well, Concord, upon the Latian throng,
now hallowed hands have established you.
Furius, the conqueror of the Etruscan people, had vowed
the old temple, and he had kept his vow's faith;
the cause was that the commons had seceded from the fathers, taking up arms,
and Rome herself feared her own strength.
The recent cause is better: Germany, with loosened hair,
offers herself to your auspices, revered leader;
hence you dedicated the spoils of the conquered nation
and made temples to the goddess whom you yourself worship.
Your mother established her by both her deeds and her altar,
she alone found worthy of great Jupiter's bed.
When these days have passed, Phoebus, leaving Capricorn behind,
you will run through the signs of the youth who bears the water.

title: Fasti
text:
When the seventh sun from this rises and sinks beneath the waves,
already no Lyre will shine in the whole sky.
After this star, on the coming night, the fire
that gleams in the middle of the Lion's breast will be sunk.
Three and four times I unrolled the calendar that marks the seasons,
and no day of the Sowing was found there;
when the Muse (for she perceived it) said to me, as this day
was being announced: 'Why do you seek a fixed rite from the calendar?
As the day is uncertain for the rite, so the season is certain:
when the seed is cast, and the field is with child.'
Stand, garlanded bullocks, at the full manger:
with the warm spring your work will return.
Let the countryman hang up the plough that has earned its rest on a stake:
the cold ground dreads every wound.
Steward, give rest to the earth, the sowing done;
give rest to the men who have tilled the earth.
Let the village keep festival: purify the village, farmers,
and give the yearly cakes to the village hearths.
Let the mothers of the crops be appeased, Tellus and Ceres,
with their own spelt and with the entrails of a sow.
Ceres and Earth keep a common office:
the one gives the cause of the crops, the other the place.
'Partners in the work, by whom antiquity was set right
and the oaken acorn was conquered by a more useful food,
satisfy the eager farmers with boundless crops,
that they may take the worthy reward of their labour.
Give perpetual growth to the tender sowings,
and let no new blade be scorched by the chill snows.
When we sow, open the sky with clear winds;
when the seed lies hidden, sprinkle it with heavenly water.
And beware lest the birds, a host that will do harm,
ravage with their flock the fields sown with Ceres' gifts.
You too, ants, spare the buried grains:
after the harvest your store of plunder will be greater.
Meanwhile let the crop grow free of rough mildew,
nor let the sickly harvest grow pale from the sky's flaw,
and let it neither fail from leanness, nor, richer than is right,
perish, run riot in its own abundance.
And let the fields be free of darnel that hurts the eyes,
nor let the barren wild oat rise from the tilled soil.
May the field render, at vast interest, the crops of wheat
and the spelt that will twice endure the fire, and the barley!'
These prayers I make for you, these pray for yourselves, farmers,
and may both goddesses make the prayers come true.
War long held men: the sword was fitter than the ploughshare,
the plough-ox yielded to the horse;
the hoes lay idle, the mattocks were turned into javelins,
and a helmet was made from the weight of the rake.
Thanks be to the gods and to your house: long since
the wars lie bound in chains beneath your feet.
Let the ox come under the yoke, the seed under the ploughed earth:
Peace nurtures Ceres, Ceres is the nursling of Peace.
But the sixth day that comes before the approaching Kalends,
on this the temples were dedicated to the Ledaean gods:
brethren gods, those brethren of the gods' race
built them by Juturna's pools.
The song itself has led me to the altar of Peace.
This will be the second day from the end of the month.
Your hair wreathed and bound with the leaves of Actium,
Peace, be present and gentle in all the world.
While foes are wanting, let the cause of triumph be wanting too:
you will be a greater glory to our leaders than war.
Let the soldier bear arms only to hold arms in check,
and let nothing but the procession be sung to the fierce trumpet.
Let the farthest world, both first and last, dread the sons of Aeneas:
if any land feared Rome too little, let it love her.
Add incense, priests, to the flames of peace,
and let the white victim fall, struck on the brow,
and ask of the gods, inclined to dutiful prayers,
that the house which secures peace may, with peace, endure.
But now the first part of my labour is done,
and with its month the little book has its end.

title: Fasti
text:
2. Janus has his end, when both the song and the year increase:
as here one month follows another, so let one book follow another.
Now for the first time, elegiacs, you go with larger sails:
of late, I remember, you were a slight work.
I myself found you ready ministers in love,
when my early youth made sport in its own measures.
Now I, the same poet, sing of sacred rites and the seasons marked in the calendar:
who would have believed there was a way from those themes to these?
This is my soldiering: I bear what arms I can,
and my right hand is not idle in every service.
If javelins are not hurled by my strong arm,
nor do I press the back of a war-horse,
nor am I covered by a helmet nor girt with a sharp sword
(in such weapons anyone can be handy),
yet I follow your titles, Caesar, with a zealous heart,
and advance through the record of your honours.
So be present, and look back a little with a kindly face
on my offerings, if you have any leisure from pacifying the foe.
The Roman fathers called expiations 'februa':
even now many signs give proof to the word.
The pontiffs ask the king and the flamen for wool,
which in the ancient tongue had the name 'februa';
and the cleansings that the lictor takes from the houses he has swept,
the roasted spelt with grain, are called the same;
the same name belongs to the branch which, cut from a pure tree,
covers the chaste brows of the priests with its leaves;
I myself have seen the flamen's wife asking for februa;
and to her asking a pine twig was given.
In short, whatever it is by which our bodies are purified
had this name among our unshorn forefathers.
The month was named from these, because the Luperci with cut hide
purify all the ground and hold it for an expiation,
or because the season is pure when the graves are appeased,
once the days of the dead have passed by.
Our elders believed that all sin and all cause of evil
could be removed by these cleansings.
Greece gave the origin of the custom: she thinks the guilty,
once purified, lay aside their impious deeds.
Peleus, son of Actor, and Phocus's slaying — Acastus freed
Peleus himself too, through the Haemonian waters;
Aegeus, all too credulous, comforted the Phasian woman,
borne through the air by bridled dragons, with his aid;
the son of Amphiaraus said to Achelous of Naupactus,
'Loose my sin,' and he too loosed his sin.
Ah! too easy of belief, you who think the grim crimes of slaughter
can be washed away by a river's water!
Yet, that you may not stray in ignorance of the ancient order,
the month of Janus was first, as it is, and was so before;
the month that follows Janus was the last of the old year:
you too, Terminus, were the boundary of the rites.
For the month of Janus is first, because the doorway is first:
the month sacred to the deep shades was the deepest.
Afterward the months once parted by a long span
are believed to have been joined by the board of ten.
At the month's beginning the Saviour, neighbour to the Phrygian Mother,
is said to have been enriched with new shrines.
Now where, you ask, are the temples consecrated to the goddess
on those Kalends? They have fallen low through length of days.
That the rest might not fall, shaken by like ruin,
the foresighted care of our hallowed leader took heed,
under whom the shrines feel no old age;
nor is he content with men: he lays gods under obligation.
Founder of temples, holy restorer of temples,
I pray the gods above may have a like care of you!
May the heavenly ones grant you the years you grant to them,
and stand on guard before your house!
Then too the grove of neighbouring Helernus is thronged,
where the stranger Tiber seeks the waters of the sea.
At Numa's sanctuary and the Capitoline Thunderer,
and on Jove's high citadel, a two-tooth victim falls.
Often the south wind, veiled in clouds, stirs up heavy rains,
or the earth lies hidden beneath a covering of snow.

title: Fasti
text:
When the Titan, about to depart into the Hesperian waves,
takes off the jewelled yoke from his crimson horses,
on that night someone, lifting his face to the stars,
will say: 'Where today is the Lyre that gleamed yesterday?'
And while he seeks the Lyre, he will mark the back of the middle Lion
suddenly plunged into the clear waters too.
The Dolphin, which you saw just now engraved with stars,
will flee your sight on the following night:
whether he was the lucky betrayer of hidden loves,
or whether he bore the Lesbian lyre with its master.
What sea does not know, what land is ignorant of Arion?
By his song he held the running waters still.
Often the wolf, pursuing the lamb, was stayed by his voice,
often the lamb, fleeing, stood still before the greedy wolf;
often hounds and hares have lain beneath one shade,
and the hind stood on the rock close by the lioness,
and without quarrel the chattering crow sat with Pallas's bird,
and the dove was joined to the hawk.
Cynthia is said often to have marvelled, tuneful Arion,
at your measures, as though at her brother's.
Arion's name had filled the Sicilian cities,
and the Ausonian shore was captivated by his lyric strains;
on his way home Arion went aboard a ship,
and so was carrying the wealth he had won by his art.
Perhaps, unhappy man, you feared the winds and waves,
but to you the sea was safer than your own ship.
For the helmsman took his stand with drawn sword,
and the rest of the crew, his accomplices, with armed hand.
What have you to do with a blade? Steer the wavering ship, sailor:
these are not weapons to be held by your fingers.
He, pale with fear, said: 'I do not beg off death,
but let me take my lyre and play a little.'
They grant it and laugh at the delay; he takes a crown
that might well grace your hair, Phoebus;
he had put on a robe twice dyed with Tyrian purple:
struck by his thumb the string gave back its sounds,
in plaintive measures, as a swan sings of its hard fate,
its temples pierced by a bright feather.
At once, in his finery, he leaps into the midst of the waves:
the dark-blue stern is sprinkled by the water he stirs.
Then (beyond belief) a dolphin, they say, with curved back
set itself beneath the strange burden;
he, sitting there, holds his lyre and, as the price of his passage,
sings, and soothes the sea-waters with his song.
The gods see his pious deeds: Jupiter received the dolphin
among the stars, and bade it have nine stars.
Now I could wish, Maeonian bard, that I had a thousand voices,
and the breast in which Achilles was sung,
while I sing in alternating measure of the sacred Nones:
here the calendar receives its greatest honour.
My talent fails, and matters greater than my strength press on:
this day must be sung by me with no common voice.
What did I, mad, mean to lay so great a weight
upon elegiacs? That was a theme for the heroic foot.
Holy father of the fatherland, this name the commons gave you,
this the senate; this name we knights gave you;
yet the facts had given it before; late, too, you took your true
titles: long since you were the father of the world.
This name on earth you bear which Jupiter bears in high heaven:
you are the father of men, he of gods.
Romulus, you will yield: this man makes your walls great by guarding them,
you had left them for Remus to leap across.
Tatius felt you, and little Cures, and Caenina:
under this man's leadership both sides of the sun are Roman.
You held some small piece of conquered land:
whatever lies beneath high Jove, Caesar holds.
You ravished women: under him the wives are bidden be chaste.
You gave refuge in a grove: he drove off wrongdoing.
Violence was pleasing to you: under Caesar the laws flourish.
You held the name of master, he that of prince;
Remus accuses you: he gave pardon to his enemies.
Your father made you a god: he made his father one.

title: Fasti
text:
Now the Idaean boy shows half his body above the waves
and pours forth clear waters mixed with nectar.
See too, if anyone was wont to shudder at the North Wind,
let him rejoice: a softer breeze comes from the Zephyrs.
When the fifth Morning-star has lifted its bright beam from the watery waves,
the season of early spring will have come.
Yet, that you be not deceived, frosts remain for you, they remain,
and departing winter has left great tokens behind.
Let the third night come: at once you will see the Guardian of the Bear
thrust out his two feet.
Among the Hamadryads and Diana the huntress
Callisto was one part of the sacred band.
Touching the goddess's bow, she said: 'By this bow we touch,
be witnesses of my virginity.'
Cynthia praised her, and said: 'Keep the compact you have promised,
and you shall be the foremost of my companions.'
She would have kept the compact, had she not been beautiful:
she guarded herself from mortals; her offence is from Jove.
Phoebe was returning, having hunted a thousand wild beasts in the woods,
when the sun held more than midday, or the midday point.
When she reached a grove (a grove dark with thick ilex,
and in its midst was a deep spring of chill water),
she said: 'Here in the wood, Tegean maiden, let us bathe!'
The girl blushed at the false name of maiden.
She had spoken to the nymphs too: the nymphs lay aside their veils,
this one is ashamed and gives the ill signs of slow delay.
She had taken off her tunic; by the swelling of her womb made plain
she is betrayed by the evidence of her own weight.
To her the goddess said: 'Forsworn daughter of Lycaon, leave
the maiden bands and do not pollute the chaste waters.'
The moon had ten times filled her new orb with her horns:
she who had been thought a maiden was a mother.
Hurt, Juno rages, and changes the girl's form.
What do you do? It was against her will she yielded to Jove.
And when she saw the foul features in her rival,
Jupiter said: 'Let him go into her embrace!'
The she-bear wandered, filthy, over the wild mountains,
she who had lately been loved by highest Jove.
Now the boy conceived in stealth was leading his third lustrum,
when the mother met her own offspring.
She, indeed, as though she knew him, stood still, beside herself,
and groaned: the groan was the words of a parent.
The boy, not knowing her, would have pierced her with his sharp spear,
had not both been snatched up to the homes above.
The signs gleam near each other: the first, which we call Arctos,
the Bear-keeper, has the form of one following her back.
Saturnia still rages, and asks white-haired Tethys
not to let the Maenalian Bear bathe in her waters.
On the Ides the altars of rustic Faunus smoke,
here where the island breaks the parted waters.
This was that day on which, by Veientine arms,
three hundred Fabii and three more fell.
One house had taken on itself the strength and the burden of the city:
the clansmen take up the arms they have professed,
a noble soldier goes forth from the same camp,
of whom any one was fit to be made the leader.
There is a road close by the right-hand Janus of the Carmental gate:
do not go through it, whoever you are; it has an omen,
for fame reports that the three hundred Fabii went out by it:
the gate is free of fault, yet it has an omen.
When with swift march they reached the rushing Cremera
(it flowed turbid with winter's waters),
they pitch camp on the spot: with drawn swords they themselves
go through the Etruscan host in valiant battle,
no otherwise than when lions of the Libyan race
fall upon flocks scattered through the broad fields.
The foes flee in all directions and take dishonourable wounds
upon their backs: the ground grows red with Tuscan blood.
So again, so often they fall, where to conquer openly
is not granted, and they prepare ambushes and hidden arms.
There was a plain; hills closed in the ends of the plain,
and a wood fit to hide the mountain beasts;
in the midst they leave a few men and scattered cattle,
the rest of the throng lies hidden, concealed in the thickets.
Behold, like a torrent swollen with rainwater
or with snow that melts, conquered by the warm Zephyr,
it is borne over the crops and over the roads, nor, as before,
keeps its waters shut within the margins of its banks:
so the Fabii fill the valley with their wide ranging,
and lay low whatever they see, and no other fear is in them.
Where do you rush, noble house? Ill do you trust the foe:
unsuspecting nobility, beware the treacherous weapons!
Valour perishes by guile: into the open plains on every side
the enemies spring forth and hold the whole flank.
What can the brave few do against so many thousands?
Or what is left for them in their wretched plight?
As a boar, driven far from the Laurentine woods,
scatters the swift hounds with his lightning jaws,
yet soon perishes himself, so they do not die unavenged
and deal wounds in turn with hand for hand.
One day had sent all the Fabii to war:
one day destroyed those sent to war.
Yet, that the seeds of the Herculean race might survive,
it is credible that the gods themselves took thought;
for a boy, not yet of age and as yet useless in arms,
one of the Fabian race, had been left behind,
that you might one day be born, Maximus,
by whom, by delay, the state was to be restored.

title: Fasti
text:
Three constellations lie in a row, the Raven and the Snake
and, in the middle between the two, the Bowl.
On the Ides they hide, and rise on the following night,
and why these three are so joined together I shall sing.
By chance Phoebus was preparing a solemn feast for Jove
(my tale will make no long delays):
'Go, my bird,' he said, 'that nothing may delay the holy rites,
and bring a little water from living springs.'
The raven lifts the gilded bowl in his curving claws
and flies high on his airy course.
A fig-tree stood there, thick with hard fruit:
he tries it with his beak; it was not fit to be picked.
Forgetful of his charge, he is said to have sat beneath the tree,
till by slow delay the fruit should grow sweet.
And now, sated, he seizes with his black talons a long water-snake
and returns to his lord and tells a made-up tale:
'This was the cause of my delay, the besieger of the living waters:
he held back the springs and my duty.'
'You add lies to your fault,' said Phoebus, 'and you dare
to try to deceive the prophet god with words?
But for you, while the milky fig clings to the tree,
no cold waters shall be drunk from any spring.'
He spoke, and as eternal memorials of that ancient deed
the Snake, the Bird, the Bowl gleam, joined constellations.
On the third day after the Ides the dawn looks upon the naked Luperci,
and the rites of two-horned Faunus come round.
Tell, Pierides, what is the origin of the rites,
and from where they were sought and reached the homes of Latium.
The Arcadians of old are said to have worshipped Pan, the god of the flock:
he was much present on the Arcadian ridges.
Pholoe will witness it, the Stymphalian waters will witness,
and Ladon, who runs to the sea with swift waters,
and the ridges of the Nonacrian grove girt with pine-woods,
and high Cyllene and the Parrhasian snows.
There Pan was the god of the herd, Pan the god of the mares;
he received a gift for keeping the sheep unharmed.
Evander brought the woodland gods with him;
here, where now the city is, was then but the site of a city.
Hence we worship the god, and the rites brought by the Pelasgians
the flamen of Jupiter still performs in the ancient manner.
Why then do they run, and why (for so it is the custom to run)
do they bear their bodies naked, their garments laid aside, you ask?
The god himself, swift, delights to range over the high
mountains, and himself takes sudden flights;
the god himself, naked, bids his ministers go naked,
nor was clothing fit enough for running.
Before Jove was born, the Arcadians are said to have held
the lands, and that people was older than the moon.
Their life was like the beasts', driven to no useful arts:
the crowd was still without skill and rude.
For houses they knew leaves, for crops grasses,
nectar was water drawn up in two cupped hands.
No bull panted beneath the curving share,
no land was under the rule of one who tilled it;
no use of the horse was yet known, each man bore himself;
the sheep went clothed in its own wool.
They lived beneath the open sky and bore their bodies naked,
schooled to endure heavy rains and the southern blasts.
Even now the unclothed Luperci recall the memorials of the ancient
custom and bear witness to the wealth of old.
But why above all Faunus flees coverings,
a tale full of ancient jest is handed down.
By chance the Tirynthian youth was going as the companion of his mistress:
Faunus saw the pair from a lofty ridge.
He saw and grew hot, and said: 'Mountain powers,
I have no business with you: here shall my passion be.'
The Maeonian woman went, her shoulders bathed in fragrant hair,
to be marvelled at in her gold-embroidered robe:
a golden parasol kept off the warm suns,
which yet the hands of Hercules held up.
Now she held the grove of Bacchus and the vineyards of Tmolus,
and dewy Hesperus came on his dusky horse.
She enters a cave panelled with tufa and living pumice;
at the very threshold was a chattering brook.
And while the attendants prepare the feast and the wine to be drunk,
she fits out Alcides in her own attire.
She gives him thin tunics dyed with Gaetulian purple,
she gives the smooth girdle with which she had just been girt.
The girdle is too small for his waist; he loosens the fastenings of the tunics,
that he might thrust out his great hands.
He had broken the bracelets, not made for those arms,
and his big feet split the little sandal-straps.
She herself takes the heavy club and the lion's spoil
and the lesser arrows stored in her quiver.
So having feasted, so they give their bodies to sleep,
and lay down apart on couches set side by side;
the reason: because they were preparing rites for the discoverer of the vine,
to perform them in purity when day should have risen.
It was midnight: what does shameless love not dare?
Through the darkness Faunus came to the dewy cave,
and when he sees the attendants undone by sleep and wine,
he conceives a hope that there is the same slumber in the masters.
He enters, and this way and that the reckless adulterer strays,
and holds his cautious hands before him and follows them.
He had come to the curtained couch of the bedstead
and was about to be happy at the first cast of the lot.
When he touched the fleeces shaggy with the bristles of the tawny lion,
he took fright and held back his hand,
and, thunderstruck with fear, drew back, as often a traveller,
startled at the sight of a snake, draws back his foot;
then he touches the soft coverings of the couch which was joined,
and is deceived by the deceiving sign.
He climbs up and reclines on the nearer side of the bed,
and the swollen part was harder than horn.
Meanwhile he draws the tunic up from its lowest edge:
the legs bristled, rough with thick hairs.
As he tries the rest, the Tirynthian hero suddenly
thrust him off: he fell from the top of the couch.
A sound is made, the Maeonian woman calls her attendants and asks for lights:
torches brought in, the deeds are laid bare.
He groans, heavily thrown down from the high bed,
and scarcely lifts his limbs from the hard ground.
Alcides laughs, and those who saw him lying there,
the Lydian girl laughs at her own lover.
Mocked by the dress, the god does not love clothing that deceives
the eyes, and calls men naked to his rites.
Add Latin reasons to the foreign, my Muse,
and let our horse run on its own dust.
A she-goat is slain in due form for goat-footed Faunus,
and the throng comes, summoned to the scanty feast.
And while the priests prepare the entrails pierced on willow spits,
the sun holding the mid path of heaven,
Romulus and his brother and the shepherd youth
gave their naked bodies to the sun on the field;
with boxing-gloves and javelins and the hurled weight of the stone
they gave their arms to be tried in sport.
A shepherd from the height cried: 'Robbers, Romulus and Remus,
are driving the bullocks through the trackless fields!'
It was long to arm: each goes out by a different side;
by meeting the robbers Remus recovered the booty.
When he returned, he draws the hissing entrails from the spits
and says: 'These surely none but the victor shall eat.'
He does as he said, and the Fabii with him; Romulus comes back there
in vain and sees the tables and the bare bones;
he laughed and grieved that the Fabii and Remus could conquer,
and that his own Quintilii could not.
The fame of the deed remains: their garments laid aside they run,
and the enterprise, because it went well, keeps a remembered fame.

title: Fasti
text:
Perhaps you may ask too why that place is the Lupercal,
or what cause marks the day with such a name.
Silvia the Vestal had brought forth heavenly seed in childbirth,
while her uncle held the kingdom.
He bids the little ones be carried off and slain in the river:
what do you do? One of these will be a Romulus.
The servants carry out the tearful orders, though they refuse them,
yet they weep, and bear the twins to the appointed place.
Albula, which Tiberinus, plunged beneath the waves,
gave back as Tiber, chanced to swell with winter's waters:
here, where now the forums are, you might see skiffs straying,
and where your valleys lie, great Circus.
When they came hither (for they could go no further),
one and another of them said:
'But how alike they are! how beautiful both!
yet of the two this one has more vigour.
If birth is shown by the face, unless the look deceives me,
I suspect some god is in you —
but if any god were the author of your origin,
in so headlong an hour he would bring help.
He would surely bring help, if your mother did not need help,
who was made a mother and bereaved on one day.
Born together, to die together, go together beneath the waves,
you bodies!' He ceased and laid them down from his arms.
Both wailed alike: you would have thought they understood;
these men return to their homes with wet cheeks.
The hollow trough bears the burden laid on it on the surface of the water:
alas, how great a destiny that little plank carried!
The trough, brought to the mud beneath the shady woods,
gradually settles as the river fails.
There was a tree: traces remain, and what is now called
the Ruminal fig was the Romulan fig.
There came to the exposed twins (a marvel!) a wolf, lately a mother:
who would believe the beast did the boys no harm?
That it did no harm is too little; it even helps them: the kindred hands
that a wolf nourishes had brought themselves to destroy.
She stood still and fawns on the tender nurslings with her tail
and shapes the two bodies with her tongue.
You would know they were Mars's sons: fear was absent; they draw the teats
and are fed by the supply of milk not promised them.
She gave her name to the place, the place itself to the Luperci.
Great is the reward the nurse has for the milk she gave.
What forbids the Luperci being named from the Arcadian mount?
Faunus Lycaeus has temples in Arcadia.
Bride, what do you wait for? Not by potent herbs,
nor by prayer, nor by magic song will you be a mother;
endure with patience the strokes of a fruitful right hand,
and soon your husband's father will have the longed-for name of grandsire.
For there was that time when, by a hard lot, the wives
gave back rare pledges of their wombs.
'What does it profit me,' Romulus cried (this was while he held the sceptre),
'to have carried off the Sabine women,
if my wrong has brought me not strength but war?
It had been more useful not to have had daughters-in-law.'
Beneath the Esquiline mount, uncut for many years,
was a grove in the name of great Juno.
When they came hither, both wives and husbands
fell down on bended knee in supplication,
when suddenly the tree-tops of the moved wood trembled
and the goddess spoke wondrous words through her groves:
'Let a sacred he-goat go in unto the Italian matrons,' she said.
The throng stood amazed, terrified at the doubtful sound.
There was an augur (his name has fallen away through the long years,
lately he had come, an exile, from Etruscan soil),
he slays a goat, and the girls, at his bidding, offered their backs
to be struck with thongs cut from its hide.
The moon was renewing her horns at the tenth course,
and suddenly the husband was a father and the bride a mother.
Thanks to Lucina! This name the grove (lucus) gave you,
or because, goddess, you hold the beginning of the light (lux).
Spare, I pray, the women with child, gentle Lucina,
and softly bring the ripe burden from the womb.

title: Fasti
text:
When the day has dawned, cease to trust the winds:
the breeze of that season has lost its faith;
the blasts are not steady, and for six days unbarred
the wide door of the Aeolian prison stands open.
Now light Aquarius has set with his slanting urn:
next, Fishes, receive the heavenly horses.
You and your brother (for you gleam as joined
signs) are said to have borne two gods on your backs.
Once, fleeing the dread Typhon, Dione,
at the time when Jupiter took up arms for heaven,
came to the Euphrates, attended by little Cupid,
and sat by the margin of the Palestinian water.
Poplars and reeds held the tops of the banks,
and the willows gave hope that these too could give shelter.
While she hides, the grove sounded with the wind; she with fear
grows pale and believes hostile bands are at hand,
and as she held her son in her bosom, 'Help, nymphs,
and bring aid to two gods!' she said.
Without delay she leaped forth. Twin fishes went beneath them:
for which now the stars hold a worthy reward.
Hence the Syrians count it sin to set this kind on the table,
and in their fear do not defile their mouths with fishes.
The next day is empty, but the third is dedicated to Quirinus,
who holds this name, but before was Romulus,
whether because the spear was called 'curis' by the ancient Sabines
(the warlike god came to the stars from a weapon),
or whether the Quirites gave their own name to their king,
or because he had joined Cures to the Romans.
For the warlike Father, after he saw the new walls
and the many wars waged by Romulus's hand,
said: 'Jupiter, the Roman power has strength:
it needs not the service of my blood.
Give the son back to his father; though one has perished,
the one who remains to me will be enough for himself and for Remus.
There will be one whom you shall raise to the blue of heaven,
you said to me: let Jove's words be made good.'
Jupiter had nodded assent. At the nod both poles
trembled, and Atlas shifted the weight of heaven.
There is a place the ancients called the Marsh of the Goat:
by chance there, Romulus, you were giving law to your people.
The sun flees, and rising clouds remove the sky,
and a heavy shower falls in poured-out streams.
Here it thunders, here the heaven is rent by hurled fires:
flight begins; the king was seeking the stars on his father's horses.
There was mourning, and the senators falsely under the charge of murder,
and perhaps that belief would have stuck in men's minds;
but Proculus Julius was coming from Long Alba,
and the moon shone, and there was no need of a torch,
when suddenly the hedges on the left trembled at a movement:
he drew back his steps, and his hair stood on end.
Beautiful and greater than human and seemly in his robe,
Romulus seemed to be present in the midst of the road,
and to have said at the same time: 'Forbid the Quirites to mourn,
nor let them violate my godhead with their tears;
let the pious throng bring incense and appease the new Quirinus,
and cultivate their fathers' arts and the soldier's calling.'
He bade it, and vanished into thin air from their eyes.
This man calls the people together and reports the bidden words.
Temples are made to the god, the hill too is named from him,
and on certain days they renew the ancestral rites.
Hear too why this same day is called the festival of Fools:
the cause is slight indeed, but fitting.
The ancient land had no skilled farmers:
fierce wars wearied the active men;
there was more glory in the sword than in the curving plough:
the field, neglected by its master, bore little.
Yet the ancients sowed spelt, they reaped spelt,
and gave the first-fruits of cut spelt to Ceres.
Taught by experience, they gave the spelt to be roasted in the flames,
and bore much loss through their own fault.
For now they swept up black ashes instead of spelt,
now the fires caught the very huts.
Fornax was made a goddess: the farmers, glad,
pray to Fornax to keep their grain at the right heat.
Now the chief Curio proclaims the Fornacalia in the lawful words,
and does not perform it on a fixed day,
and in the forum, with many tablets hanging round,
each ward is marked by its certain sign;
and the foolish part of the people, who do not know their ward,
perform the rite on the last day, postponed.

title: Fasti
text:
There is honour for the tombs too. Appease the souls of your fathers
and bring small gifts to the extinguished pyres.
The shades ask little, piety is welcome in place of a rich
gift: deep Styx holds no greedy gods.
A tile veiled with stretched-out garlands is enough,
and scattered fruits and a sparing grain of salt,
and Ceres softened in wine and loosened violets:
let the potsherd left in the middle of the road hold these.
Nor do I forbid greater gifts, but with these too the shade is appeased;
add prayers and their own words at the hearths set up.
This custom Aeneas, a fitting author of piety,
brought into your lands, righteous Latinus;
he bore solemn gifts to his father's Genius:
from this the peoples learned the pious rites.
But once, while they wage long wars with fighting arms,
they forsook the Days of the Fathers.
It did not go unpunished; for from that omen, it is said,
Rome grew hot with pyres in the suburbs.
I scarcely believe it: the forefathers are said to have come forth from their tombs
and to have made complaint in the silent time of night,
and through the city's streets and over the broad fields
they say the misshapen souls, an empty crowd, howled.
After this the neglected honours are restored to the tombs,
and an end came to the prodigies and the deaths.
While these things, however, are being done, cease, widowed maidens:
let the pine torch await pure days,
and let not the curved spear comb your maiden locks,
you who will seem ripe to your eager mother.
Hide your torches, Hymenaeus, and take them away
from the dark fires! The mournful graves have other torches.
Let the gods too be hidden behind the closed temple doors,
let the altars be without incense and the hearths stand without fire.
Now the thin souls and the bodies buried in tombs
wander, now the shade feeds on the food set out.
Yet not beyond this, than as many Morning-stars remain of the month
as our verses have feet.
This day they called the Feralia, because they bring the due rites;
that is the last day for appeasing the shades.
Behold, an aged crone, sitting among the girls,
performs the rites of the Silent Goddess (yet she herself is not silent),
and with three fingers sets three bits of incense under the threshold,
where the small mouse has made itself a hidden passage;
then she binds enchanted threads with dark lead
and turns seven black beans in her mouth,
and the head of a sprat, which she has sealed with pitch and pierced
with a bronze needle, she roasts, sewn up, in the fire;
she drips wine on too: whatever wine is left,
either she or her companions, but mostly she, drinks.
'We have bound hostile tongues and unfriendly mouths,'
the crone says as she departs, and goes out drunk.
At once you will ask of me who the Mute Goddess is:
learn what is known to me from the old men of old.
Jupiter, overcome by an immoderate love of Juturna,
endured many things not to be borne by so great a god:
now she hid in the woods among the hazel-thickets,
now leaped down into her kindred waters.
He calls together the nymphs, all who held Latium,
and casts such words into the midst of the band:
'Your sister grudges herself and shuns what is good for her,
to have lain with the highest god.
Take thought for both; for what is my great pleasure
will be a great profit for your sister.
Do you, as she flees, stand in her way on the brink of the bank,
that she may not plunge her body in the river-water.'
He had spoken: all the Tiberine nymphs nodded assent,
and those who haunt your chambers, divine Ilia.
There chanced to be a naiad, Lara by name, but to her
the first syllable, said twice, was her old name,
given from her fault. Often Almo's
daughter had said to her, 'Hold your tongue,' yet she does not hold it,
who, as soon as she touched the pools of her sister Juturna,
said: 'Flee the banks,' and reports the words of Jove.
She even went to Juno, and pitying the wives
said: 'Your husband loves the naiad Juturna.'
Jupiter swelled with anger, and from her, who had used her tongue immodestly,
he tears it out, and calls Mercury:
'Lead her to the shades; that place is fit for the silent.
A nymph she shall be, but a nymph of the infernal marsh.'
The orders of Jove are done; the grove received them as they went:
she is said then to have pleased the god who led her.
Here he prepares violence; she pleads with her face instead of words,
and strives in vain to speak with her dumb mouth.
And she becomes pregnant and bears twins, who guard the crossroads
and keep watch ever in our city, the Lares.

title: Fasti
text:
The next day the kindred dear called the Caristia,
and the throng of relatives comes to the gods of kin.
No doubt it is pleasant to turn the face away from the tombs
and those who have perished, and back to the living,
and after so many lost, to look upon whatever of the blood remains
and to number the degrees of the family.
Let the innocent come: far, far from here be the impious
brother, and the mother harsh toward her own offspring,
he whose father lives too long, who reckons up his mother's years,
the unjust mother-in-law who oppresses the hated daughter-in-law.
Let the brothers, sons of Tantalus, be absent, and Jason's wife,
and she who gave the roasted seeds to the farmers,
and the sister and Procne and Tereus, unjust to both,
and whoever increases his wealth through crime.
Give incense to the gods of the family, you good (Concord, they say,
is present, gentle, especially on that day),
and offer the feast, that, as a pledge of grateful honour,
the dish set out may feed the girdled Lares.
And now when damp night counsels gentle sleep,
take up the wine in generous hand for your prayers,
and say: 'Well to you, well to you, father of the fatherland, best Caesar!'
say it through the sacred words, the wine poured out.
When night has passed, let the god who marks off the fields by his own sign
be honoured with his accustomed rite.
Terminus, whether you are a stone, or a stake buried in the field,
you too have had divinity from of old.
Two owners crown you from opposite sides,
and bring you two garlands and two cakes.
An altar is made: hither the rustic farmer's wife
brings fire in a broken crock, taken from the warm hearth.
The old man cuts wood and builds it, chopped, with skill,
and strives to fix the branches in the firm ground;
then he kindles the first flames with dry bark,
the boy stands and holds in his hands the wide baskets.
Then when he has thrown the grain three times into the midst of the fire,
the little daughter offers the cut honeycombs.
Others hold the wine; each thing is offered to the flames;
they watch, and the white-robed throng keeps silence.
The shared Terminus is sprinkled with the blood of a slain lamb
and does not complain when a suckling pig is given him.
The simple neighbourhood gathers and celebrates the feast
and sings your praises, holy Terminus:
you set bounds to peoples and cities and great kingdoms;
without you every field would be a thing of strife.
You have no ambition, by no gold are you corrupted,
you guard the lands entrusted to you in lawful faith.
If you had marked off the Thyrean land of old,
three hundred bodies would not have been sent to death,
nor would Othryades have lain upon the heaped-up arms.
Oh, how much blood he gave to his fatherland!
What of the time when the new Capitol was being built? No doubt
the whole throng of gods yielded to Jove and gave him place:
Terminus, as the ancients tell, found in the shrine,
stood his ground and holds the temple with great Jove.
Even now, that he may see nothing above him but the stars,
the temple roof has a small opening.
Terminus, after that you are not free to wander:
in the post where you have been set, stay,
and yield nothing to your neighbour at his asking,
lest you seem to have set a man before Jove;
and whether you are struck by ploughshares or by mattocks,
cry out: 'This is your field, that is his!'
There is a road that leads the people to the Laurentine fields,
the kingdom once sought by the Dardanian leader:
on that road the sixth milestone from the city sees the rites
done to you, Terminus, with the entrails of a wool-bearing flock.
To other nations land is given with a fixed boundary:
the space of the city of Rome and of the world is the same.

title: Fasti
text:
Now I must tell of the king's flight: from it the sixth day
from the month's end took its name.
Tarquin held the last reign of the Roman race,
an unjust man, yet brave in arms.
He had taken some cities, overthrown others,
and made Gabii his own by base craft.
For the youngest of three, the manifest offspring of the Proud,
came to the midst of the foe in the silent night.
They had bared their swords: 'Slay me, unarmed!' he said;
'this my brothers and my father Tarquin would wish,
who tore my back with cruel scourging.'
That he might say this, he had endured the scourge.
There was moonlight: they look at the youth and sheathe their swords,
and see his back, marked, his garment drawn aside;
they weep too, and pray him to wage their wars with them:
the cunning one nodded assent to the unsuspecting men.
And now in power he names his father by a friend sent,
to show him the road to Gabii's ruin.
There was below a garden, most cultivated with fragrant herbs,
its ground cut by a stream of softly sounding water:
there Tarquin received his son's hidden message
and with his staff mowed off the topmost lilies.
When the messenger returned and said the lilies were struck off,
the son said: 'I recognize my father's commands.'
Without delay, the chief men slain, the walls of the Gabine city
are handed over, bare of their leaders.
Behold, dreadful to see, a snake comes forth from the midst of the altars
and seizes the entrails from the quenched fires.
Phoebus is consulted: the oracle was given thus: 'He who first
shall give kisses to his mother will be the victor.'
Each one hastened to bear kisses to his mother,
the credulous throng not understanding the god.
Brutus was a wise man feigning folly, that he might be
safe from your plots, dread Proud One;
he, lying prone, gave kisses to his mother Earth,
thought to have fallen by a stumbling foot.
Meanwhile Ardea is girt with Roman standards
and endures the long delays of a siege,
while there is leisure and the foe fear to join battle,
they play in the camp, the soldier spends his idle hours.
Young Tarquin receives his comrades with feast and wine;
from among them the king's son spoke:
'While Ardea holds us anxious in a sluggish war
and does not let us bear our arms back to our fathers' gods,
is the marriage-bed kept faithful by our wives? And are we
a mutual care to our spouses?'
Each praises his own: in their zeal the rivalry grows,
and tongue and heart boil with much wine.
He rose to whom Collatia had given a famous name:
'No need of words, believe the facts!' he said.
'The night is left: let us mount our horses and seek the city!'
The words please, the horses are bridled,
they bore their masters, and at once they seek the royal
palace: there was no guard at the door.
Behold, they find the king's daughters-in-law, with garlands flung about their necks,
keeping wakeful, the wine set out.
Thence with swift step Lucretia is sought: she was spinning,
before the bed were baskets and soft wool.
By the scant light the maids drew out their assigned tasks,
among whom she spoke thus with a low voice:
'A cloak must be sent to your master (now, now hasten, girls!),
made by our hand as soon as may be.
But what do you hear? For you can hear more news:
how much is said to be left of the war?
Soon you shall fall, conquered: Ardea, you hold out against your betters,
shameless, who force our husbands to be away.
Let them but return! But indeed mine is reckless
and rushes anywhere with drawn sword.
My mind goes, and I die, whenever the image of him fighting
comes upon me, and a cold chill holds my breast.'
She ends in tears and lets fall the stretched threads,
