and laid her face in her lap.
This itself became her: her tears, chaste, became her,
and her face was worthy of her mind and equal to it.
'Lay aside fear, I have come!' her husband says. She revived
and hung, a sweet burden, from her husband's neck.
Meanwhile the royal youth conceives the frenzied fires
and, seized by blind love, raves;
her beauty pleases, her snow-white colour and golden hair,
and the grace that was there, wrought by no art;
her words and her voice please, and that she could not be corrupted,
and the less the hope, the more he desires it.
Now the bird, herald of the light, had given its song,
when the young men bring their steps back to their camp.
That man's stunned senses are gnawed by the image of the absent one;
as he recalls her, more and more things please him:
'So she sat, so was she adorned, so she spun the threads,
so her neglected locks lay on her neck,
this face she had, these were her words to me,
this her colour, this her look, this the grace of her face.'
As after a great blast the wave is wont to grow calm,
yet from the wind that was, the wave still swells,
so, though the presence of the form he loved was gone,
the love that her present beauty had given remained.
He burns, and, goaded by the stings of unjust love,
he plots violence and guile against the unworthy bed.
'The outcome is in doubt: we will dare the utmost!' he said,
'Let her see to it! Chance and a god help the daring.
By daring we took Gabii too.' So having spoken
he girt his side with a sword and pressed his horse's back.
Bronze-gated Collatia received the youth,
the sun now preparing to hide its face.
As a guest, the foe enters the house of Collatinus:
he is kindly received; he was joined to him by blood.
How much error is in the mind! Unwitting of the matter,
the unhappy woman prepares a feast for her foes.
He had finished the feast: the hour demands sleep;
it was night, and no lights in the whole house;
he rises and frees his sword from the gilded sheath,
and comes into your chamber, chaste bride.
And when he pressed the bed, 'The steel, Lucretia, is with me,'
he said, 'and I, a king's son, am Tarquin, who speak!'
She says nothing: for she has neither voice nor strength to speak,
nor any sense of mind in her whole breast,
but trembles, as once a little lamb, caught when it has left
the fold, lies beneath a hostile wolf.
What is she to do? Fight? A woman fighting will be beaten.
Cry out? But in his right hand was a sword to forbid it.
Flee? Pressing palms bear hard upon her breast,
then for the first time touched by a stranger's hand.
The foe-lover presses on with prayers and bribes and threats;
neither by prayer nor bribe nor threats does he move her.
'You do nothing: I will take your life by a false charge,' he said;
'I, the adulterer, will be a false witness of adultery:
I will kill a slave, and say I caught you lying with him.'
The girl, overcome by fear of disgrace, gave way.
Why, victor, do you rejoice? This victory will destroy you.
Alas, how much one night cost your kingdom!
And now day had risen: she sits with disordered hair,
as a mother is wont, about to go to her son's pyre,
and calls her aged father and her faithful husband from the camp,
and both come, their delay laid aside.
And when they see her state, they ask the cause of her grief,
for whom she prepares the funeral rites, or by what ill she is stricken.
She is long silent, and ashamed hides her face
in her robe: her tears flow like an ever-running stream.
On this side father, on that husband console her tears and beg
that she tell, and they weep and fear with blind dread.
Three times she tried to speak, three times gave up, and daring a fourth
she still did not for that lift up her eyes.
'This too shall we owe to Tarquin? Shall I speak,' she says,
'shall I, unhappy, myself tell my own shame?'
And what she can, she tells; the end remained: she wept,
and her matron's cheeks blushed.
Her father and husband grant pardon for the deed forced upon her:
'The pardon you grant,' she said, 'I myself refuse.'
Without delay she pierced her breast with a hidden steel
and falls, bloodstained, at her father's feet.
Then too, even dying, she takes care that she fall decently,
this concern was hers as she fell.
Behold, over her body, lamenting their common losses,
her husband and father lie, forgetful of seemliness.
Brutus comes, and at last belies his name in spirit,
and snatches the weapon fixed in the half-living body,
and holding the knife dripping with noble blood
uttered fearless sounds with threatening mouth:
'By this brave and chaste blood I swear to you,
and by your shade, which shall be a divinity to me,
that Tarquin with his exiled stock shall pay the penalty.
Long enough now has my valour been disguised.'
She, lying there, moved her lightless eyes at the words
and seemed to approve the speech with shaken hair.
She is borne to her funeral, a matron of manly spirit,
and draws tears and hatred along with her.
The gaping wound lies open. Brutus with a cry rouses
the Quirites and tells the king's unspeakable deeds.
Tarquin flees with his offspring; the consul takes the yearly
authority: that day was the last for the kingship.

title: Fasti
text:
Are we deceived, or has the swallow come, herald of spring,
nor fears lest winter, turned back, should return?
Yet often, Procne, you will complain you hurried too much,
and your husband Tereus will be glad at your cold.
And now two nights remain of the second month,
and Mars urges his swift horses with the chariot yoked:
the name Equirria, fittingly set, has lasted,
which the god himself looks down upon in his own Field.
You come by right, Gradivus: your season demands the place,
and the month marked by your name is here.
We have come into harbour with the book and the month finished:
let my skiff now sail hence on other water.
3. Warlike Mars, lay aside your shield and spear a while,
be present, and free your shining locks from the helmet.
Perhaps you yourself may ask what a poet has to do with Mars:
from you the month I sing takes its name.
You see yourself that fierce wars are waged by Minerva's hands:
is she, for that, the less free for the liberal arts?
By Pallas's example take a time for laying aside
the spear: you will find something also to do unarmed.
Then too you were unarmed, when the Roman priestess
took you, that you might give great seed to this city.
Silvia the Vestal (for why should I not begin from there?)
was seeking water in the morning to wash the sacred things;
she had come to the bank that slopes by a gentle path:
the earthen urn is set down from the top of her head.
Weary, she sat upon the ground and took the winds with open
breast, and set her ruffled hair in order.
While she sits, the shady willows and the singing birds
brought on sleep, and the soft murmur of the water.
Sweet rest stole stealthily over her conquered eyes,
and her hand, grown languid, falls from her chin.
Mars sees her, and seeing desires, and possesses her he desired,
and hid his stealth by his divine power.
Sleep departs; she lies, heavy: for now within
her womb was the founder of the city of Rome.
Languid she rises, nor knows why she rises languid,
and, leaning on a tree, utters such words:
'May it be useful and of good omen, I pray, what in a dream's image
we have seen — or was it clearer than a dream?
I was at the Ilian fires, when, slipped from my hair,
the woollen fillet fell before the sacred hearths.
Then two palm-trees, wondrous to see, rose up together:
of these the one was the taller,
and with heavy branches had covered the whole world
and had touched the topmost stars with its foliage.
Behold, my uncle plies his sword against them:
I am terrified at the warning, and my heart throbs with fear.
A woodpecker, the bird of Mars, fights for the twin trunks
and a she-wolf: by these both palms were kept safe.'
She had spoken, and lifted the full urn with no firm
strength; she had filled it while she told her dream.
Meanwhile, as Remus grew, as Quirinus grew,
her belly was swollen with the heavenly burden.
With two signs now left for the bright god
before the year should run out its finished course,
Silvia becomes a mother. The images of Vesta are said
to have put their virgin hands before their eyes;
the goddess's altar surely trembled as her handmaid gave birth,
and the frightened flame sank down into its own ashes.
When Amulius learned this, that scorner of right
(for he held in victory the wealth seized from his brother),
he bids the twins be drowned in the river; the wave shrinks from the crime;
the boys are left upon the dry ground.
Who does not know the infants grew on the milk of a wild beast,
and that a woodpecker often brought food to the exposed ones?
Nor would I pass you in silence, Larentia, nurse of so great a race,
nor your humble service, poor Faustulus.
Your honour shall come, when I tell of the Larentalia:
December, welcome to the spirits, holds that feast.
The offspring of Mars had grown to thrice six years,
and a new beard was now beneath their golden hair;
to all the farmers and the masters of the herds
the brothers, sons of Ilia, gave justice when it was sought.
Often they come home, glad with the blood of robbers,
and drive back the rustled oxen into their own fields.
When they heard their birth, the revealing of their father lifts their spirits,
and they are ashamed to bear a name in a few huts.
Amulius falls, pierced by Romulus's sword,
and the kingdom is restored to the aged grandsire.
Walls are founded, which, however small they were,
it was yet not well for Remus to have leaped across.
Now what had lately been woods and the haunts of cattle
was a city, when the father of the eternal city said:
'Arbiter of arms, from whose blood I am believed
to be born (and, that I may be believed, I shall give many pledges),
from you we name the beginning of the Roman year:
the first month shall be from my father's name.'
The word is ratified, and he names the month from his father's name.
This piety, they say, was pleasing to the god.
And yet before all others the men of old worshipped Mars:
this the warlike crowd had given to its own pursuits.
The sons of Cecrops worship Pallas, Minoan Crete Diana,
the land of Hypsipyle worships Vulcan,
Sparta worships Juno, and Mycenae of Pelops's line,
the Maenalian country the pine-crowned head of Faunus;
Mars was to be revered by Latium, because he presides over
arms: arms gave to a fierce nation both substance and glory.
And if perhaps you have leisure, look into foreign calendars:
in these too there will be a month with the name of Mars.
It was the third with the Albans, the fifth with the Faliscans,
the sixth among your people, Hernican land.
Between the Aricians and the Alban dates it stands,
and the high walls built by Telegonus's hand.
The Laurentines have it fifth, fierce Aequiculus tenth,
the people of Cures hold it first of three;
and with you, Pelignian soldier, and your Sabine forefathers
it agrees: to each of these nations the god is fourth.
That Romulus might surpass all these at least in order,
gave the first place in time to the author of his blood.
Nor did the ancients have as many Kalends as now:
their year was shorter by two months.
Greece had not yet handed her conquered arts to her conquerors,
a race eloquent but ill-suited to war;
he who fought well had known the Roman art:
he who could throw javelins was the eloquent one.
Who then had marked the Hyades or the Atlantean Pleiades,
or that there were twin poles beneath the sky?
That there are two Bears, of which Cynosura is steered by
the Sidonians, while the Greek keel marks Helice?
That the signs which the brother surveys in a long year,
through these the sister's horses go in a single month?
The stars ran free and unobserved through the year;
yet it was agreed that there were gods.
They did not hold the signs gliding in the sky,
but their own, which it was a great crime to lose.
They had standards of hay, indeed; but there was reverence for the hay,
as much as you see your eagles have now.
A long pole carried the bundles hung upon it,
from which the common soldier (manipularis) has his name.
So minds untaught and as yet without reason
spent their lustres in less than ten months.
It was a year when the moon had taken back her tenth orb:
this number was then in great honour;
whether because so many are the fingers by which we are wont to count,
or because in the twice fifth month a woman gives birth,
or because by counting upward the increase comes as far as ten,
and from there a beginning is taken for new spans.
From there Romulus divided the fathers, a hundred at a time, into bands of ten,
and established the spearmen, ten companies;
and as many in the front rank, as many in the rear the rear-rank held,
and the same number who served on the lawful horse.
Nay more, he gave as many divisions to the Titienses,
and to those they call the Ramnes, and to the Luceres.
So he kept the accustomed numbers in the year.
For this span the mourning wife laments her husband.
And that you may not doubt that the Kalends of March were first,
to these tokens you may turn your mind:
the laurel which has stood through the whole year for the flamens
is taken down, and the new leaves are in honour;
then the king's door grows green with the planted tree of Phoebus:
the same is done before your doors, ancient senate-house.
That Vesta too may shine, veiled in fresh leaf,
the white laurel yields from the Ilian hearths;
add that a new fire is said to be made in the secret shrine,
and the renewed flame takes on strength.
Nor is it a small proof to me that the years went from here before,
because Anna Perenna began to be worshipped in this month.
Hence too the ancient honours are recorded, gently won,
up to the time of your war, treacherous Carthaginian.
In short, the fifth from this was Quintilis, and from there
begins whoever has a name from a number.
Pompilius, brought to Rome from the olive-bearing fields,
first perceived that two months were lacking,
whether taught this by the Samian, who thinks that we
can be born again, or at his own Egeria's prompting.
But yet the seasons were still going astray, until
this too was among Caesar's many cares.
That god, the author of so great a line, did not think
these things beneath his offices,
and wished to know in advance the heaven promised to him,
nor as a god to enter unknown homes a stranger.
He is said to have set in order, the records being worked out,
the delays of the sun by which it returns to its own signs.
He joined to the three hundred sixty days five more,
and a fifth part of a full day.
This is the measure of the year: to the lustrum should be added
one day, which is made up of the parts.

title: Fasti
text:
'If it is allowed to hear the hidden warnings of the gods
from poets, as fame surely thinks is allowed,
since you are fit, Gradivus, for manly offices,
tell me why the matrons keep your festival.'
So I. So Mavors, his helmet laid aside, said to me,
yet in his right hand was a throwing-spear:
'Now for the first time I, a god useful in arms,
am summoned to the pursuits of peace and bring my steps into a new camp,
nor do I regret the venture; I am glad to linger in this field too,
lest Minerva think that she alone has this power.
Learn, laborious poet of the Latin days,
what you seek, and mark my words in a mindful heart.
Rome was small, if you wish to recall her first beginnings,
yet in that small place was hope of this present greatness.
The walls already stood, too narrow for the peoples to come,
but then thought too ample for their own throng.
If you ask what the palace of my son was,
look at his house of reed and straw.
On straw he took the gifts of peaceful sleep,
and yet from that couch he came to the stars.
And now the Roman had a name greater than his place,
yet he had neither wife nor any father-in-law.
The wealthy neighbours scorned poor sons-in-law,
and I was ill believed to be the author of his blood.
It harmed him to have dwelt in stables and pastured sheep
and to hold a few acres of untilled soil.
Birds and beasts each mate with their own kind,
and the snake too has some mate from which to breed;
the right of marriage is given to the farthest nations: but no woman
was there who would wed a Roman.
I grieved, and gave you, Romulus, your father's spirit:
"Lay aside prayers," I said; "what you seek arms will give."
He prepares a feast for Consus. Consus will tell you the rest
done on that day, when you sing his rites.
Cures swelled with anger, and those whom the same grief touched:
then for the first time a father-in-law brought arms against his kin.
And now the ravished women had almost the name of mothers too,
and the kindred wars had been drawn out by long delay:
the wives gather in the temple named of Juno,
among whom my daughter-in-law dared to speak thus:
"O ravished alike (since we hold this in common),
we can no longer be slow in our piety.
The battle-lines stand; but choose for which side the gods
are to be asked: on this side a husband, on that a father holds arms.
The question is, whether you would rather be made widows or orphans:
I will give you counsel, brave and pious."
She had given counsel: they obey and loose their hair
and clothe their sad bodies in funeral garb.
Now the lines had stood, ready for the sword and for death,
now the trumpet was about to give the signal for battle:
when the ravished women come between fathers and husbands,
and hold in their bosoms their children, dear pledges.
When with streaming hair they reached the middle of the field,
they fell down on bended knee to the earth,
and, as though they understood, the grandchildren with coaxing cries
stretched their little arms to their grandfathers:
who could, cried 'grandfather' to the one then first seen,
and who scarcely could, was forced to be able.
The weapons and the spirits fall from the men, and the swords laid aside
the fathers-in-law give and take the hands of their sons-in-law,
and hold their praised daughters, and on his shield the grandfather
carries his grandchild: this was the sweeter use of the shield.
Hence the matrons of Oebalia hold it no slight task
to keep the first day, my Kalends,
either because, daring to engage with drawn swords,
they had ended the wars of Mars with their tears;
or because Ilia was happily made a mother by me,
the matrons duly keep my rites and my day.
What of this, that winter, veiled in frost, then at last yields,
and the snows, fallen, perish in the warming sun;
the leaves, shorn by the cold, return to the trees,
and the moist bud swells on the tender shoot,
and the fertile grass, which long lay hidden, now finds
hidden ways by which it may rise into the air?
Now the field is fruitful, now is the hour for breeding the flock,
now the bird on the branch makes its roof and home:
rightly do the Latin mothers keep the fruitful season,
in whose childbearing is their warfare and their vows.
Add that, where the Roman king kept his watch,
on the hill that now has the name Esquiline,
there by the Latin wives temples to Juno
were on this day, if I remember, dedicated to the public.
Why do I delay and burden your breast with various reasons?
What you seek, behold, stands plain before your eyes.
As mother I love the wives: the throng of mothers thronged about me:
this so pious cause especially befits me.'
Bring flowers to the goddess: this goddess delights in flowering
herbs: with the tender flower bind your head;
say: 'You, Lucina, gave us the light';
say: 'You are present at the vow of the woman in travail.'
Yet if any is with child, let her pray with loosened hair,
that the goddess may softly loose her labour.

title: Fasti
text:
Who will tell me now why the Salii bear the heavenly arms
of Mars and sing of Mamurius?
Instruct me, nymph who serve the grove and pool of Diana;
nymph, wife of Numa, come to recount your deeds.
In the Arician valley, girt by a shady wood,
is a lake, sacred by ancient observance.
Here Hippolytus lies hidden, torn apart by his horses' reins,
whence no horses are admitted to that grove.
Threads hang down, veiling the long hedges,
and many a tablet is set up to the deserving goddess.
Often a woman whose prayer is granted, her brow wreathed with garlands,
carries lighted torches from the city.
There the strong of hand and swift of foot hold the kingship,
and each afterward perishes by his own example.
A stony stream flows down with uncertain murmur:
often, but in scanty draughts, I have drunk from it.
Egeria it is who supplies the waters, a goddess dear to the Camenae;
she was the wife and the counsel of Numa.
At first it pleased to soften the Quirites, too prone to war,
by law and by the fear of the gods;
hence laws were given, lest the stronger should have power over all,
and rites handed down began to be kept in purity.
Wildness is put off, and right is more powerful than arms,
and it is shameful to have joined hands in strife with a fellow citizen;
and a man, just now fierce, is changed at the sight of an altar
and gives wine and salted meal to the warm hearths.
Behold, the father of the gods scatters ruddy flames through the clouds
and dries the air with the poured-out waters;
never at other times did the hurled fires fall more thickly:
the king is afraid, and terror holds the breasts of the crowd.
To him the goddess said: 'Be not too greatly terrified! The thunderbolt
can be expiated,' she said, 'and the anger of fierce Jove is bent;
but Picus and Faunus will be able to teach the rite
of expiating, both divinities of the Roman soil.
Yet they will not teach it without force: do you put bonds on them when caught.'
And so she told by what art they could be caught.
There was a grove below the Aventine, dark with the shade of ilex,
on seeing which you could say 'a divinity is within.'
In the midst was grass, and from a rock covered with green moss
flowed a perennial vein of water:
from it Faunus and Picus almost alone used to drink.
King Numa came hither and slays a sheep to the spring,
and sets out full cups of fragrant wine,
and with his own men hides himself, buried in a cave.
The woodland powers come to their accustomed springs
and relieve their dry breasts with much wine.
Rest follows the wine; Numa comes forth from the chill cave
and puts close bonds on their slumbering hands.
When sleep withdrew, they try by struggling to break
the bonds: the more strongly they struggle, the more it holds them.
Then Numa: 'Gods of the groves, pardon my deeds,
if you know that crime is absent from my nature;
and show by what means the thunderbolt can be expiated.'
So Numa; so, shaking his horns, Faunus said:
'You seek great things, nor such as it is right for you to learn
by our warning: our divinities have their limits.
We are rustic gods and such as rule over the high
mountains: over his own weapons Jove has the choice.
Him you will not be able by yourself to draw down from heaven,
but you will be able, perhaps, by using our aid.'
Faunus had said this; Picus's opinion is the same:
'Yet take the bonds from us,' Picus says;
'Jupiter will come hither, drawn down by powerful art.
The cloudy Styx shall be my witness of the promise.'
Released from the snares, what they do, what songs they say,
and by what art they drew Jove from his heavenly seat,
it is not lawful for man to know: what is granted to us
shall be sung, and what may be said by a pious poet's mouth.
They draw you down from heaven, Jupiter, whence even now
lesser men honour you and call you Elicius.
It is agreed that the tops of the Aventine wood trembled,
and the earth sank, pressed by the weight of Jove.
The king's heart throbs, and from his whole body the blood
flees, and his bristling hair stood stiff.
When his spirit returned, 'Give sure expiations,' he said,
'of the thunderbolt, king and father of the gods on high,
if with pure hands I have touched your offerings,
and if a pious tongue asks this also that is sought.'
He nodded assent to the prayer, but hid the truth in remote
riddling, and terrified the man with doubtful speech.
'Cut off a head,' he said; to whom the king: 'We will obey,'
he said; 'an onion, dug from my gardens, must be cut.'
He added, 'Of a man's':
'You shall take,' said the other, 'the hairs.'
He demands a life; to him Numa: 'Of a fish.'
He laughed and said: 'See that you settle my weapons with these,
O man not to be driven from converse with the gods.
But to you, when tomorrow's Cynthian has brought forth his whole orb,
I will give sure pledges of empire.'
He spoke, and with a mighty thunder was borne above the moved
heaven, and left Numa worshipping.
He returns glad and tells the Quirites what was done:
belief comes to his words slow and difficult.
'But surely we shall be believed,' he says, 'if the outcome
follows my words: come, hear, whoever is present, tomorrow's signs.
When the Cynthian has brought forth to the lands his whole orb,
Jupiter will give sure pledges of empire.'
They depart in doubt, and the promises seem slow,
and belief hangs on the coming day.
The earth was soft, dewed with frost in the morning:
before his king's threshold the people are present,
and he comes forth and sat in their midst on a throne of maple-wood.
Countless men stand around and keep silence.
Phoebus had risen only just at the topmost edge:
their anxious minds quake with hope and fear,
and he stood and, his head veiled with a snow-white robe,
lifted those hands now well known to the gods,
and thus he said: 'The time of the promised gift is at hand;
make good, Jupiter, the faith pledged by your words.'
While he speaks, the sun had now wholly moved its orb,
and a heavy crash came from the heavenly axis.
Thrice the god thundered without a cloud, three thunderbolts he hurled.
Believe me as I speak: wondrous things, but done, I tell.
From the mid-region the sky began to gape;
the throng with their leader lowered their eyes.
Behold, a shield, gently turned by a light breeze,
fell down; a shout went up from the people to the stars.
The man lifts the gift from the ground, a heifer first slain,
one that had given her neck to no yoke to be pressed,
and calls it 'ancile,' because it was cut away on every side,
and, search with your eyes, every angle is gone.
Then, mindful that the fate of empire stood in it,
he forms a plan of much cunning.
He bids many be made, engraved in a like shape,
that error might go before the eyes of the plotter.
Mamurius (whether more exact in character or in the smith's
art, it is hard for any to say) finished the work.
To him Numa, generous, said: 'Ask the rewards of your deed;
if my faith is known, you will ask nothing in vain.'
He had already given the Salii names called from their leaping,
and the arms, and the words to be sung to certain measures.
Then thus Mamurius: 'Let glory be given me for wages,
and let my name sound at the end of the song.'
Hence the priests pay the rewards promised
for the ancient work, and call out 'Mamurius.'
If any girl would marry, however much you both will hasten,
put it off; a small delay has great advantages.
Arms stir up battles, battle is unfitting for the married;
when they are stored away, the omen will be more apt.
On these days too the holy wife of the mitred flamen of Jove
must keep her hair uncombed.

title: Fasti
text:
When the third night of the month has stirred its fires,
one of the twin Fishes will be hidden.
For there are two: this one is nearest the south winds, that one
the north; each holds its name from the wind.
When the wife of Tithonus with saffron cheeks
begins to drop dew and brings on the season of the fifth light,
whether it is the Bear-keeper, or that lazy Bootes,
he will be plunged and flee your sight.
But the Vintager will not flee: whence this star too
draws its cause, it is a short delay to teach.
Ampelos, the unshorn, son of a satyr and a nymph,
Bacchus is said to have loved on the Ismarian ridges:
he gave him a vine hanging from the foliage of an elm,
which now has its name from the boy's name;
while reckless he plucks the bright grapes on the branch,
he fell: the lost one Liber bore to the stars.
When the sixth Phoebus climbs steep Olympus from the ocean
and cleaves the air with his winged horses,
whoever you are that worship the inner shrine of chaste Vesta,
rejoice, and set incense on the Ilian hearths.
To Caesar's numberless titles (which would he rather earn?)
the pontifical honour was added.
The divine powers of eternal Caesar preside over the eternal
fires: you see the pledges of empire joined.
Gods of ancient Troy, most worthy spoil for him who bore you,
by whom weighty Aeneas was kept safe from the foe,
a priest sprung from Aeneas touches kindred
divinities: guard, Vesta, your kinsman's head!
You fires whom that holy hand cherishes, you live well:
live unextinguished, both flame and leader, I pray.
There is one note for Mars on the Nones, because on that day they think
temples were consecrated before the two groves of Vediovis.
When Romulus surrounded the grove with a high rock,
'Whoever you are,' he said, 'flee here, you will be safe.'
O from how slender a beginning did the Roman grow!
How free from envy that ancient throng was!
Yet, lest the newness of the name baffle you in your ignorance,
learn who that god is, and why he is so called.
He is Jupiter the youth: look at his youthful face;
look then at his hand, it holds no thunderbolts.
Thunderbolts were taken up by Jove after the Giants dared
to assail the sky; in the first time he was unarmed.
With new fires Ossa, and Pelion higher than Ossa,
blazed, and Olympus fixed on the solid ground.
A she-goat too stands by: the Cretan nymphs are said
to have pastured her; she gave milk to the infant Jove.
Now I am called to the name: the country folk call spelt that has grown
ill, undersized, 'vegrandia,' and small, poor things 'vesca.'
If this is the force of the word, why may I not suppose
the shrine of Vediovis to be the shrine of no great Jove?
And now, when the stars dapple the dark-blue sky,
look up: you will see the neck of the Gorgon's horse.
He is believed to have leaped forth, when the neck of pregnant Medusa
was cut, his mane spattered with blood.
As he glided above the clouds and beneath the stars,
the sky was his earth, a wing his foot,
and now he had taken the new bit in his indignant mouth,
when his light hoof dug up the Aonian waters.
Now he enjoys the heaven which before he sought on wings,
and gleams bright with fifteen stars.
At once you will see, when night comes, the Cnossian
Crown: by Theseus's crime she was made a goddess.
Now she had happily exchanged her forsworn husband for Bacchus,
she who had given the thread to be gathered by the thankless man;
glad in her wedded lot, 'Why did I weep, a country girl?' she said;
'his faithlessness was useful to me.'
Meanwhile Liber had conquered the smooth-haired Indians
and returns rich from the eastern world;
among the captive girls of surpassing beauty
the king's daughter was too pleasing to Bacchus.
His loving wife wept, and pacing the curving shore
uttered such words with disordered hair:
'Lo, again, you waves, hear like complaints!
Lo, again, sand, receive my tears!
I said, I remember, "Forsworn and faithless Theseus!"
he went off; the same charges Bacchus has.
Now too I will cry, "Let no woman trust a man!"
my case is repeated, only the name changed.
O would that my fate had gone the way it first had begun,
and that at this present time I were no more!
Why, Liber, did you save me, doomed to die on the deserted
sands? I could have ended my grief once for all.
Bacchus, light, and lighter than the leaves that wreathe your
temples, Bacchus known to my tears,
have you dared, a rival brought before our eyes,
to disturb a bed so well composed?
Alas, where is the troth you pledged? Where the oaths you used to swear?
Wretched me, how often shall I speak these words?
You blamed Theseus and yourself called him deceiver:
by your own judgement you sin the more basely.
Let no one know this, and let me burn with silent griefs,
lest I be thought to have deserved to be so often deceived!
Above all I would have it hidden from Theseus, lest he
rejoice that you are a partner in his fault.
As I suppose, a fair rival is set before me, the dark one:
may that complexion befall my enemies!
Yet what does this matter? She is dearer to you for the very fault.
What do you do? She defiles your embrace.
Bacchus, keep faith, and prefer no woman before the love
of a wife; I have grown used always to love one man.
A handsome bull's horns captivated my mother,
yours captivated me: mine they praise, hers was a shameful love.
Let it not harm me that I love; for it did not harm you, Bacchus,
that you confessed your own flames to me.
Nor is it strange that you set us on fire: born in fire,
they say, and snatched by a father's hand from fire.
I am she to whom you used to promise heaven.
Ah me, what gifts I bear in place of heaven!'
She had spoken: Liber had long been hearing the words of her lament,
as he chanced to follow at her back.
He seizes her with an embrace and dries her tears with kisses,
and 'Together,' he said, 'let us seek the heights of heaven!
You, joined to me in marriage, shall take a name joined to mine,
for to you, transformed, the name of Libera shall belong;
and I will make that there be with you memorials of your crown,
which Vulcan gave to Venus, and she to you.'
He does as he said, and changes the nine gems into fires:
now that golden crown gleams with nine stars.

title: Fasti
text:
When he who carries the bright day on his swift axle
has lifted six orbs and sunk as many,
you will watch another Equirria on the grassy Field,
which Tiber presses on the flank with its curving waters.
Yet if perhaps it is held by the wave cast out,
the dusty Caelian will receive the horses.
On the Ides is the merry festival of Anna Perenna,
not far from your banks, you stranger Tiber.
The common folk come, and scattered here and there over the green grass
they drink, and each reclines with his own partner.
Some endure beneath the open sky, a few set up tents,
some have made a leafy hut of branches,
some, where they have set up reeds for stiff columns,
have laid their stretched-out togas above.
Yet they grow warm with sun and wine, and pray for as many years
as the cups they take, and drink to the number.
There you will find one who drinks down Nestor's years,
one who by her cups has been made a Sibyl.
There too they sing whatever they learned in the theatres,
and fling their ready hands to their own words,
and lead rough dances, the mixing-bowl set down,
and the dressed-up girl dances with her hair flung loose.
When they come home they stagger and are a spectacle for the crowd,
and the throng they meet calls them fortunate.
Lately a procession met me (it seemed worth telling):
a tipsy old woman dragged a tipsy old man.
Yet who this goddess is, since rumour goes astray,
no tale shall be hidden by my purpose.
The pitiable Dido had burned with the fire of Aeneas,
had burned on the pyre built up for her own death;
and her ashes were gathered, and on the tomb's marble was this
brief song, which she herself, dying, left:
'Aeneas furnished both the cause of death and the sword.
Dido herself fell, using her own hand.'
At once the Numidians invade the kingdom without a defender,
and the Moor Iarbas takes possession of the captured palace,
and, mindful that he was scorned, 'Behold,' he said, 'in Elissa's
chamber, I, whom she so often repulsed, hold sway.'
The Tyrians scatter, as wandering error drives each, as once
the bees, their king lost, stray in doubt.
The third threshing-floor had received the grain to be laid bare,
and into the hollow vats the third new wine had gone:
Anna is driven from her home and weeping leaves the walls
of her sister: first she gives the due rites to her sister.
The soft ashes drink unguents mixed with tears,
and receive the locks offered from her head;
and 'thrice farewell!' she said, and thrice pressed the ashes
brought to her lips, and to her the sister seemed to be present.
Having got a ship and companions for her flight, she glides on an even keel,
looking back at the walls, her sister's sweet work.
Fertile Melite, the island neighbour to barren Cosyra,
which the wave of the Libyan strait beats,
she seeks, trusting in the old friendship of its king:
King Battus, rich in wealth, was a host there.
When he had learned the misfortunes of each sister,
'This land,' he said, 'however small, is yours.'
And he would have kept the gift of hospitality to the last,
but he feared the great power of Pygmalion.
Twice the sun had counted over his signs; a third year
was passing, and a new land must be sought for exile.
Her brother comes and seeks her with war. The king, hating arms,
'We are unwarlike,' he said, 'do you flee unharmed!'
At his bidding she flees, and commits her ship to wind and waves:
her brother was harsher than any sea.
There is, near the fishy streams of stony Crathis,
a little field: the dwelling folk call it Camere.
Thither was her course, nor was it farther off from there
than a sling can cast nine times.
The sails fall at first and waver from the uncertain breeze.
'Cleave the waters,' the sailor said, 'with the oar!'
And while they prepare to take in the canvas with twisted line,
the curved stern is struck by the swift south wind,
and into the open sea, the master struggling in vain,
it is borne, and the land seen flees from their eyes.
The waves leap up, and from the lowest depth the sea
is churned, and the hull swallows the white waters.
Skill is conquered by the wind, nor does the steersman now
use the reins; he too asks for help by vows.
The Phoenician exile is tossed through the swollen waves
and covers her wet eyes with the robe held before them:
then for the first time Dido was called happy by her sister,
and any woman who has pressed some ground with her body.
The ship is driven by a mighty blast upon the Laurentine
shore, and, all being put off, swallowed up it perishes.
Now dutiful Aeneas had been enriched with the kingdom and the daughter
of Latinus, and had mingled the two peoples.
Accompanied only by Achates, on the dowry-shore,
while with bare foot he takes a lonely path,
he sees Anna wandering, nor can he bring himself to believe
it is she: why should she come into the Latin fields?
While Aeneas thinks thus to himself, 'It is Anna!' cries Achates:
at the name she lifted up her face.
Alas! should she flee? what should she do? what gaping of the earth should she seek?
Before her eyes was her wretched sister's fate.
The hero, son of Cytherea, perceived and addresses the trembling woman
(yet he was moved at the reminder of you, Elissa):
'Anna, by this land I swear, which once you used to hear
was given me by a more prosperous fate,
and by the gods, my companions, lately settled in this seat,
that they often chid me for my delays,
yet I did not fear for her death; that dread was absent.
Ah me! she was braver than I could believe.
Do not recall it: I saw wounds unworthy of that body,
when I dared to enter the Tartarean homes.
But you, whether reason has driven you to our shores
or a god, enjoy the comforts of my kingdom.
Many things, mindful, we owe to you, nothing not to Elissa:
you shall be welcome for your own name, welcome for your sister's.'
To him so speaking (for no other hope remained)
she gave belief, and told her wanderings.
And when she entered the house, clad in Tyrian array,
Aeneas begins (the rest of the throng is silent):
'I have a pious cause why I give her to you, Lavinia my wife:
a castaway, I lived on her wealth.
She was born in Tyre, possessed a kingdom on the Libyan shore;
I pray you love her as a dear sister.'
Lavinia promises all, but the false wound
she presses in her silent mind and, fuming, conceals it;
and when she sees many gifts borne openly before her eyes,
she thinks many are sent in secret too;
she has not decided what to do; with fury she hates,
and prepares a plot, and longs to die avenged.
It was night: before the bed her sister seemed to stand,
Dido, bloodstained, with squalid hair,
and 'Flee, do not doubt, flee the mournful house!' to say;
at the word a breeze pushed the creaking doors.
She leaps up and swift through the low window over the fields
she throws herself: fear itself had made her bold.
And where dread carries her, veiled in her ungirt tunic,
she runs, as a doe terrified at the sound of wolves.
Horned Numicius is believed to have carried her off in his swollen waves
and hidden her in his pools.
Meanwhile the Sidonian woman is sought with great clamour
through the fields: the signs and marks of feet appear:
they had come to the banks: there were footprints on the banks.
The knowing river held its silent waters.
She herself seemed to speak: 'I am the nymph of the calm Numicius:
hidden in a perennial stream, I am called Anna Perenna.'
At once they feast, glad, in the fields where they had strayed,
and celebrate themselves and the day with abundant wine.
Some hold that she is the Moon, because she fills the year with months;
some think she is Themis, some the Inachian heifer.
You will find those who call you a nymph, daughter of Atlas,
and say you, Anna, gave the first food to Jove.
This tale too, which I shall tell, has come to our ears,
nor does it depart from the trust of truth.
The old commons, not yet safe even then under tribunes,
had fled and were on the crest of the Sacred Mount;
already too the food they had brought with them had failed,
and the bread fit for human use.
There was a certain Anna, born at suburban Bovillae,
poor, but an old woman of much diligence.
She, her grey hair bound in a light cap,
kept shaping rustic cakes with trembling hand,
and so among the people, while they smoked, in the morning was wont
to share them out: this supply was welcome to the people.
When peace was made at home, they set up a statue of Perenna,
because she had brought help to them in their need.
Now it remains for me to tell why the girls
sing obscene songs; for they gather and sing certain abuse.
She had lately been made a goddess: Gradivus came to Anna
and, drawing her aside, makes such words:
'In my month you are worshipped, I have joined my season to yours:
on your service hangs a great hope of mine.
I, the arm-bearer, smitten with love of arm-bearing Minerva,
burn, and this wound I nurse a long time.
Bring it about that we, gods alike in pursuits, be joined in one:
these parts befit you, a kindly old woman.'
He had spoken; she mocks the god with an empty promise
and draws on his foolish hope with doubtful delay.
Often, as he pressed, 'I have done your bidding,' she said,
'she is won over, she scarcely gave her hands to my prayers.'
The lover believes and prepares a chamber; thither Anna is led,
veiling her face like a new bride.
About to take kisses, Mars suddenly sees Anna:
now shame, now anger steals upon the deluded god.
The new goddess laughs at the lover of dear Minerva,
nor was any matter more pleasing to Venus than this.
Hence the old jests and obscene words are sung,
and it pleases that she tricked the great god.

title: Fasti
text:
I was about to pass over the swords driven into the prince,
when Vesta spoke thus from her chaste hearths:
'Do not hesitate to remember: he was my priest;
sacrilegious hands sought me with their weapons.
I myself snatched away the man and left a bare likeness:
what fell by the sword was Caesar's shade.'
He, indeed, set in heaven, saw Jove's halls
and holds a temple dedicated in the great forum.
But all who dared the crime, against the forbidding power
of the gods, and had polluted the pontifical head,
lie in deserved death; be witnesses, Philippi,
and you whose scattered bones whiten the ground.
This was the work, this the piety, these the first beginnings
of Caesar: to avenge his father by lawful arms.
When the next dawn has refreshed the tender grasses,
the Scorpion will be visible from his foremost part.
The third light after the Ides is most thronged for Bacchus:
Bacchus, favour your poet, while I sing your festival.
Nor will I tell of Semele, to whom, unless Jupiter had brought
his thunderbolts with him, you would have been a small, defenceless thing;
nor how, that you might be born a boy at the ripe time,
your mother's task was completed in your father's body.
It would be long to tell of the Sithonian and Scythian triumphs,
and the nations you tamed, incense-bearing Indian.
You too shall be told of, the ill prey of the Theban mother,
and you, Lycurgus, driven by furies upon your own knee.
Behold, I would gladly tell of the sudden fishes and the Tyrrhenian
monsters, but it is not the task of this song;
the task of this song is to set forth the reasons why
a worthless old woman calls the people to her cakes.
Before your birth the altars were without honour,
Liber, and grass was found on the chilly hearths.
You are said, when the Ganges and all the East were subdued,
to have set apart the first-fruits for great Jove.
You first gave cinnamon and captive frankincense
and the roasted entrails of a vanquished ox.
From the founder's name the libations take their name,
and the cakes (liba), because a part of them is given to the holy hearths.
Cakes are made for the god, because he likewise delights in sweet
juices, and they say honey was discovered by Bacchus.
He was going, attended by satyrs, from sandy Hebrus
(my tale has no ungracious jests),
and now he had come to Rhodope and flowery Pangaeus:
the bronze-clashing hands of his companions clanged.
Behold, new winged creatures gather, driven by the ringing,
and the bees follow the sounds that the bronze makes.
Liber collects the wanderers and shuts them in a hollow tree
and has the reward of the honey he found.
When the satyrs and the smooth old man had tasted the savour,
they sought the yellow combs through all the grove.
The old man hears the hum of a swarm in a hollow elm,
sees the wax, and feigns not to.
And as he sat idly on the back of the swaybacked ass,
he brings it up to the elm and its hollow bark,
he himself took his stand, leaning on a branching stake,
and greedily seeks the honey stored in the trunk.
Thousands of hornets gather and on his bare crown
fix their stings and mark his snub face.
He falls headlong and is struck by the ass's heel,
and calls his own and asks for help.
The satyrs run together and laugh at the swollen face
of their father: he limps with his struck knee.
The god himself laughs and shows him to smear on mud;
he obeys the advice and smears his face with clay.
The father enjoys the honey, and rightly, poured on the warm cake,
we give white honey to the discoverer.
Why a woman presses it is no hidden reason:
he stirs the female bands with his thyrsus.
Why an old woman does this, you ask? That age is more given
to wine and loves the gifts of the laden vine.
Why is she wreathed with ivy? The ivy is most dear to Bacchus:
why this too is so, there is no delay in telling.
They say the Nysaean nymphs, when the stepmother sought the boy,
set this foliage before his cradle.
It remains for me to find why the free toga is given
to boys on your Morning-star, bright Bacchus:
whether because you yourself seem ever a boy and a youth,
and your age is midway between the two;
or because you are a father, and fathers commend their pledges, their sons,
to your care and to your divine power;
or because you are Liber, and so the free (libera) garment too
is taken through you, and the path of a freer life;
or because, when the ancients tilled their fields more zealously,
and the senator did work on his father's land,
and the consul took the rods from the curved plough,
and it was no reproach to have hard hands,
the country people came to the games in the city
(but the honour was given to the gods, not to amusements:
the discoverer of the grape held his games on his own day,
which now he holds with the torch-bearing goddess):
so, that a throng might attend to celebrate the recruit,
the day seemed not unfitting for giving the toga?
Turn hither, father, your gentle head and your appeased horns,
and give favouring sails to my talent.

title: Fasti
text:
To the Argei it is gone (who they are, their own page shall tell)
on this day, if I remember rightly, and the day before.
The Kite-star slopes, declining, toward the Lycaonian Bear:
this comes to be seen on that night.
What gave the bird a place in heaven, if you wish to know:
Saturn had been driven from his kingdom by Jove;
in anger he stirs the strong Titans to arms,
and tries the help that was due to him by the fates.
There was a bull, born of mother Earth, a wondrous monster,
which in its hinder part was a serpent:
this, by warning of the three Fates, fierce Styx had shut up
with a triple wall in the dark groves.
There was an oracle that whoever should give the bull's entrails
to be burned in the flames could conquer the eternal gods.
Briareus slays it with an axe made of adamant,
and was now, now about to give the entrails to the flames:
Jupiter bids the birds snatch them; the kite brought them to him
and came into the stars by his deserts.
One day is in the middle, and the rites of Minerva are held,
which have their name from the five joined days.
The first is free of blood, nor is it right to clash with steel:
the cause is that Minerva was born on that day.
The next and the three after are kept on the strewn sand:
the warlike goddess delights in drawn swords.
Now pray to Pallas, boys and tender girls:
whoever has well appeased Pallas will be learned.
Pallas appeased, let the girls learn to soften the wool
and to unload the full distaffs.
She also teaches to run the shuttle over the standing webs
and packs the loose work close with the comb.
Worship her, you who take stains from damaged garments,
worship her, whoever prepares the bronze vats for fleeces;
nor will anyone make the sandal-thongs well against Pallas's
will, though he be more skilled than Tychius;
and though, compared in his hands to ancient Epeus,
he be the better, with Pallas angry he will remain helpless.
You too who drive away diseases by Phoebus's art,
bring a few gifts of your own to the goddess;
nor do you, you teachers, a crew often defrauded of pay,
scorn her; she draws new pupils on:
you too who work the burin and burn the panel with colours,
and you who make soft stones with skilled hand.
A goddess of a thousand works is she: surely she is the goddess of song;
if I deserve it, may she be a friend to my pursuits.
Where the Caelian hill descends from its height to the level,
here, where the road is not flat, but nearly flat,
you may see the small shrine of Minerva Capta,
which the goddess began to have on her birthday.
The cause of the name is in doubt. We call clever
genius 'capital': the goddess is full of genius.
Or because she is said to have leaped forth without a mother
from the crown of her father's head, with her shield?
Or because she came to us captive (capta), the Faliscans subdued?
This very thing an ancient inscription teaches.
Or because she has a law which bids that thefts found in that place
pay penalties with their heads (capitis)?
From whatever reason you draw the name, Pallas,
ever hold your aegis before our leaders.
The last of the five days warns to purify the tuneful trumpets
and to sacrifice to the brave goddess.
Now you may say, your face lifted toward the sun:
'Here yesterday he pressed the fleece of the Phrixean ewe.'
By the crime of a wicked stepmother the seeds were roasted,
and the corn, as it does, put forth no blades.
One is sent to the tripods, to bring back a sure response,
what aid the Delphic god might grant to the barren land.
He too, corrupted like the seed, reports that the death
of Helle and of young Phrixus is asked by the oracle;
and when the citizens and the time and Ino
compelled the unwilling king to suffer the unspeakable command,
both the sister and Phrixus, their temples veiled with fillets,
stand together before the altars and bewail their joined fates.
Their mother, as she chanced to be hanging in the air, sees them
and strikes her bare breast with stunned hand,
and into the dragon-born city, with clouds attending,
she leaps down and there snatches away her children;
and that they may take flight, a ram, most gleaming with gold,
is given: he bears the two over the long straits.
The girl is said to have held the horn with weak left hand,
when she gave her name to the water from herself.
Almost at the same time her brother perished, while he would help her as she slipped,
and stretches out his hands as far as he can,
he wept that he had lost the partner of their twin peril,
not knowing she was joined to the sea-blue god.
The shores reached, the ram becomes a constellation, but his
golden fleece came to the Colchian homes.

title: Fasti
text:
When the coming Dawn has sent before her three Morning-stars,
you will keep the daylight hours equal to the nights.
Then four times when the shepherd has shut up his sated kids,
four times when the grasses have whitened with fresh dew,
Janus must be adored, and with him gentle Concord
and Roman Safety and the altar of Peace.
The Moon rules the months: the season of this month too
the Moon ends, to be worshipped on the Aventine ridge.
4. "Kind mother of the twin Loves, smile on me," I said.
She turned her face toward the poet
and asked, "What do you want with me? Surely you were singing of greater things.
Do you carry some old wound in your soft heart?"
"You know, goddess," I answered, "about the wound." She laughed, and at once
the sky on that side cleared and was serene.
"Wounded or whole, have I ever deserted your standards?
You are always my theme, you always my work.
What was fitting I played at without blame in my early years;
now a larger field is worked by my horses:
I sing the seasons with their causes, dug from ancient annals,
and the constellations that sink below the earth and rise.
We have come to the fourth month, in which you are most honoured:
you know, Venus, that both the poet and the month are yours."
Moved, she lightly touched my brow with Cytherean myrtle
and said, "Finish the work you have begun."
I felt it, and at once the reasons of the days lay open:
while it is allowed and the breezes blow, let the ship sail on.
If any part of the calendar should touch you, however,
Caesar, in April you have what claims you.
This month comes down to you with a great lineage
and becomes yours by the nobility of adoption.
The father of the Iliad saw this, when he set down the long year,
and named his own ancestors:
and as he gave fierce Mars first place in the order,
since Mars was the nearest cause of his own birth,
so he wished Venus, found many degrees back in his line,
to hold the place of the second month;
and seeking the origin of his race and the rolling
ages, he came at last to the gods, his kin.
Could he not know that Dardanus was born of Electra, Atlas' daughter,
that Electra had lain with Jove?
From him came Erichthonius; Tros was begotten of him;
he fathered Assaracus, and Assaracus Capys.
Next was Anchises, with whom Venus did not disdain
to share the name of parent.
From him sprang Aeneas, whose piety was proved, who through the fires
bore on his shoulders the sacred things and his father, another sacred thing.
At last we come to the auspicious name of Iulus,
through whom the Julian house touches its Trojan forebears.
From him came Postumus, who, because he was born deep in the woods,
was called Silvius among the Latin people.
He, Latinus, is your father. Alba follows Latinus:
next after you, Alba, in the records is Epytus.
He gave to Capys the renewed name of Troy,
and the same man, Calpetus, became your grandfather.
And when Tiberinus held his father's kingdom after him,
he is said to have drowned in the swirling waters of the Tuscan stream.
Yet he had already seen Agrippa his son and Remulus his grandson:
they say lightning was hurled at Remulus.
After these came Aventinus, from whom the place takes its name,
and the hill as well; after him the kingdom passed to Proca.
He is followed by Numitor, brother of harsh Amulius.
Ilia and Lausus were the children of Numitor.
Lausus falls by his uncle's sword; Ilia pleases Mars,
and bears you, Quirinus, joined with your twin Remus.
He always called Venus and Mars his parents,
and earned the right to have his word believed;
and so that the descendants to come could not fail to know it,
he gave the seasons of his race in unbroken succession.
But I judge that the month of Venus was named in the Greek tongue:
the goddess took her name from the foam of the sea.
Do not be surprised that the thing is called by a Greek name;
for the land of Italy was Greater Greece.
Evander had come with his whole company of ships;
Alcides had come, both of them Greek by birth
(the club-bearer pastured his herd on the Aventine grass,
and Albula's water was drunk by so great a god);
the Neritian leader came too; the Laestrygonians stand as witnesses,
and the shore that still bears the name of Circe,
and already the walls of Telegonus, already those of well-watered Tibur
stood, founded by Argive hands.
Halesus came, driven on by the fates of the son of Atreus,
from whom the Faliscan land thinks itself named.
Add Antenor, who urged the Trojans to make peace,
and the son of Oeneus, your son-in-law, Daunus of Apulia.
Late, after the Trojan flames and after Antenor,
Aeneas brought his gods to our country.
One of his companions was Solymus, from Phrygian Ida,
from whom the walls of Sulmo take their name,
Sulmo the cool, my native town, Germanicus.
Wretched me, how far it lies from the Scythian soil!
So am I so far away—but check your complaints, my Muse!
You must not sing the sacred rites with a mournful lyre.
Where does envy not reach? There are those who would rob you, Venus,
of the honour of the month, and grudge it to you.
For because spring then opens all things, and the thick
harshness of the cold gives way, and the teeming earth lies open,
they say April was named from the time of opening,
which gentle Venus claims, laying her hand on it.
She indeed most worthily governs the whole world;
she holds a realm no less than any god's,
and gives laws to heaven, to earth, to the waters of her birth,
and through her comings preserves every kind alive.
She created all the gods (it would be long to count them);
she gave to crops and trees their causes;
she gathered the rude minds of men into one
and taught each to be joined with his own mate.
What creates all the race of birds, if not coaxing pleasure?
Nor would the flocks couple, if light love were absent.
The savage ram fights with his horn against another ram,
yet he spares the brow of the ewe he loves.
The bull, laying his fierceness aside, follows the heifer,
the bull at whom all the woods, all the grove, tremble.
The same power preserves whatever lives beneath the broad sea
and fills the waters with countless fish.
This power first stripped from man his savage manner; from her
came refinement and the neat care of oneself.
The first lover, they say, sang a song wakeful through a night denied,
serenading before the closed doors,
and eloquence was the means of softening the hard girl,
and each man was made fluent for his own cause.
A thousand arts were set in motion by her; in the eagerness to please,
much that lay hidden before, they say, was found.
Would anyone dare to strip this goddess of the title
of the second month? Far from us be that madness.
What of this, that though everywhere powerful and enriched with thronging temples,
yet the goddess holds a greater right in our city?
For your Troy, Roman, Venus bore arms,
when she groaned, her tender hand grazed by a spear-point;
and by a Trojan's judgement she defeated two of the heavenly goddesses
(ah, I would not have the conquered goddesses remember this!);
and she was called the daughter-in-law of Assaracus, so that one day
great Caesar might have the line of Iulus for his forebears.
No season was ever more fitting for Venus than spring:
in spring the lands gleam, in spring the soil is soft,
now the grasses lift their tips through the broken earth,
now the vine-shoot puts out buds on the swelling bark.
And lovely Venus is worthy of the lovely season,
and, as always, she is set beside her Mars:
in spring she warns the curved ships to go out
over the maternal seas and fear no longer the winter's threats.

title: Fasti
text:
Worship the goddess rightly, you matrons and brides of Latium,
and you who lack the fillet and the long robe.
Take the golden chains from her marble neck,
take away her riches: the whole goddess must be bathed.
Restore the golden chains to her neck when it is dry;
now other flowers must be given her, now a fresh rose.
She herself bids you too to bathe beneath the green myrtle:
and the reason why she bids it (learn it!) is sure.
Naked on the shore she was drying her dripping hair:
the satyrs, a wanton crowd, saw the goddess.
She felt it, and screened her body with myrtle set before her:
she was safe by doing so, and she bids you do the same.
Learn now why you offer incense to Manly Fortune
in the place that is warm with hot water.
That place receives all women with their garments laid aside
and sees every flaw of the naked body;
so that Manly Fortune may hide and conceal this from the men,
she grants it, and does so when asked with a little incense.
And do not be reluctant to take poppy ground with snow-white milk
and the honey pressed from the clear combs;
when Venus was first led to her eager husband,
she drank this: from that time she was a bride.
Appease the goddess with words of supplication: under her care
remain both beauty and good behaviour and good name.
In our forefathers' day Rome lapsed from chastity:
you consulted, men of old, the Cumaean crone.
She bids a temple be made for Venus, and when it was duly built,
from this Venus holds her name from the turned heart.
Always, fairest, look back with a kindly face upon the sons of Aeneas,
and guard, goddess, your many brides.
While I speak, dreaded with the point of his raised tail,
Scorpio plunges into the green waters.
When the night has passed, and the sky has begun
to redden with the first light, and the dew-touched birds complain,
and the traveller who has watched through the night sets down
his half-burnt torch, and the countryman goes to his usual work,
the Pleiades will begin to ease their father's shoulders,
they who are called seven, yet are commonly six:
whether because six of them came into the embrace of gods
(for they say Sterope lay with Mars,
Alcyone with Neptune, and you, lovely Celaeno,
Maia and Electra and Taygete with Jove);
the seventh, Merope, married a mortal, you, Sisyphus;
she repents, and alone hides for shame of the deed:
or because Electra could not bear to look on the ruin
of Troy, and set her hand before her eyes.
Let the sky turn three times on its unceasing axle,
let Titan three times yoke and three times unyoke his horses,
and at once the Berecyntian flute with its curved horn
will blow, and the festival of the Idaean Mother will come.
Her half-male priests will go and beat the hollow drums,
and bronze struck on bronze will give its clashing notes;
seated, she herself will be borne on the soft necks of her attendants,
howled along through the middle of the city's streets.
The stage resounds, the games call: look on, Quirites,
and let the courts, contentious with their own Mars, be empty.
I would gladly ask many things, but the sound of the shrill bronze
frightens me and the curved flute with its dreadful tone.
"Grant me, goddess, someone whom I may question." Cybele's
learned granddaughters she saw, and bade them attend to my care.
"Mindful of your charge, nurslings of Helicon, make plain
why the Great Goddess delights in ceaseless sound."
So I; and so Erato (the Cytherean month fell to her,
because she holds the name of tender love):
"This lot was given to Saturn: 'Best of kings,
you will be cast from your sceptre by a son.'
Fearing it, he devoured his offspring as each was born,
and held them sunk within his belly.
Often Rhea complained, so often fertile yet never
a mother, and grieved at her own fruitfulness.
Jove was born (the great witness of antiquity
is believed; do not lightly disturb the accepted faith):
a stone wrapped in cloth went down the heavenly throat;
so the father was destined to be deceived by the fates.
Long now steep Ida resounds with clashing,
so that the child may cry safely with his infant mouth.
Some beat shields with staves, some beat empty helmets:
this is the task of the Curetes, this of the Corybantes.
The thing was hidden; and the imitations of the old deed remain;
the goddess's attendants strike the bronze and the harsh hides,
they beat cymbals instead of helmets, drums instead of shields;
the flute gives the Phrygian measures, as it gave of old."
She had ceased. I began: "Why do the fierce race of lions
offer their unaccustomed manes to her curved yoke?"
I had ceased. She began: "Their wildness is believed
to have been softened by her; she proves it by her car."
"But why is her head burdened with a turreted crown?
Did she give towers to the first cities?"
She nodded. "Where," I said, "did the impulse come from to cut
their own limbs?" When I was silent, the Muse began to speak:
"A Phrygian boy in the woods, beautiful to look upon, Attis,
bound the turret-bearing goddess to him with a chaste love.
She wished to keep him for herself, to guard her temple,
and said, 'See that you wish to remain a boy forever.'
He gave his pledge to her commands, and said, 'If I lie,
let the love by which I deceive you be my last.'
He deceives her, and ceases to be what he was, in the nymph
Sagaritis: from this the goddess's anger exacts its penalty.
She cut down the Naiad by wounds made in her tree;
the Naiad perished: the tree was the fate of the Naiad.
He goes mad, and believing the roof of his chamber falling,
he flees and in his course makes for the heights of Dindymus,
and now he cries, 'Take away the torches! now remove the whips!'
often he swears the Palaestinian goddesses are present.
He even mangled his body with a sharp stone,
and his long hair was dragged in the filthy dust,
and his cry was, 'I have deserved it! I pay the just penalty in blood.
Ah, let the parts perish that have harmed me!
Ah, let them perish,' he was still saying, and he takes away the weight of his groin,
and suddenly no signs were left of his manhood.
This madness became a model, and the soft ministers
cut their worthless members, tossing their hair."
With such words the eloquent voice of the Aonian Muse
gave back to me the cause of the madness I had asked.
"This too, my work's guide, I pray you teach: from where was she
fetched and brought? Or was she always in our city?"
"The Mother always loved Dindymus and Cybele and Ida
lovely with its springs, and the wealth of Ilium:
when Aeneas was bringing Troy into the Italian fields,
the goddess almost followed the ships that bore the sacred things,
but she felt that the fates did not yet ask her divinity
for Latium, and she stayed in her accustomed places.
Afterwards, when mighty Rome had now seen five
ages of her power, and raised her head over a conquered world,
the priest examined the fateful words of the Euboean song;
they say what he examined was such as this:
'The Mother is absent: Roman, I bid you seek the Mother.
When she comes, she must be received by a chaste hand.'
The fathers wander in the riddles of the dark oracle,
which parent was absent, and in what place she was to be sought.
Paean is consulted: 'Summon the Mother of the gods,'
he said, 'she is to be found on the Idaean ridge.'
The nobles are sent. Attalus then held the Phrygian
sceptre: he refuses the thing to the men of Ausonia.
I shall sing a marvel: the earth trembled with a long rumbling,
and thus the goddess spoke from her inner shrine:
'I myself wished to be sought; let there be no delay; send me willing.
Rome is a place worthy that every god should go there.'
Trembling in fear at the terror of the sound, he said, 'Set out,
you shall be ours: Rome traces back her line to Phrygian forebears.'
At once the countless axes cut down the pine-woods,
those that the pious Phrygian had used in his flight:
a thousand hands join, and a hollow ship, painted
with burnt colours, holds the Mother of the gods.
She is carried most safely through the waters of her own son
and reaches the long pools of the Phrixean sister;
she passes ravenous Rhoeteum and the Sigean shores
and Tenedos and the old wealth of Eetion.
The Cyclades receive her, Lesbos left behind,
and the wave that breaks on the Carystian shallows.
She crosses too the Icarian sea, where Icarus lost
his fallen wings and gave his name to the vast water.
Then leaving Crete on the left, the Pelopid waters on the right,
she makes for Cythera, sacred to Venus.
From here the Trinacrian sea, where Brontes and Steropes
and the son of Acmon are wont to dip the glowing iron,
and she skirts the African waters, looks back on the Sardinian
realms from the left of her oars, and reaches Ausonia.
She had reached Ostia, where Tiber divides himself
into the deep and swims in a freer plain:
all the knights and the grave senate, mingled with the common folk,
came to meet her at the mouth of the Tuscan river.
Mothers and daughters and brides advance together,
and those who tend the holy hearths with their virginity.
The men weary their arms with the taut rope:
the foreign ship scarcely makes its way against the waters,
the land had long been dry, thirst had scorched the grass:
the keel sat fast, pressed into the muddy shallows.
Everyone who is there toils more than his share,
and helps the strong hands with a ringing voice.
She sits there like an island fixed in the middle of the sea:
the men, struck by the marvel, stand and are afraid.
Claudia Quinta traced her descent from high Clausus,
nor was her beauty unequal to her nobility:
chaste indeed, but not believed so; an unjust rumour
had wronged her, and she was charged with a false crime;
her elegance and her habit of going out with varied hairstyles
had counted against her, and her ready tongue against the stern old men.
Her mind, conscious of the right, laughed at the lies of rumour,
but we are a crowd ready to believe in fault.
When she had come forward from the line of chaste matrons
and drawn the river's pure water in her hands,
three times she sprinkles her head, three times lifts her palms to the sky
(all who look on think she has lost her wits),
and bending her knee she fixes her eyes on the goddess's image
and, her hair loose, utters these words:
"Kind and fruitful mother of the gods, receive
the prayers of your suppliant on one sure condition.
They deny that I am chaste. If you condemn me, I shall confess I deserved it;
beaten, with a goddess for judge, I shall pay the penalty with death.
But if the charge is false, you will give a pledge of my innocence
by the deed, and, chaste yourself, follow my chaste hands."
She spoke, and with a slight effort drew the rope
(a marvel, but the stage attests what I tell):
the goddess is moved and follows her leader, and praises her by following:
the sound that signals joy is carried to the stars.
They come to the bend of the river (the ancients called it
the Halls of Tiber), where it turns away to the left.
Night was at hand: they fasten the rope to an oaken stump
and give their bodies, fed lightly, to easy sleep.
Day was at hand: they loose the rope from the oaken stump;
but first they set down a hearth and offered incense,
first they garlanded the stern and sacrificed a heifer
without blemish, untried by toil or by mating.
There is a place where the gliding Almo flows into the Tiber
and the lesser stream loses its name in the great river:
there a hoary priest in purple robe washed the Mistress
and her sacred things in the waters of Almo.
Her attendants howl, the frenzied flute is blown,
and soft hands strike the leather of the drums.
Claudia walks in front, renowned with a joyful face,
her chastity at last believed on a goddess's witness;
the goddess herself, seated on a wagon, was carried in through the Capene gate:
the yoked oxen are sprinkled with fresh flowers.
Nasica received her: the founder of the temple did not survive;
now Augustus is, before him Metellus was."
Here Erato paused; there is a delay; so I ask the rest:
"Tell me," I say, "why she seeks her wealth with a small coin."
"The people contributed the bronze from which Metellus
built the shrine," she says; "from there remains the custom of giving the coin."
"Why do they hold banquets by turns," I ask,
"and then most of all celebrate uninvited feasts?"
"Because the Berecyntian goddess changed her seat with good fortune,"
she said; "by changing seats they catch the same omen."
I had pressed on to ask why the Megalesian games were the first
in our city, when the goddess (for she perceived it)
said, "She gave birth to the gods; they yielded to their parent,
and the Mother holds the privilege of the honour granted first."
"Why then do we call those who castrate themselves Galli,
since the Gallic land lies so far from Phrygia?"
"Between green Cybele and lofty Celaenae," she says,
"flows a river of mad water, Gallus by name.
Whoever drinks of it goes mad: stay far away, you who have
any care for a sound mind: whoever drinks of it goes mad."
"I am not ashamed," I said, "that a dish of herbs is set
on the Mistress's tables: or is there a reason of its own?"
"The men of old, they tell, used pure milk and herbs
that the earth bore of its own accord," she says.
"White cheese is mixed with the pounded herb,
so that the ancient goddess may know the ancient foods."

title: Fasti
text:
When, after her stars have moved across the sky, the daughter of Pallas
has shone, and the Moon has lifted her snowy horses,
whoever says, "On this day in the past, on the hill of Quirinus,
Public Fortune was hallowed," will speak the truth.
It was the third day of the games (I remember), and a certain
older man, sitting next to me as I watched,
said this: "That was the day on which Caesar, on the Libyan shores,
crushed the treacherous arms of great-souled Juba.
Caesar was my leader, under whom I am proud to have served
as tribune: he presided over my service.
This seat I won by soldiering, you in peace,
through the office held among the board of ten."
We were about to say more, when we were suddenly parted by a shower:
the hanging Scales were stirring the waters of heaven.
Yet before the final day brings the spectacles to a close,
sword-bearing Orion will be sunk in the sea.
When next the Dawn looks upon victorious Rome,
and the routed star has yielded its place to Phoebus,
the Circus will be crowded with the procession and the throng of gods,
and the first palm will be sought by the wind-swift horses.
Now come the games of Ceres. There is no need to point out the cause;
the goddess's gift and her merit are plain of themselves.
The bread of the first mortals was the green grasses
that the earth gave with none to coax it;
and now they plucked the living turf from the sod,
now the tip of tender foliage was their banquet,
later the acorn was born: it was well, the acorn once found,
and the hard oak held magnificent wealth.
Ceres first called man to better nourishment
and changed acorns for a more useful food.
She forced the bulls to offer their necks to the yoke:
then for the first time the upturned soil saw the sun.
Bronze was prized, the iron ore lay hidden:
alas, it ought to have been hidden forever.
Ceres rejoices in peace; and you, farmers, pray
for unending peace and a peace-making leader.
You may give the goddess spelt and the honour of the leaping
grain of salt, and grains of incense on the ancient hearths;
and if incense is lacking, light resinous torches:
small offerings please good Ceres, if only they be pure.
You ministers, gird up your robes and take the knives from the ox:
let the ox plough; sacrifice the idle sow.
The neck fit for the yoke is not to be struck by the axe:
let the ox live and often labour in the hard ground.
The place itself requires that I tell the rape of the maiden:
much you will recognize, in a few things you will be taught.
The Trinacrian land runs out into the vast sea with three crags,
having taken its name from the lay of the place,
a home dear to Ceres; she possesses many cities,
among them Henna, fertile with its cultivated soil.
Cool Arethusa had summoned the mothers of the gods:
the golden goddess too had come to the sacred feast.
Her daughter, attended as ever by her usual girls,
was wandering barefoot through her own meadows.
In a shady valley there is a place wet with much spray
from the water leaping down from on high.
There were as many colours there as nature holds,
and the ground gleamed, painted with varied flowers.
As soon as she saw it she said, "Come, my companions,
and bring back with me your laps full of flowers."
The empty prize lures their girlish hearts,
and in their busyness the toil is not felt.
This one fills baskets woven of pliant osier,
this one her bosom, another weighs down her loose folds:
this one gathers marigolds, to this one the violet-beds are dear,
this one nips off the poppy-heads with her nail:
you, hyacinth, these hold; these, amaranth, you delay:
some love thyme, some rosemary, some the melilot.
Roses most of all are gathered, and flowers without a name;
she herself plucks the slender crocus and the white lilies.
In the eagerness of gathering they wander little by little farther,
and by chance no companion followed her mistress.
Her uncle sees her, and seeing swiftly carries her off,
and bears her to his realm on his dark-blue horses.
She indeed kept crying, "Dearest mother, oh,
I am being carried away!" and she had torn her dress.
Meanwhile a road opens for Dis, for his horses,
unused to it, can scarcely bear the light of day.
But the band of her companions, their baskets heaped with flowers,
cry out, "Persephone, come to your gifts!"
When she who was called is silent, they fill the hills with their howls
and strike their bare breasts with mournful hands.
Ceres was stunned by the lament (she had just come to Henna),
and at once said, "Wretched me! daughter, where are you?"
Out of her mind she rushes off, like the Thracian
maenads we hear of, going with streaming hair.
As a mother cow bellows when her calf is torn from her udder
and seeks her young through every grove:
so the goddess does not hold back her groans, and driven on in her course
is carried off, and begins from your fields, Henna.
There she finds the prints of a girl's foot
and saw the ground pressed by the familiar weight;
perhaps that day might have been the end of her wandering,
had not the pigs disturbed and spoiled the tracks she found.
And now in her course she passes Leontini and the streams of Amenanus
and your banks, grass-bearing Acis;
she passes Cyane and the springs of gentle Anapus
and you, Gela, not to be approached for your whirlpools.
She had left Ortygia and Megara and Pantagias,
and where the sea receives the waters of Symaethus,
and the caves of the Cyclopes, scorched by the furnaces set within,
and the place that takes its name from the curved sickle,
and Himera and Didyme and Acragas and Tauromenium
and the glad pastures of Melas with its sacred herds.
From here she comes to Camerina and Thapsus and the Heloran Tempe,
and where Eryx lies forever open to the Zephyr.
And now she had traversed Pelorias and Lilybaeum and Pachynus,
the three horns of her own land.
Wherever she goes, she fills all places with her wretched
laments, as the bird grieves over the lost Itys,
and by turns she cries now "Persephone!" now "daughter!"
she cries and calls out each name in turn.
But neither does Persephone hear Ceres, nor the daughter her mother,
and by turns each name is lost upon the air;
and whether she had seen a shepherd or one tilling the fields,
her one cry was, "Has any girl passed this way?"
Now one colour is in all things, and all are covered
