by darkness, now the watchful dogs are silent:
high lies vast Aetna above the mouth of Typhoeus,
whose ground burns with the fires he breathes out;
there she kindled two pines for a lamp:
hence to this day a torch is given at the rites of Ceres.
There is a cave, a rough mass of eaten-away pumice,
a region not to be approached by man or beast:
as soon as she came there she yokes serpents bridled
to her chariot and roams dry-shod over the watery seas.
She flees the Syrtes and you, Zanclaean Charybdis,
and you, Nisaean dogs, monsters of shipwreck,
and the Adriatic spreading wide and the two-sea'd Corinth:
so she comes to your harbours, land of Attica.
Here she first sat down, most sorrowful, on a cold rock:
even now the children of Cecrops call that rock the Sorrowful.
She endured many days unmoved beneath the open sky,
patient under the moon and the rain;
each place has its own destiny: what is now called Cerealian Eleusis
was then the lands of old Celeus.
He carries home acorns and blackberries shaken from the brambles
and dry wood for the hearths that were to burn.
His little daughter was driving two she-goats down from the mountain,
and his tender son lay sick in his cradle.
"Mother!" said the girl (the goddess was moved by the name of mother),
"what are you doing in lonely places without a companion?"
The old man stopped too, though his burden pressed him, and begged her
to come under the roof of his cottage, however small.
She refused; she had taken the shape of an old woman, and had bound
her hair with a cap. To his urging she answered thus:
"May you go safe and ever be a parent! my daughter has been snatched from me.
Alas, how much better is your lot than mine!"
She spoke, and as a tear (for it is not for gods to weep)
fell, a bright drop, into her warm bosom,
the tender-hearted girl and old man weep alike;
and these were the words of the just old man:
"So may your daughter, whom you seek as stolen, be safe,
rise up and do not scorn the roof of a small cottage."
The goddess said to him, "Lead on! you have found the way to compel me,"
and she lifts herself from the rock and follows the old man.
As leader he tells his companion how sick his son is,
and that he gets no sleep and lies awake in his pains.
About to enter the little house, she gathers the sleep-bringing
gentle poppy from the wild ground;
while she gathers, they say she tasted it with forgetful lips
and unwittingly broke her long fast.
Because she ended her fasting at the beginning of night,
the initiates take their time of food at the appearing of the stars.
As she crossed the threshold she sees everything full of grief:
already there was no hope of the boy's recovery.
Having greeted the mother (Metanira the mother is called),
she deigned to join her lips to the boy's.
His pallor goes, they see sudden strength in his body:
so great a vigour came from the heavenly mouth.
The whole house is glad—that is, the mother and father
and daughter: those three were the whole household.
Soon they set out a meal, curds melted in milk
and apples and golden honey in its combs.
Kind Ceres refrains, and gives you, boy, the poppy,
cause of sleep, to drink in warm milk.
It was the middle of the night and the silence of peaceful sleep:
she took Triptolemus up into her lap
and stroked him three times with her hand, said three charms,
charms not to be repeated by mortal voice,
and in the hearth, with the living embers, she covered
the boy's body, that the fire might purge the human burden.
The well-meaning but foolish mother starts from sleep, and frantic,
cries, "What are you doing?" and snatches the limbs from the fire.
The goddess said to her, "Though not wicked, you have been so:
my gifts are made vain by a mother's fear.
He indeed shall be mortal, but the first to plough
and to sow and to lift the rewards from the tilled soil."
She spoke, and going out trailed a cloud, and changed into her dragons,
and was lifted up by Ceres on her wing-bearing car.
She leaves Sunium jutting out and the Piraeus safe in its recess
and the shore that lies on the right hand.
From here she enters the Aegean, where she looks on all the Cyclades,
and skirts the ravenous Ionian and Icarian seas,
and through the cities of Asia seeks the long Hellespont,
and wanders her high path, varied by its places.
For now she looks down on the incense-gathering Arabs, now on the Indians,
on this side Libya, on that Meroe and the parched land lie beneath;
now she comes to the Hesperians, the Rhine and the Rhone and the Po,
and you, Tiber, father-to-be of a mighty water.
Where am I being carried? It would be endless to tell the lands she wandered:
no place in the world was passed over by Ceres.
She wanders too in the sky, and addresses the constellations
nearest the cold pole, free from the liquid sea:
"You Parrhasian stars (for you can know all things,
since you never sink into the watery deep),
show wretched Persephone to her unhappy mother!"
She had spoken, and Helice answers her with these words:
"The night is free of the crime; consult the Sun about the stolen
maiden, who sees far and wide the deeds of day."
The Sun, approached, says, "Not to weary you in vain, she whom you seek
is married to Jove's brother and holds the third realm."
After long lamenting to herself, she addressed the Thunderer,
and the greatest signs of grief were on her face:
"If you remember by whom Proserpina was born to me,
she ought to have half your care.
The whole world traversed, the wrong alone of the deed
is known: the ravisher keeps the rewards of his crime.
But Persephone does not deserve a robber for a husband,
nor was this the way for us to gain a son-in-law.
What heavier thing could I have borne, a captive of victorious Gyges,
than now I have borne with you holding the sceptres of heaven?
But let him go unpunished, we shall endure this unavenged;
let him give her back and amend his former deeds with new ones."
Jove soothes her and excuses the deed by love,
and says, "He is no son-in-law for us to be ashamed of.
I am no nobler: a palace was set for me in heaven,
another holds the waters, another the empty void.
But if your heart is not to be changed,
and you are set on breaking the bonds of a marriage once joined,
let us try this too, if only she has remained fasting;
if not, she will be the wife of the lord below."
The wand-bearer, bidden, takes wings and goes to Tartarus,
and returns sooner than hoped and reports for certain what he saw:
"The stolen maid," he said, "broke her fast with three seeds
that the Punic apple hides within its tough rind."
No less did the sorrowing parent grieve than if she had just
been stolen, and was long, and scarcely, restored after the delay,
and said thus, "Heaven is not habitable for me either;
bid me too be received in the Taenarian vale."
And she would have done it, had not Jove agreed
that for thrice two months of the year she should be in heaven.
Then at last Ceres recovered her face and her spirit,
and placed garlands of grain upon her hair;
and the harvest came forth abundant in the long-idle fields,
and the threshing-floor scarcely held the heaped wealth.
White suits Ceres: at the Cerealia put on white
garments; now there is no use for dark fleece.

title: Fasti
text:
Jupiter the Victor takes the Ides of April for his title:
on this day temples were given to him.
On this day too, if I am not mistaken, Liberty
began to have her own halls, most worthy of our people.
On the day that follows, sailor, make for safe harbours:
the wind from the west will be mixed with hail.
Yet be that as it may, on this day Caesar with hail
struck down the arms raised against him in the war at Mutina.
When the third light has risen after the Ides of Venus,
priests, sacrifice a pregnant cow.
The forda is a cow bearing young and fertile, named from bearing:
from this too they think the foetus takes its name.
Now the herds are heavy with young, the lands too are heavy with seed:
to teeming Earth a teeming victim is given.
Part falls on the citadel of Jove; the senate-house receives thrice ten
cows and is wet, sprinkled with abundant blood.
But when the ministers have snatched the calves from the wombs
and laid the cut entrails on the smoking hearths,
the eldest virgin burns the calves with fire,
that on the day of Pales the ashes may purge the people.
In Numa's reign, when the harvest did not answer the labour,
the vows of the deceived husbandman were made in vain,
for now the year was dry with chill north winds,
now the field ran riot with ceaseless rain:
often Ceres failed her master in the first blades,
and the light oat-stalk stood on the choked soil,
and the flock bore its young before the time, untimely,
and often the lamb in its birth killed the ewe.
An old wood, long unviolated by any axe,
stood, left sacred to the Maenalian god:
he gave answers to a quiet mind in the silent
nights; here King Numa sacrifices two ewes.
The first falls to Faunus, the second to gentle Sleep:
both fleeces are spread on the hard ground.
Twice his unshorn head is sprinkled with spring water,
twice he covers his temples with beech leaves,
he abstains from the use of love, no flesh may be set
on the tables, nor any ring be on his fingers,
covered in rough garb he lays his body upon
fresh fleeces, having worshipped the god in his own words.
Meanwhile night comes, her calm brow wreathed with poppy,
and draws dark dreams along with her.
Faunus is present, and pressing the sheep's fleeces with his hard hoof,
uttered such words from the right side of the couch:
"By the death of two cattle, king, Earth must be appeased:
let one heifer give two lives to the rites."
Sleep is shaken off by terror: Numa turns over the vision
and ponders to himself the riddles and the dark commands.
His wife, most dear to the grove, frees him from his perplexity
and said, "You are asked for the entrails of a pregnant cow."
The entrails of a pregnant cow are given, a more fruitful year
came on, and the earth and the cattle bore their fruit.
Once the Cytherean goddess bade this day go more swiftly
and hurried on her loosed horses,
so that on the following day the prosperous wars might give
to the youthful Augustus the title of empire as soon as possible.
But already the fourth Morning-star looks back on the Ides
now past: on this night the Hyades hold Doris.
When the third light has risen after the distant Hyades,
the Circus will hold the horses parted in their stalls.
Why then do the foxes that are loosed carry on their backs
torches blazing and bound—the cause must be told by me.
The land at Carseoli is cold and unfit for bearing olives,
but a soil suited to corn-crops;
this way I was making for the Pelignians, my native fields,
small but always moist with constant streams.
I entered the familiar house of my old host;
Phoebus had now taken the yokes from his weary horses.
He used to tell me many things, but this among them,
from which my present work might be furnished:
"In this plain," he said (and he pointed out the plain), "a thrifty
country-woman had a small farm with her hard husband.
He worked his own ground, whether the use was of the plough
or of the curved sickle or of the mattock.
She now would sweep the cottage propped on its post,
now set the eggs to be warmed under the mother's feathers,
or gather green mallows or white mushrooms,
or warm the lowly hearth with a welcome fire,
and yet keeps her arms busy with the constant loom
and prepares weapons against the threats of cold.
Her son was, in his early years, playful,
and had added two years to his ten:
he catches a fox at the far end of a willow-thicket:
she had carried off many of the farmyard birds.
He wrapped his captive in straw and hay and brings up
the fire: she escapes his burning hands:
where she fled she set fire to the fields clothed with crops;
a breeze gave strength to the destructive flames.
The deed is gone, the memorials remain; for even now
a fixed law forbids the men of Carseoli to name a fox;
and that this race may pay the penalty, a fox is burnt at the Cerealia,
and in the way it destroyed the crops, it perishes itself."

title: Fasti
text:
When next the saffron-robed mother of Memnon comes
on her rosy horses to look upon the open lands,
the sun departs from the leader of the wool-bearing flock,
who betrayed Helle: as it goes out, a greater victim is present.
Whether it be a cow or a bull is not easy to tell:
the front part appears, the hinder is hidden.
But whether the sign is a bull or a female,
it holds the gift of love against Juno's will.
Night has gone, and Aurora rises. I am summoned to the Parilia:
not summoned in vain, if kind Pales favours me.
Kind Pales, favour me as I sing the shepherds' rites,
if I honour your festival with my service.
Surely I have often carried in my full hands the ashes of a calf
and bean-stalks, chaste means of purging:
surely I have leapt over the flames set three in a row,
and the wet laurel-branch sprinkled its dewy waters.
The goddess is moved and favours the work: the ship goes out
from the docks, my sails already have their winds.
Go, people, seek the fumigant from the virgin's altar:
Vesta will give it; by Vesta's gift you will be pure.
The blood of a horse will be the fumigant, and the ashes of a calf,
the third thing the empty stalk of the hard bean.
Shepherd, purify the well-fed sheep at the first twilight:
let water first sprinkle, and the besom sweep the ground.
Let the sheepfolds be adorned with leaves and fixed boughs,
and let a long garland cover the decked doors.
Let blue smoke be made from pure sulphur,
and let the sheep bleat, touched by the smoking sulphur.
Burn the male olive-wood and the pine and the Sabine herbs,
and let the scorched laurel crackle in the middle of the hearths,
and let cakes of millet follow the basket of millet:
the rustic goddess delights especially in this food.
Add the feast and her own milk-pail, and when the feast is cut,
pray to woodland Pales with warm milk.
Say, "Watch alike over the flock and the masters of the flock:
let harm be driven off and flee from my stalls.
If I have grazed on sacred ground, or sat under a sacred tree,
and my sheep have unknowingly cropped fodder from the graves:
if I have entered a forbidden grove, or the nymphs
and the half-goat god have been put to flight by my eyes:
if my sickle has stripped the grove of a shady branch,
from which a basketful of leaves was given to a sick sheep:
grant pardon for the fault, nor let it harm me, while it hails,
to have sheltered the flock beneath a rustic shrine,
nor let it hurt that I disturbed the pools; forgive me, nymphs,
that a hoof in motion has made the waters murky.
Do you, goddess, appease for us the springs and the spring-deities,
appease the gods scattered through every grove.
Let us not see the Dryads, nor Diana's bath,
nor Faunus, when he lies in the fields at midday.
Drive the diseases far off; let men and flocks be well,
and well the watchful, foreseeing band of dogs.
Let me not drive home fewer than there were in the morning,
nor groan as I bring back fleeces snatched by the wolf.
Let unjust famine be absent: let grass and leaves abound,
and waters both to wash the limbs and to drink.
Let me press full udders, let the cheese bring me money,
and let the wide wicker give a way to the liquid whey.
Let the ram be lusty, and let my mate give back the conceived
seed, and let there be many a lamb in my stall.
Let wool come forth to wound no girls,
soft and fit for tender hands of every kind.
Let what I pray come to pass, and we shall make next year
great cakes for Pales, the mistress of the shepherds."
With these words the goddess must be appeased: this, turned toward the east,
say four times, and wash your hands in the living dew,
then you may take, in a wooden bowl set out as a mixing-bowl,
snow-white milk and the purple new wine;
and at once through the burning heaps of crackling straw
hurl your nimble limbs with a quick foot.
The custom is set out: the origin of the custom remains for me:
the crowd of explanations makes me doubt and holds back my task.
The devouring fire purges all things and refines the dross
from metals: therefore it purges the sheep with the shepherd.
Or is it because the contrary seeds of all things
are two discordant gods, fire and water,
and the fathers joined the elements and thought it fit
to touch the body with fire and sprinkled water?
Or because in these is the cause of life, which the exile loses,
and by these the bride is made new, and they think these two great things?
I scarcely believe it: there are those who think Phaethon
is referred to, and the excessive waters of Deucalion.
Some too say that when the shepherds struck stones with stones,
a spark suddenly leapt out;
the first indeed died, the second was caught by the straw:
does the flame of the Parilia have this for its reason?
Or did the piety of Aeneas rather make this custom,
to whom the fire gave a harmless passage when he was conquered?
Yet is it not nearer the truth that, when Rome was founded,
the Lares were ordered to be moved into new homes,
and changing their house, the country folk set fire
beneath their rural dwellings and the cottage soon to be left,
that the flock leapt through the flames, that the farmers leapt,
which is done even now, Rome, on your birthday?

title: Fasti
text:
The place itself gives the poet his theme: the founding of the city
comes; be present, great Quirinus, at your own deeds!
Now Numitor's brother had paid the penalty, and all
the herdsmen's crowd was under the twin leaders.
It pleased both to gather the country folk and lay walls:
the question was, which should lay the walls.
"There is no need of any contest," said Romulus;
"great is the trust in birds; let us try the birds."
The plan pleases: one goes to the rocks of the wooded Palatine,
the other in the morning climbs the height of the Aventine.
Remus sees six birds, Romulus twelve in order; by the pact
they abide, and Romulus holds the rule of the city.
A fit day is chosen on which to mark the walls with the plough.
The rites of Pales were near: from this the work is begun.
A trench is dug down to the solid ground, fruits are thrown into the bottom
and earth fetched from the neighbouring soil.
The trench is filled with earth, an altar set on the full ground,
and a new hearth busies itself with the kindled fire.
Then pressing the plough-handle he marks the walls with a furrow;
a white cow bore the yoke with a snowy ox.
These were the king's words: "Jupiter, and father Mavors,
and mother Vesta, be present as I found this city;
and all you gods whom it is right to summon, attend, every one.
Under your auspices may this work of mine rise.
Long be its life, and the power of this land its mistress,
and beneath it both the rising and the setting day."
He prayed, and Jove gave omens with thunder on the left,
and lightning hurled from the left pole.
Glad at the augury the citizens lay the foundations,
and in a short time there was a new wall.
Celer hastens this work, whom Romulus himself had called,
and had said, "Celer, let these be your care,
and let no one cross the walls or the trench made by the share:
put to death any who dares such a thing."
Remus, not knowing this, began to scorn the lowly walls
and to say, "Will the people be safe behind these?"
At once he leapt over. Celer strikes the one who dared with his spade;
he, bloodied, presses the hard ground.
When the king learned this, he swallowed the tears that rose
within him and kept the wound shut in his breast.
He will not weep openly, and keeps the example of fortitude,
and says, "So let the enemy cross my walls."
Yet he grants the funeral rites, and can no longer hold back
his weeping, and the piety he concealed is laid bare;
he pressed his last kisses on the bier set down,
and said, "Brother, taken against my will, farewell!"
He anointed the limbs that were to burn; Faustulus did the same,
and Acca, her sorrowing hair unbound.
Then the Quirites, not yet so named, wept for the youth;
and at last the fire was set beneath the bewailed pyre.
The city rises (who then could have believed it of any?)
destined to set its conquering foot upon the lands.
Rule all things, and be ever beneath a great Caesar,
and often hold many bearers of that name;
and as often as you stand sublime over a conquered world,
let all things be lower than your peaks.
I have spoken of Pales, and I shall speak of the Vinalia;
yet one day lies between the two.
Common girls, celebrate the divinity of Venus:
Venus suits well the gains of those who profess the trade.
With incense offered, ask for beauty and the people's favour,
ask for charm and words fit for jesting,
and give the mistress her own grateful mint with myrtle
and rush-bonds covered with arranged rose.
Now it is fitting that her temple near the Colline gate
be thronged; it takes its name from a Sicilian hill;
and when Claudius took with arms Syracuse of Arethusa
and captured you too, Eryx, in war,
Venus was brought over by the song of the long-lived Sibyl,
and chose rather to be worshipped in the city of her own stock.
You ask why then they call the festival of Venus the Vinalia,
and why this day belongs to Jove.
There was war over whether Turnus or Aeneas should be
the son-in-law of Latian Amata: Turnus implores the Etruscan power.
Mezentius was renowned and, with arms taken up, fierce,
great on horseback, and greater on foot;
the Rutulians and Turnus try to win him to their side,
but against them the Tuscan leader spoke thus:
"My valour stands me in no small worth: I call to witness my wounds
and the arms I have often stained with my own blood.
You who seek my aid, share with me no great
reward—the next new wine from your vats.
There is no delay in the service: yours to give, ours to conquer.
How Aeneas would wish that this were denied me!"
The Rutulians had nodded assent. Mezentius put on his arms,
Aeneas put them on too, and addressed Jove:
"The enemy's vintage is vowed to the Tyrrhenian king:
Jupiter, you shall have new wine from the Latian vine!"
The better vows prevail: huge Mezentius falls
and beats the ground with his indignant breast.
Autumn had come, foul with the trodden grapes:
the wine owed is duly paid to Jove.
Hence the day is called the Vinalia: Jupiter claims it for his own
and rejoices to be present at his own festivals.

title: Fasti
text:
When April has six days left of those that remain,
the seasons of spring will be at mid-course,
and in vain will you seek the ram of Helle, daughter of Athamas;
the rains give the signs, and the Dog rises.
On this day, as I was returning to Rome from Nomentum,
a white-robed crowd blocked the middle of the road.
A flamen was going to the grove of ancient Robigo,
to give the entrails of a dog and the entrails of a sheep to the flames.
At once I drew near, that I might not be ignorant of the rite:
your flamen, Quirinus, uttered these words:
"Rough Robigo, spare the corn-blades of Ceres,
and let the smooth tip tremble at the top of the soil.
Suffer the crops, nourished by the favouring stars of heaven,
to grow until they are ripe for the sickle.
Your power is not slight: the grain you have marked,
the mournful farmer counts among his losses;
neither winds nor rains have harmed Ceres so much,
nor does she grow so pale, scorched by the marble frost,
as when Titan warms the wet stalks:
then is there room for your anger, goddess to be feared.
Spare, I pray, and take your rough hands from the harvest,
and harm not the tilled fields: it is enough that you can harm.
Embrace not the tender crops, but the hard iron,
and what can destroy others, destroy first.
More usefully will you seize on swords and harmful weapons:
there is no need of them, the world is at leisure.
Now let the hoes and the hard mattock and the curved share,
the wealth of the country, shine; let rust foul the arms,
and let anyone who tries to draw the sword from its sheath
feel that it is stuck fast from long disuse.
But do not you defile Ceres, and may the farmer ever
be able to pay his vows to you in your absence."
He had spoken: at his right was a napkin with its loose nap,
and a casket of incense with a saucer of pure wine.
He gave incense and wine to the hearths, and the entrails of a sheep,
and the foul entrails (we saw it) of an obscene dog.
"Then why," you ask, "is a strange victim given to the rites?"
(I had asked.) "Hear the cause," the flamen said.
"There is a Dog, the Icarian they call it, at whose rising
the parched earth thirsts and the crop ripens too soon.
For the starry dog this dog is set on the altar,
and the only reason it dies is its name."
When Tithonus' bride, leaving behind the brother of Phrygian
Assaracus, has lifted her radiance three times over the vast world,
a goddess comes wreathed with a thousand garlands of varied flowers:
the stage holds the manner of freer jesting.
The rite of Flora goes out also to the Kalends of May;
I shall take it up then, now a greater work presses me.
Take the day, Vesta! Vesta has been received on her kinsman's
threshold: so the righteous fathers decreed.
Phoebus holds a part, a second part fell to Vesta;
what is left over the third himself holds.
Stand, laurels of the Palatine, and let the house stand
decked with oak: one house holds three eternal gods.
5. You ask from where I think the month of May was given its name?
The cause is not clearly enough known to me.
As a traveller stands uncertain, not knowing which way to go,
when he sees a road on every side:
so, since it is possible to give differing causes,
I do not know which way to turn; the very abundance harms me.
Tell me, you who hold the springs of Aganippean Hippocrene,
the cherished signs of the Medusan horse.
The goddesses disagreed, of whom Polyhymnia began
first; the others are silent and note her words in mind.
"After chaos, as soon as the three bodies were given to the world,
and all the work withdrew into new shapes,
the earth sank by its own weight and drew down the seas,
but lightness bore the sky to the highest places;
the sun too, with the stars, held back by no heaviness,
and you, the horses of the moon, leapt up.
But for a long while neither Earth yielded to Sky, nor the other
constellations to Phoebus; the honour was equal for all.
Often some god from the common throng dared
to sit on the throne which you, Saturn, held,
nor did any newcomer god take his place beside Ocean,
and Themis was often received in the last seat,
until Honour and Reverence, comely with a calm face,
laid their bodies on the lawful marriage-couch.
From these was born Majesty, who governs the whole world.
On the day she was brought forth she was great.
Without delay she sat aloft in the middle of Olympus,
golden, conspicuous in her purple robe.
Modesty and Awe sat down with her: you might see every
divinity compose its face toward her.
At once respect for honours entered their minds:
worth has its reward, and no one pleases himself.
This state remained in heaven for many years,
until the elder god fell by the fates from the citadel.
Earth brought forth fierce offspring, monstrous Giants,
who would dare to go against the house of Jove;
she gave them a thousand hands and serpents for legs,
and said, 'Take up arms against the great gods.'
They prepared to pile up mountains to the highest stars
and to harass great Jove with war;
Jupiter, hurling thunderbolts from the citadel of heaven,
turned the vast masses back upon their makers.
Well defended by these arms, the Majesty of the gods
remains, and from that time stays honoured;
thence she sits by Jove, she is Jove's most faithful guardian
and grants Jove to hold his sceptre without force.
She came to earth as well: Romulus worshipped her
and Numa, and then others, each in his own time.
She guards the fathers and mothers in their pious honour,
she comes as companion to boys and maidens,
she commends the bestowed rods and the curule ivory,
she rides high in triumph on garlanded horses."
Polyhymnia had ended her words: Clio approved what was said,
and Thalia skilled in the curved lyre.
Urania takes up the tale: all kept silence,
and no voice could be heard but hers.
"Great once was the reverence for a grey head,
and the old man's wrinkle was held in its own esteem.
The young men did the work of Mars and waged spirited wars,
and stood on guard for their gods:
the old man, lesser in strength and unfit to bear arms,
often brought help to his country by counsel.
The senate-house then was not open except after ripe years,
and the senate was a name gentle with age.
The elder gave laws to the people, and a definite
law fixed the age at which office might be sought;
and a man went among the young, they themselves not resenting it,
and on the inner side, if one companion walked with him.
Who would dare to speak words deserving a blush before
an old man? Long old age conferred the right of censure.
Romulus saw this and called his chosen spirits 'fathers':
to these the chief affairs of the new city were referred.
Hence I am moved to think the elders gave their name to May
and took thought for their own time of life.
And Numitor could have said, 'Romulus, give this month
to the old,' and the grandson could not refuse his grandfather,
nor does June, named from the name of the young,
hold a light pledge of the design of an honour bestowed in turn."
Then thus, her neglected hair wreathed with ivy,
Calliope, first of her choir, began:
"Ocean once married the Titaness Tethys,
he who encircles the earth, as far as it reaches, with flowing waters.
From them, it is said, was born Pleione, who is joined
to sky-bearing Atlas, and bears the Pleiades.
Of these, Maia is said to have surpassed her sisters in beauty
and to have lain with most high Jove.
She gave birth, on the ridge of cypress-bearing Cyllene,
to him who plucks the airy path with winged foot.
The Arcadians duly worship him, and ravenous Ladon
and huge Maenalus, a land believed older than the moon.
Evander, an exile from Arcadia, had come into the Latian fields,
and had brought his gods set on his ship.
Here, where now Rome is, the head of the world, there was tree and grass
and a few cattle and a rare cottage.
When they came there, 'Halt!' said the foreseeing mother,
'for that countryside will be the seat of empire.'
The Nonacrian hero obeys his mother and the seer
and settled as a guest on the foreign soil,
and taught these peoples many rites, but first those of two-horned
Faunus and of the wing-footed god.
Half-goat Faunus, you are worshipped by the girded Luperci,
when their thronging companies purify the streets with the cut hide.
But you, inventor of the curved lyre, fitted to its bounds,
gave the month its name from your mother.
Nor is this your first act of devotion: you are thought to have given
the lyre seven strings, the number of the Pleiades."
This one too had ended: she was praised by her sisters' voices.
What am I to do? Every part of the throng holds the same view.
May the favour of the Pierides attend me equally,
and let none be praised by me more or less.

title: Fasti
text:
Let the work rise from Jove. On the first night a star is to be seen,
the dutiful star at Jove's cradle:
the rainy sign of the Olenian Goat is born;
she has the sky as the reward of the milk she gave.
The Naiad Amalthea, famous on Cretan Ida,
is said to have hidden Jove in the woods.
She had a beautiful she-goat, mother of two kids,
conspicuous among the Dictaean flocks,
with high horns curving back over her own back,
with an udder such as the nurse of Jove might have.
She gave milk to the god; but she broke a horn on a tree
and was robbed of half her beauty.
The nymph took it up and bound it with fresh herbs
and brought it, full of fruit, to the mouth of Jove.
When he held the affairs of heaven and sat on his father's
throne, and there was nothing greater than unconquered Jove,
he made his nurse a constellation, and the fruitful horn of his nurse
a constellation, which now too bears its mistress's name.
The Kalends saw an altar set up to the Tutelary Lares of Maia
and small images of the gods:
Curius had indeed vowed it; but much antiquity
destroys, and long age harms the stone.
The cause of the surname given to them was this,
that they keep all things safe with their eyes.
They stand on our behalf and watch over the city walls
and are present and bring help.
But a dog, made of the same stone, stood before
their feet: what cause was there for its standing with the Lar?
Each guards the house, each is faithful to the master too:
the crossroads are dear to the god, the crossroads dear to the dog.
Both the Lar and the band of Diana drive off thieves:
wakeful are the Lares, and wakeful the dogs.
I sought the twin images of the twin gods,
made to fall by the strength of long age:
a thousand Lares and the Genius of the leader, who gave them,
the city holds, and the districts worship the threefold powers.
Where am I being carried? The month of Augustus has the right
of this song: meanwhile the Good Goddess must be sung.
There is a natural mass in the place; the thing made the name:
they call it the Rock; it is a good part of the hill.
On this Remus had stood in vain, at the time when
the Palatine birds gave the first signs to your brother.
There the Fathers founded a temple that hates male eyes,
on the gently sloping ridge.
This was dedicated by an heiress of the old Clausan name,
who had suffered no man to touch her virgin body:
Livia restored it, so that she might not fail to imitate her husband
and to follow her own in every respect.
When next, with the stars of Hyperion driven off, the Dawn
lifts her rosy lamp on her morning horses,
the chill Argestes will soothe the topmost ears of corn,
and white sails will be spread from the Calabrian waters.
But as soon as the dim twilight brings on the night,
no part of the Hyades from the whole flock is hidden.
The face of the Bull shines, radiant with seven flames,
which the Greek sailor calls the Hyades from the rain;
some think they nursed Bacchus, some believed them
the granddaughters of Tethys and old Ocean.
Not yet did Atlas stand with his shoulders laden by Olympus,
when Hyas was born, conspicuous for his beauty;
the offspring of Ocean, Aethra, brought him forth
in due labour, and the nymphs, but Hyas was born first.
While his down is new, he frightens the timid deer
with terror, and the hare is a welcome prey to him.
But after his manhood ripened with the years, he dares
to go against boars and shaggy lionesses hand to hand,
and while he seeks the lairs and cubs of a lioness with young,
he himself became the bloody prey of the Libyan beast.
His mother wept for Hyas, and his sorrowing sisters wept for Hyas,
and Atlas, soon to set his neck beneath the pole.
Yet the love of the sisters overcame both parents:
it gave them the sky; Hyas gave the name.

title: Fasti
text:
"Mother of flowers, come, to be honoured with playful games!
I had put off your part in the month before.
You begin in April, you cross into the season of May:
the one holds you as it flees, the other as it comes.
Since the borders of the months are yours and yield to you,
either one or the other suits your praises.
The Circus games end in this month, and the palm acclaimed in the theatres:
let this song too go along with the Circus's gift.
Teach me yourself who you are. The opinion of men is deceptive:
you yourself will be the best author of your own name."
So I; and so the goddess answered my questions
(while she speaks, she breathes spring roses from her mouth):
"I was Chloris, who am called Flora: the Greek letter
of my name was corrupted by the Latin sound.
I was Chloris, a nymph of the happy field, where, you hear,
in old time there was wealth for fortunate men.
What my beauty was, it is hard for a modest one to tell,
but it found a god for a son-in-law to my mother.
It was spring, I was wandering: Zephyrus saw me, I was going away.
He pursues, I flee: he was the stronger,
and Boreas had given his brother every right of rape,
who had dared to bear off plunder from the house of Erechtheus.
Yet he makes amends for the force by giving me the name of wife,
and there is no complaint about my marriage-bed.
I enjoy perpetual spring: the year is always brightest,
the tree has leaves, the ground its fodder always.
I have a fruitful garden in the fields of my dower:
a breeze cherishes it, it is watered from a spring of clear water.
My husband filled it with noble flowers
and said, 'Have, goddess, the rule of the flower.'
Often I have wished to count the ordered colours
and could not: the abundance was greater than the number.
As soon as the dewy frost has been shaken from the leaves,
and the varied foliage has warmed in the sun's rays,
the Hours, girt with painted robes, gather
and pick our gifts into light baskets.
At once the Graces approach and weave garlands
and wreaths to entwine the locks of the gods.
I was first to scatter new seeds among countless peoples!
The earth before was of one colour.
I first made a flower from Therapnaean blood,
and the lament remains written on its leaf.
You too have a name through the cultivated gardens, Narcissus,
unhappy, because you were not another and another.
Why should I tell of Crocus, or Attis, or the son of Cinyras,
from whose wound an honour rises through me?
Mars too, if you do not know, was brought forth by my arts:
may Jupiter, as until now, never know it, I pray.
Holy Juno grieved that Jove had not needed her service,
since Minerva was born without a mother.
She went to complain to Ocean of her husband's deed;
weary with the labour she stopped at our doors.
As soon as I saw her, I said, 'What has brought you here,
daughter of Saturn?' She tells what place she seeks,
and added the reason; I was consoling her with friendly words:
'No,' she said, 'my care is not to be lightened by words.
If Jupiter has become a father by neglecting the use of a wife,
and alone holds both names,
why should I despair of becoming a mother without a husband,
and of bearing, while still chaste, untouched by man?
I will try all the drugs in the wide lands,
and search the seas and the depths of Tartarus.'
Her speech was in mid-course: I had the look of one who doubts.
'You seem, nymph, able to do something,' she said.
Three times I wished to promise help, three times my tongue held back:
the wrath of great Jove was the cause of my fear.
'Bring help, I pray!' she said; 'the author will be concealed,
and I will call to witness the divinity of the Stygian water.'
'What you ask,' I said, 'a flower sent to me from the Olenian
fields will give: it is the only one in my gardens.
He who gave it said, "Touch with this even a barren heifer,
and she will become a mother." I touched, and at once she was a mother.'
At once with my thumb I plucked the clinging flower:
she is touched, and being touched in the bosom she conceives.
And now, heavy with child, she enters Thrace and the left side of Propontis,
and the wish is fulfilled, and Mars was begotten.
He, mindful that his birth was granted through me, said,
'Have you too a place in the city of Romulus.'
Perhaps you may think my realm lies only in tender garlands?
My power touches the fields as well.
If the crops have flowered well, the threshing-floor will be rich;
if the vine has flowered well, there will be wine;
if the olives have flowered well, the year will be brightest,
and the apples have the yield of this season.
The flower once harmed, the vetches and the beans perish,
and your lentils perish, foreign Nile.
Wines too, laboriously stored in great cellars,
flower, and mist covers the surface of the jars.
Honey is my gift: I call the bees that will give honey
to the violet and the cytisus and the grey thyme."
I silently marvelled as she spoke such things, but she said,
"You have the right to learn, if you ask anything."
"Tell me, goddess," I answered, "what is the origin of the games."
I had scarcely well finished, when she replied to me:
"The other instruments of luxury did not yet flourish;
the rich man had either cattle or broad land;
from this came the word for 'wealthy,' from this 'money' itself.
But now each was gathering riches from what was forbidden:
it had become a custom to graze the public pastures bare,
and this was long allowed, and there was no penalty.
The common folk guarded their public lands with no protector;
and now it was a mark of sloth to graze on private ground.
Such licence was brought before the plebeian aediles,
the Publicii: men had lacked the spirit before.
The people takes up the case, the guilty pay a fine:
public concern was a credit to the protectors.
A great part of the fine was given to me, and with great favour
the victors instituted new games.
With part they let out the slope, which was then a steep cliff:
now it is a useful road, and they call it the Publician."
I had believed the spectacles were made yearly; she denied it,
and added other words to her speech:
"Honour touches us too: we delight in festivals and altars,
and we heavenly ones are an ambitious throng.
Often someone has made the gods unjust by sinning,
and a coaxing victim atoned for the offences;
often I have seen Jove, when he was already about to hurl
his thunderbolts, hold back his hand at the offering of incense.
But if we are neglected, the wrong is paid for with great penalties,
and anger passes the just measure.
Look at the son of Thestius: he burned with flames that were absent;
the cause is that the altar of Phoebe was without fire.
Look at the son of Tantalus: the same goddess held back his sails;
a virgin, yet she avenged her slighted hearths twice over.
Unhappy Hippolytus, you would have wished to worship Dione,
when you were torn apart by your terrified horses.
It would be a long delay to tell of forgetfulness corrected by losses.
Me too the Roman fathers passed over.
What was I to do, by which I might make my grief plain?
What punishment was I to exact for the slight to my name?
My care fell from me in my grief. I guarded no
fields, nor was the fertile garden in esteem:
the lilies had fallen, you might see the violets wither,
and the threads of the crimson crocus grow languid.
Often Zephyrus said to me, 'Do not corrupt
your own dowry': my dowry was worthless to me.
The olives were in flower; the wanton winds harmed them:
the crops were in flower; the crop was struck by hail:
the vine was in promise; the sky blackens from the south winds,
and the leaves are shaken down by sudden rain.
I did not wish it to happen, nor am I cruel in my anger,
but I had no care to drive the harm away.
The fathers gathered, and vowed yearly festivals
to my divinity, if the year should flower well. I assented
to the vow. Laenas the consul, with his colleague Postumius,
the consul, paid the games to me."
I tried to ask why there should be greater wantonness
in these games, and freer jesting,
but it came to my mind that the divinity is not stern
and brings gifts fitted to delights.
The drinkers' brows are bound with stitched garlands,
and the bright table is hidden under scattered roses;
the drunken guest, his hair girt with linden bark,
dances and unwittingly practises the art of wine;
the drunken lover sings at the hard threshold of his lovely
mistress, and soft garlands deck his anointed hair.
Nothing serious is done with a garlanded brow,
nor are clear waters drunk by those bound with flowers;
as long as you, Achelous, were mixed with no grapes,
there was no charm in taking a rose.
Bacchus loves flowers: that a garland pleased Bacchus
you may know from the star of Ariadne.
The light stage suits this goddess: she is not, believe me, not
to be counted among the buskined goddesses.
Why the harlot throng should celebrate these games,
the reason sought is not far to seek.
She is not of the gloomy ones, nor of those who profess greatness,
she wishes her rites to lie open to the plebeian choir,
and warns us to use the bloom of our age while it flowers;
the thorn is scorned when the roses have fallen.
Yet why, as white garments are given at the Cerealia,
is she becoming in many-coloured dress?
Is it because the harvest grows white with ripe ears,
and flowers have every colour and shape in them?
She nodded, and as her hair moved the flowers fell,
as a rose set on the tables is wont to fall.
The lamps remained, the cause of which was hidden from me,
when she thus took away my error:
"Either because the fields glow with crimson flowers,
the lamps were thought to suit our days;
or because neither the flower nor the flame is of dull colour,
and each splendour draws the eyes to itself;
or because nightly licence suits our delights,
the third cause comes from the truth."
"There is one short thing besides, on which it remains for me to ask,
if I may," I said: she too said, "You may."
"Why instead of Libyan lionesses are the harmless does
and the anxious hare shut up in your nets?"
She answered that not the woods had been given to her, but the gardens
and fields not to be approached by a warlike beast.
She had ended all: she withdrew into the thin air,
the fragrance remained: you might know a goddess had been there.
That the song of Naso may flower for all time,
sprinkle, I pray, my heart with your gifts.

title: Fasti
text:
On the fourth night Chiron will bring out his stars,
half-man and mingled with the body of a tawny horse.
Pelion is a mountain of Haemonia facing the south winds:
its top is green with pine, oak holds the rest.
The son of Phillyra dwelt there; the caves stand of ancient rock,
which they recall the just old man inhabited.
He is believed once to have detained in lyric measures
the hands that would send Hector to his death.
Alcides had come, part of his labours drained,
and the last commands almost remained for the hero.
You might see by chance the two fates of Troy standing together:
here the boy son of Aeacus, here the one born of Jove.
The Phillyrean hero receives the young man in hospitality,
and asks the cause of his coming; the other tells.
Meanwhile he looks at the club and the lion's spoil,
and the man says, "These arms are worthy of the man, the man of the arms!"
Nor could the hands of Achilles hold back from daring
to touch the fleece bristling with its hairs.
And while the old man handles the shafts foul with poisons,
an arrow fell and was fixed in his left foot.
Chiron groaned and drew the iron from his body,
and Alcides groans, and the Haemonian boy.
Yet he himself tempers herbs picked on the Pagasaean hills
and soothes the wounds with idle aid:
the devouring venom overcame the aid, and the plague
had entered deep into the bones and the whole body.
The blood of the Lernaean serpent, mixed with the Centaur's blood,
gave no time for help.
Achilles stood, bathed in tears, as before a father:
so was Peleus to be wept for, if he were dying.
Often he pressed the sick hands with friendly hands
(the teacher had the reward of the character he made);
often he gave kisses, and often said to him as he lay,
"Live, I pray, and do not leave me, dear father!"
The ninth day was at hand when you, most just Chiron,
girt your body with twice seven stars.
The curved Lyre would wish to follow him, but the way
is not yet fit: the third night will be the suitable time.
Scorpio will be in the sky, when we say that tomorrow
the Nones will dawn, to be marked from its middle.
When from here the lovely Evening-star has thrice put forth
his face, and the stars have thrice given Phoebus his place,
there will be the rite of an old sacred thing, the nightly Lemuria:
they will give offerings to the silent shades.
The year was shorter, nor did they yet know the pious purgations,
nor were you, two-faced Janus, the leader of the months:
yet even then they brought their gifts to the extinguished ash,
and the grandson appeased the tomb of his buried grandfather.
The month was May, named from the name of the elders (maiores),
which still holds a part of the ancient custom.
When the night is now at its midst and gives silence to sleep,
and you, dog and varied birds, have grown still,
he, mindful of the old rite and fearing the gods,
rises (his twin feet have no bonds)
and makes a sign with his fingers, the thumb joined to the middle,
lest a light shade meet him in his silence.
And when he has washed his pure hands in spring water,
he turns and first takes black beans,
and throws them with face averted; but as he throws he says,
"These I cast; with these beans I redeem myself and mine."
This he says nine times and does not look back: the shade is thought
to gather them and to follow behind, with none seeing.
Again he touches the water and clashes Temesaean bronze
and asks the shade to go out from his house.
When he has said nine times, "Go forth, ancestral shades,"
he looks back and thinks the rite duly done.
From where the day was named, what is the origin of the name,
escapes me: it must be found out from some god.
Son of the Pleiad, instruct me, you to be revered with the mighty wand:
often have you seen the palace of Stygian Jove.
The wand-bearer came at my prayer: receive the cause
of the name; the cause was learned from the god himself.
When Romulus had buried his brother's shade in the tomb,
and the rites were paid to too-swift Remus,
unhappy Faustulus and Acca with loosened hair
were sprinkling the burnt bones with their tears.
Then they return home, sad, at the first twilight,
and lay down, as they were, on the hard couch.
The bloody shade of Remus seemed to stand by the bed
and to speak these words in a faint murmur:
"Behold, I who was half of you, the other part of your vow,
see what I am, who was lately what I was!
I who lately, had I had the birds bidding me to rule,
might have been the greatest among my people,
now am an empty image, slipped from the flames of the pyre:
this is the shape left to me from that Remus!
Alas, where is Mars our father? If you spoke the truth lately,
and he gave us, exposed, the beast's udders,
him whom the she-wolf saved, the rash hand of a citizen
destroyed: how much gentler was she!
Cruel Celer, may you yield up your cruel soul through wounds,
and go, bloodied, beneath the earth, as I did.
My brother did not wish this; his love equals mine:
what he could, he gave—his tears to my shade.
Ask him, by your tears, by your nursing of us,
to mark a day to be honoured in my honour."
They long to embrace him as he charges them, and stretch out their arms:
the slippery shade escapes their grasping hands.
When the fleeing image had drawn off sleep with it,
both bear the brother's words to the king.
Romulus complies and calls that day Remuria,
on which the rites are paid to the buried forefathers.
In long course of time the rough letter that stood
first in the whole name was changed to a soft one;
soon too they called the souls of the silent dead lemures:
this was the sense of the word, this the force of the sound.
The ancients, however, closed the shrines on those days,
as you now see them shut at the time of the dead,
nor are the times fit for the torches of widow or maiden:
she who married then did not live long.
For this cause too, if proverbs touch you,
the common folk say it is ill to marry in the month of May.
But these three festivals fall at the same season,
none of them joined to another by a continuous day.

title: Fasti
text:
If in the middle of these you seek Boeotian Orion,
you will be deceived. The cause of the sign must be sung by me.
Jupiter, and his brother who reigns in the broad sea,
and Mercury were treading the road together.
It was the time when the inverted ploughs are brought back from the yoke,
and the lamb, lying down, drinks the milk of the full ewe.
By chance old Hyrieus, the tiller of a narrow plot,
sees them as he stood before his small cottage;
and thus he said, "The road is long, nor is much time
left, and our door lies open to guests."
He added a look to his words and asked again:
they obey his promises and hide that they are gods.
They enter the old man's hut, foul with black smoke;
there was a little fire in yesterday's log.
He himself, kneeling, kindles the flames with his breath
and brings out and breaks up the shattered torches.
Cups stand ready; the smaller held beans, the other greens,
and each foams, pressed under its own lid.
And while there is delay, he gives the red wine with trembling
right hand: the sea-god receives the first cups.
When he had drained them, "Now give Jupiter to drink
in turn," he said. At the name of Jove the old man grew pale.
When his spirit returned, he sacrifices the ploughing-ox
of his poor field and roasts it in the great fire;
and the wine that he as a boy had once stored in his early years,
he brings out from the smoky jar.
Without delay they reclined on couches, not high,
stuffed with river sedge covered with linen.
Now with the feast, now with Bacchus set out, the tables shone:
the mixing-bowl was red earth, the cups were beech-wood.
The words of Jove were these: "If your heart prompts anything, choose:
you shall have it all." The peaceful old man's words were these:
"Dear was my wife, known to me in the bloom of my early youth;
where is she now, you ask? The urn covers her.
To her I swore, calling you to witness the words,
'You alone shall enjoy my marriage.'
I both swore and keep it; but indeed a different wish
is mine: I wish to be not a husband, but a father."
All had nodded assent: all stood at the bullock's back—
shame forbids to tell what followed—
then they covered the wet ground with earth heaped over it;
and now ten months had passed, and a boy was born.
Him Hyrieus, because he was begotten thus, calls Urion:
the first letter lost its ancient sound.
He had grown immense; the Delian goddess took him as her companion,
he was the goddess's guard, he her attendant.
Words not considered move the anger of the gods:
"There is no beast," he said, "that I cannot conquer."
Earth sent a scorpion: it was its impulse
to bear its curved stings against the goddess who bore twins;
Orion stood in the way. Latona added him to the shining
stars and said, "Have the reward of your merit."
But why do Orion and the other stars hasten
to give place to the world, and the night cuts short its course?
Why does the bright day, with the Morning-star going before,
lift its radiance from the clear sea sooner than usual?
Am I deceived, or do arms sound? I am not deceived, arms were sounding:
Mars comes, and coming gave the signs of war.
The Avenger himself came down from heaven to his own honours
and his temple to be admired in the forum of Augustus.
Both the god is mighty and the work: in no other way
ought Mars to dwell in the city of his son.
This shrine is worthy of the trophies over the Giants:
from here it is fitting that Gradivus should stir fierce wars,
whether some impious foe provoke us from the Eastern world,
or whether one must be tamed from the setting sun.
The lord of arms looks up at the peaks of the lofty work
and approves that unconquered gods hold the heights.
He looks at the weapons of varied shape on the doors,
and the arms of the lands conquered by his soldier.
Here he sees Aeneas burdened with his dear weight
and the many forebears of Julian nobility;
here he sees the son of Ilia bearing the leader's arms on his shoulders,
and the famous deeds set beneath the ordered men.
He looks too at the temple inscribed with the name of Augustus,
and the work seemed greater for the reading of Caesar's name.
The youth had vowed this then, when he took up his pious arms:
a Princeps had to begin from deeds so great.
He, stretching out his hands, with the just soldier standing here,
the conspirators there, gave such words:
"If my father and the priest of Vesta is the author
of my warring, and I prepare to avenge both divinities:
Mars, be present and sate the iron with the guilty blood,
and let your favour stand for the better cause.
You shall have a temple and, when I am victor, shall be called Avenger."
He had vowed, and returns rejoicing from the routed foe.
Nor is it enough to have earned the surname for Mars once:
he pursues the standards held by the Parthian's hand.
There was a race safe in its plains, its horses, and its arrows,
and unapproachable, ringed by rivers.
The deaths of the Crassi had given the race its courage,
when soldiers and standards and leader perished together.
The Parthian held the Roman standards, the glory of war,
and an enemy was the standard-bearer of the Roman eagle.
And that shame would still have remained, had not the brave arms
of Caesar protected the resources of Ausonia.
He removed the old marks and the disgrace of a long age:
the recovered standards knew their own again.
What now availed you, Parthian, your wonted arrows
sent behind your backs, what your country, what the use of the swift horse?
You bring back the eagles, you stretch out your conquered bows too:
now you hold no pledges of our shame.
Rightly to the god twice avenger a temple and a name were given,
and the merited honour pays the debts of the vow.
Celebrate the solemn games in the Circus, Quirites!
The stage seemed not to suit the brave god.

title: Fasti
text:
You will see all the Pleiades and the whole band
of sisters, when there is one night left before the Ides.
Then, by no doubtful authorities, summer begins for me,
and the season of warm spring has its end.
The Ides show the Bull lifting his starry face
before the others; a well-known tale lies beneath this sign.
As a bull Jupiter offered his back to the Tyrian girl
and bore false horns on his brow,
she held the mane with her right hand, her garments with the left,
and the very fear was a cause of new beauty.
The breeze fills her robe, the breeze stirs her golden hair:
Sidonian, so were you to be looked upon by Jove.
Often she drew up her girlish feet from the sea
and feared the touch of the leaping water:
often the god knowingly let down his back into the waves,
that she might cling more strongly to his neck.
When the shores were reached he stood without any horns,
Jupiter, turned from a bull into a god.
The bull enters the sky: Jupiter, he fills you, Sidonian,
and a third part of the earth bears your name.
Others have called this sign the Pharian heifer,
who from a human became a cow, from a cow became a goddess.
Then too the maiden is wont to send the images of ancient
men of rushes from the oaken bridge.
The old story is that, when the land was called Saturnia,
such were the words said to be spoken by Jove:
"Send to the old man with the sickle two bodies, you peoples,
offered up, to be received by the Tuscan waters."
Until the Tirynthian came into these fields, every year
the gloomy rites were performed in the Leucadian manner;
he, they say, threw straw figures into the water,
that by the example of Hercules false bodies might be cast.
Some think that, so the young alone might cast their votes,
they hurled the feeble old men from the bridges.
He who believed that bodies were sent to death after sixty
years condemns his ancestors of a charge of crime.
Tiber, teach the truth: your bank is older than the city,
you can well know the origin of the rite.
Tiber lifted his reed-bearing head from the middle of his channel
and parted his hoarse lips with such sounds:
"I have seen these places as deserted grass without walls:
each bank pastured scattered cattle,
and I, whom now the nations know and fear as Tiber,
was then even to be despised by the herd.
The name of Arcadian Evander is often recalled to you:
he, a stranger, churned my waters with his oars.
Alcides came too, attended by an Achaean throng
(Albula, if I remember, was then my name):
the Pallantian hero receives the young man in hospitality,
and at last the deserved penalty came upon Cacus.
The victor departs and drags off with him the cattle,
the Erythean spoil. But his companions refuse to go farther
(and a great part of them had come from deserted Argos):
on these hills they set their hope and their home.
Yet often they are touched by the sweet love of their country,
and one dying gives this brief command:
'Cast me into the Tiber, that, borne on the Tiberine waves,
I may go as empty dust to the Inachian shore.'
The heir dislikes the charge of the commanded tomb:
the dead guest is buried in Ausonian ground,
and a rush image is thrown into the Tiber for the master,
to seek again, over the long seas, his Greek home."
So far he spoke, and went into caves dripping
with living rock: light waters, you stayed your course.
Famous grandson of Atlas, be present, whom once on the Arcadian
mountains a Pleiad bore to Jove,
arbiter of peace and arms for the gods above and below,
who pluck your path with winged foot,
glad in the lyre's stroke, glad too in the shining wrestling-ground,
by whose teaching the tongue learned to speak with elegance,
the fathers set a temple to you facing the Circus
on the Ides: from then this day is your festival.
You, whoever profess to sell their wares,
with incense offered, ask that you grant them profit.
There is a water of Mercury near the Capene gate;
if it helps to believe those who have tried it, it has a divine power.
Here comes the merchant, girt in his tunic, and with an urn
fumigated and pure draws the water he is to carry,
from this the laurel is wetted, and with the wet laurel
all things are sprinkled that are to have new masters;
he sprinkles too his own hair with the dripping laurel
and pours out prayers in his wonted deceiving voice:
"Wash away the perjuries of past time," he says,
"wash away the treacherous words of the past day.
Whether I have made you a witness, or falsely invoked
the great divinity of Jove, who would not hear,
or whether I have knowingly deceived another god or goddess,
let the swift south winds carry off the wicked words,
and let the perjuries lie open to me as the day comes,
and let the gods not care for anything I shall have said.
Only give me profits, give me joys in the profit made,
and grant that it may please me to have cheated the buyer."
At one asking such things Mercury laughs from on high,
remembering that he himself stole the Ortygian cattle.

title: Fasti
text:
But unfold to me, I pray, since I seek far better things,
from what time Phoebus passes into the Twins.
"When you see as many days left of the month
as are the labours of Hercules' toil," he said.
"Tell me," I answered, "the origin of this sign for me."
The god gave the cause with eloquent mouth:
"The brothers, sons of Tyndareus, had carried off
Phoebe and Phoebe's sister, the one a horseman, the other a boxer.
Idas and his brother prepare war and demand back their own,
both pledged to become the son-in-law of Leucippus.
Love urges these to demand them back, those not to give them up;
and from a like cause each fights.
The sons of Oebalus could have escaped by running from their pursuers,
but it seemed shameful to conquer by swift flight.
There is a place free of trees, a fitting field for battle:
they had taken their stand there; Aphidna is the name of the place.
Pierced through the breast by the sword of Lynceus, Castor,
by a wound he did not expect, pressed the ground.
Pollux comes as avenger and pierces Lynceus with his spear,
where the neck, continuous with the shoulders, presses on them.
Idas was going against him and was scarcely repelled by Jove's fire,
yet they say his weapons were not snatched from his right hand by the lightning.
And now the high heaven lay open to you, Pollux,
when you said, 'Receive my words, father:
the heaven that you give to me alone, share between two:
half will be greater than the whole gift.'
He spoke, and redeemed his brother by alternate station.
Each star is useful to the anxious ship."
Let him who asks what the Agonia are return to Janus:
yet they too have this time in the calendar.
On the night that follows the day, the Erigonian dog goes out:
the cause of the sign has been given in another place.
The next day is Vulcan's, the Tubilustria they call it:
the pure trumpets that he makes are purified.
From here there is a place with four marks, in which, read in order,
is either the custom of the rites or the flight of the king.
Nor do I pass you by, Public Fortune of the powerful
people, to whom a temple was given on the following day.
When Amphitrite, rich in waters, has received this day,
you will see the beak of the tawny bird dear to Jove.
The coming dawn will take Bootes from our eyes,
and on the day after there will be the star of Hyas.
6. This month too has uncertain causes for its name;
of all that I set out, you yourself shall choose which please.
I shall sing of facts; but there will be those who say I invented them
and think that no divine powers were ever seen by a mortal.
There is a god within us; we grow warm when he stirs us:
this impulse holds the seeds of a sacred mind.
It is especially lawful for me to have seen the faces of the gods,
whether because I am a poet, or because I sing of sacred things.
There is a grove thick with trees, a place secret from every
sound, were it not for the noise of waters.
Here I was seeking what was the origin of the month
I had begun, and I was busy with the care of its name.
Behold, I saw goddesses, not such as the teacher of ploughing
had seen, when he followed his Ascraean sheep,
nor such as the son of Priam compared in the valleys of watery
Ida: yet one of them was from those.
One of them was there, the sister of her own husband;
this was she (I knew her) who stands on the citadel of Jove.
I had shuddered and confessed my heart by my silent pallor;
then the goddess herself took away the fears she had made,
for she said, "O poet, founder of the Roman year,
who have dared to tell great things in slender measures,
you have made for yourself the right to see a heavenly power,
when it pleased you to set festivals down in your verse.
But that you may not be ignorant and led by the error of the crowd,
June takes its name from my name.
It is something to have married Jove, to be the sister of Jove:
whether by my brother or by my husband I should rather boast, I doubt.
If lineage is regarded, I first made Saturn a parent,
I was the first offspring of Saturn.
Rome was once called Saturnia from my father:
this land was nearest to him from heaven.
If the marriage-bed is prized, I am called the matron of the Thunderer,
and my temple is joined to Tarpeian Jove.
Could a mistress give her name to the month of May,
and shall this honour in me be a thing of envy?
Why then am I called queen and chief of the goddesses?
Why have they given a golden sceptre to my right hand?
Shall days make the month, and shall I be called Lucina from them,
and yet draw my name from no month?
Then I should repent of having faithfully laid aside my wrath
against the race of Electra and the Dardanian house,
the cause of my anger was double: I grieved at the rape of Ganymede,
and my beauty too was defeated by the Idaean judge.
I should repent that I do not cherish the citadels of Carthage,
though my chariot and my arms are in that place;
I should repent of having set beneath Latium Sparta and Argos
and my own Mycenae and old Samos;
add old Tatius and the Juno-worshipping Faliscans,
whom I suffered to fall beneath the Romans.
But let me not repent, nor is any nation dearer to me:
here may I be worshipped, here may I hold the temple with my Jove.
Mavors himself said to me, 'I commend these walls
to you. You shall be powerful in your grandson's city.'
His word is followed by deed: I am honoured at a hundred altars,
nor is the honour of the month a lighter thing to me.
Nor does Rome alone grant me this honour:
the towns nearby give me the same gift.
Look at the calendars that wooded Aricia holds,
and the people of Laurentum and my Lanuvium;
there is a month of Juno there. Look at Tibur
and the sacred walls of the Praenestine goddess;
you will read the season of Juno there, and Romulus did not
found those towns: but Rome was my grandson's."
Juno had ended. We looked back: the wife of Hercules
stood there, and on her face were signs of vigour.
"I would not, if my mother bade me yield the whole heaven,
linger against my mother's will," she said.
"Now too I do not contend over the name of this season:
I coax, and almost play the part of one who asks,
and I would rather have held what is my right by entreaty,
and perhaps you yourself may favour my cause.
My mother holds the golden Capitol in a shared temple
and, as is fitting, holds the heights with Jove.
But all my glory comes from the origin of the month:
the only honour I am anxious for is this.
What harm is it, Roman, if you gave the title of a month
to the wife of Hercules, and posterity remembers it?
This land too owes me something, by the name of my great
husband; here he drove the captured cattle,
here, ill defended by his flames and his father's dowry,
Cacus stained the Aventine ground with his blood.
But I am called to nearer matters. Romulus divided the people
by their years, and distributed them into two parts:
the one is readier to give counsel, the other to fight;
this age advises war, but that wages it.
So he ordained, and marked the months by the same distinction:
June belongs to the young (iuvenes); the one before, to the old."
She spoke, and they would have gone to strife in their zeal for contest,
and piety would have been hidden by anger:
Concordia came, her long hair bound with Apollo's
laurel, the divinity and the work of a peaceful leader.
When she had told how Tatius and brave Quirinus
and their two realms had united with their peoples,
and how the fathers-in-law and sons-in-law had been received under a common home,
"June," she said, "from these joined takes its name."
The cause is told threefold. But pardon me, you goddesses:
the matter is not to be decided by my judgement.
Go from me equal. By a judge of beauty Pergamum
perished: two harm more than one can help.

title: Fasti
text:
The first day is given to you, Carna; she is the goddess of the hinge:
by her power she opens the closed and closes the open.
From where she has the powers granted to her, the tale is obscured
by age, but from my song you shall be certain.
Near the Tiber lies the ancient grove of Helernus:
the pontiffs even now bring their rites there.
A nymph was born there (the earlier ones called her Crane),
often sought in vain by many suitors.
She used to follow the fields and hunt wild beasts with javelins
and to spread the knotted nets in the hollow valley.
She had no quiver, yet they believed her to be the sister
of Phoebus; nor were you ashamed of her, Phoebus.
If any young man spoke loving words to her,
she at once gave back such sounds as these:
"These places have too much light, and with the light too much shame:
if you lead the way into more secret caves, I follow."
While the credulous man went ahead, she, finding the thickets,
stops and hides and is in no way to be found.
Janus had seen her, and caught by desire of what he saw,
had used soft words to the hard girl.
The nymph, as her custom was, bids him seek a more secluded cave,
and follows as his companion, and leaves her leader.
Foolish one! Janus sees what is done behind his back:
you achieve nothing, and he looks back at your hiding-place.
"You achieve nothing, look!" I say: for as you lie hidden under the rock
he seizes you in his embrace, and having had his hope, he says:
"For our coupling, let the power of the hinge be yours:
have this as the price of your lost virginity."
So speaking he gave a thorn, with which she could drive off
the gloomy harms from the doors (this was white).
There are greedy birds, not those that cheated the throat
of Phineus at his tables, but they draw their race from these:
a great head, staring eyes, beaks fit for plunder,
grey in their feathers, a hook on their talons.
They fly by night and seek out children deprived of a nurse
and defile the bodies they snatch from the cradle.
They are said to tear the milk-fed entrails with their beaks
and have a throat full of the blood they drink.
Striges is their name; but the cause of this name
is that they are wont to screech horribly by night.
Whether therefore they are born birds, or are made so by a charm,
and a Marsian crone shapes them into birds by her song,
they came into the chambers of Proca. Proca, born in those days,
was fresh prey for the birds, five days old,
and they suck the infant breast with their greedy tongues;
but the unhappy child wails and seeks help.
Frightened by the voice of her charge, the nurse runs up
and finds the cheeks cut by the rigid claw.
What was she to do? The colour of his face was such as leaves
are wont to have late in the year, harmed by the new winter.
She comes to Crane and tells the matter; she says, "Lay aside
your fear: your charge will be safe."
She had come to the cradle: mother and father were weeping:
"Stop your tears, I myself will cure him," she said.
At once she touches the doorposts three times in order with arbutus
foliage, three times marks the threshold with arbutus leaf;
she sprinkles the entrance with waters (and the waters held a remedy)
and holds the raw entrails of a two-month-old sow;
and thus she says, "Birds of the night, spare the boy's
entrails: for a little one a little victim falls.
Take, I pray, a heart for a heart, fibres for fibres.
This life we give you in place of a better one."
When she had thus made offering, she lays the cut pieces under the open sky,
and forbids those present at the rite to look back;
and a wand of Janus, made of the white thorn, is set
where a little window gave light to the chamber.
After that, they say, the birds did no violence to the cradle,
and the colour that was before returned to the boy.

title: Fasti
text:
You ask why rich lard is tasted on those Kalends,
and why beans are mixed with hot spelt?
She is an ancient goddess and is fed on the foods she used before,
nor, in her luxury, does she seek imported feasts.
The fish still swam for that people without treachery,
and the oysters were safe in their shells.
Latium did not know the bird that rich Ionia offers,
nor the one that delights in Pygmy blood;
and nothing but its feathers pleased in the peacock,
nor had the earth before sent its captured beasts.
The pig was prized; with a slain pig they kept their feasts:
the earth gave only beans and hard spelt.
Whoever shall eat these two mixed together on the sixth Kalends,
they say his bowels cannot be harmed.
On the highest citadel too, they tell, a temple to Juno Moneta
was made from your vow, Camillus:
before it had been the house of Manlius, who once
drove the Gallic arms from Capitoline Jove.
How well, great gods, had he fallen in that battle,
defender of your throne, lofty Jupiter!
He lived, only to die condemned on a charge of seeking kingship:
this title long old age gave him.
The same day is a festival of Mars, whom the Capene gate,
set beside the Covered Way, looks upon outside.
You too, Tempest, we confess deserved a shrine,
when the fleet was almost overwhelmed by the Corsican waters.
These memorials of men lie open; if you seek the stars,
then rises the curved-beaked bird of great Jove.
The next light calls forth the Hyades, the horns of the Bull's
brow, and the earth grows wet with much water.
When the morning has come twice and Phoebus has twice repeated his rising,
and the crops have been twice wet with the falling dew,
on this day Bellona is said to have been consecrated in the Tuscan
war, and she is always favourable to Latium.
Appius is the author, who, when peace was denied to Pyrrhus,
saw much in his mind, though he was robbed of sight.
A small open space looks out from the temple upon the top of the Circus,
there is a small column there of no small mark:
from here it is the custom for a spear, the herald of war, to be cast by hand,
when it is resolved to take up arms against a king and peoples.
The other part of the Circus is kept safe under Hercules the Guardian:
a charge the god holds by the Euboean song.
The time of the charge is the day of the Morning-star before the Nones:
if you seek the giver of the title, Sulla approved the work.
I was asking whether to refer the Nones to Sancus or to Fidius,
or to you, father Semo; then Sancus said to me:
"To whichever of these you give it, I shall have the gift:
I bear three names: so the men of Cures willed it."
Him, therefore, the old Sabines endowed with a shrine
and set up on the Quirinal ridge.
I have a daughter (and may she, I pray, outlast my years),
in whose safety I shall always be happy.
When I wished to give her to a son-in-law, I sought the times
fit for the wedding torches, and which were to be avoided:
then it was shown to me that, after the sacred Ides, June
is useful for brides, useful for husbands,
but the first part of this month was found unsuited to weddings;
for thus the holy wife of the Flamen Dialis told me:
"Until the calm Tiber has carried the sweepings from Iliac
Vesta down to the sea in its tawny waters,
it is not lawful for me to comb my hair with the toothed boxwood,
nor to cut my nails with iron,
nor to touch my husband, although he is the priest of Jove,
although he was given to me by a perpetual law.
Do not you hasten either; better will your daughter marry
when fiery Vesta shines on a clean floor."

title: Fasti
text:
On the third day after the Nones, Phoebe is said to remove
Lycaon, and the Bear has no fear from behind.
Then I remember that I saw the games on the grass of the Campus
and that they were called yours, gliding Tiber.
It is a festal day for those who draw the dripping nets,
and who cover the curved bronze with little baits.
The Mind too has its divinity. We see the shrine of Mind
vowed in fear of your war, treacherous Carthaginian.
Carthaginian, you had renewed the war, and at the death of the consul
all, struck with dread, greatly feared the Moorish bands.
Fear had driven out hope, when the senate took up
the vows to Mind, and at once she came in a better mood.
That day on which the vows were paid to the goddess
sees the Ides pressing on at the sixth light from then.
Vesta, be favourable! To you now, with my mouth devoted, I unloose my lips,
if it is granted me to come to your rites.
I was wholly in prayer: I felt the heavenly powers,
and the ground shone glad with a purple light.
I did not indeed see you (away with the lies of poets),
goddess, nor were you to be looked upon by a man;
but the things I had not known, and in error of which I was held,
were made known to me with no one teaching.
They tell that Rome had kept forty Parilia,
when the goddess, the guardian of the flame, was received into her temple,
the work of a peaceful king, than whom no land
bore a more god-fearing nature than the Sabine.
What you now see in bronze, you would then have seen roofed with straw,
and the wall was woven of pliant osier.
This narrow place, which holds the hall of Vesta,
was then the great palace of unshorn Numa.
Yet the form of the temple, which remains now, is said to have been so
before, and the cause of the form is to be approved.
Vesta is the same as the earth: a watchful fire lies beneath both:
the earth and the hearth signify their seat.
The earth is like a ball, resting on no support,
and as far as it is withdrawn from the heights, so far from the depths
is the earth; and the round shape makes this come about.
The form of the temple is the same: no corner juts out in it;
a dome defends it from the rainy shower.
You ask why the goddess is served by virgin ministers?
I shall find for this part too its proper reasons.
They tell that Juno and Ceres were born of Ops
by the seed of Saturn; Vesta was the third.
Both the others married, both are said to have borne children,
of the three one alone remained, refusing a husband.
What wonder, if a virgin, glad in a virgin minister,
admits only chaste hands to her rites?
Understand Vesta as nothing other than the living flame,
and you see no bodies born of the flame.
Rightly therefore she is a virgin, who sends out no seeds
nor takes any, and loves the companions of virginity.
Long, foolish, I thought there were images of Vesta;
